Her past life was fading away, leaving her a hollow shell, defined by her new reality as an object of service and humiliation. She was no longer upset by it—it was simply the way things were. Obedience kept the pain at bay, and that was all that mattered now.
Keiko understood that her fate had been sealed from the moment the nanomaterial touched her skin. She never had a chance. Hartmann had planned everything, and she had been naïve to think she could have control over her destiny. Now, he ruled over her life, like an unreachable god, and she belonged to him and his servants.
Her days settled into an unchanging pattern. She worked as ordered, cleaned, and carried out the maid’s endless commands. She knelt and serviced the butler when called upon, her mind empty, her body compliant. The constant humiliation and degradation no longer cut as deep; they had simply become the fabric of her existence.
Keiko’s inner world became blank, her past washed away by relentless conditioning. She lived in the present, performing tasks without thought or emotion. She was an object, stripped of agency, purpose, and hope. In rare moments of reflection, she understood that this was her life now. She existed to serve, to endure, and to obey.
Hartmann’s design had succeeded. She was no longer a person but a possession, her will extinguished, her identity dissolved. She moved through her days as if in a trance, responding only to the commands of those who controlled her. And as the weeks turned into months, Keiko accepted her fate fully. Her spirit was gone, and she was nothing more than a plaything, living only to please her captors.
Entertainment# Keiko’s transformation into a silent, obedient ornament was complete. She moved through Hartmann’s villa with practiced ease, her every action graceful and automatic. Each command was met with a smile and a polite curtsy, just as she had been trained.
Hartmann felt secure in her obedience, proudly displaying her as his trophy. For special occasions, the nanomaterial molded into a striking black outfit that emphasized her role. A tight corset cinched her waist, pushing her breasts up provocatively, while the material flared into an ornate skirt, resembling luxurious fabric. Her legs were wrapped in high-heeled boots that forced her into an elegant posture. A half-hood covered her head, leaving only her eyes and mouth visible. Her hands were free, allowing her to serve the guests more efficiently. Looking at her, there was no mistaking her role—she was a living symbol of submission.
The guests at Hartmann’s parties were as cruel as he was. They took delight in commanding her, knowing that she had no choice but to obey. Keiko walked among them, serving drinks and offering smiles that never reached her eyes. Each interaction was a fresh humiliation, a reminder of her complete and utter defeat.
Sometimes Hartmann would order her to smile, ensuring her expression matched the perfect, polished demeanor he demanded. Other times, he had her wear the Diadem of Lyria, showing it off to guests, emphasizing her servitude. And always, he made sure she was available for their pleasure. The guests took advantage of her, ordering her around with no room for refusal. The suit and her training made sure she complied with every request.
She was only to speak when spoken to, always polite, always respectful. The guests reveled in her compliance, each interaction stripping away more of her humanity. Keiko’s existence had become a constant cycle of enforced obedience, her role as a living trophy solidified.
As Keiko moved among the guests, her actions were smooth and well-practiced. She carried trays of canapés and drinks, keeping her gaze down. When addressed, she responded with a soft “Yes, Sir” or “Yes, Ma’am,” her voice devoid of emotion. The guests treated her as an object, a public plaything.
“What’s your story, girl?” one guest asked, a cruel curiosity flickering in his eyes.
Keiko recited what she had been taught. “My name was Keiko Toda. I was caught trying to steal from Mr. Hartmann, and I have been taught to serve. I am grateful for the lessons he has given me.”
“And what do you offer?” another guest asked with a lecherous tone.
“I offer drinks, entertainment, and pleasure,” Keiko replied without hesitation. “I am here for your enjoyment.”
Throughout the night, Keiko was used in various ways. Some guests made her kneel and service them, while others ordered her to perform degrading tasks for their amusement. One particularly cruel guest enjoyed making her repeat her story, delighting in the way her voice cracked slightly with each telling.
“Such a lovely addition to the party,” he sneered. “A reminder of what happens when you cross Viktor Hartmann.”
Occasionally, guests would compliment Hartmann on his ’trophy.’ In response, Keiko would say, “I am thankful to Mr. Hartmann for teaching me these valuable lessons. I am honored to serve.”
In the center of the room stood her cage, a clear symbol of her captivity. Keiko’s eyes were constantly drawn to it, the bars a stark reminder of her imprisonment. Some guests would point at it, laughing about her time spent confined within its black steel.
Hartmann watched with satisfaction as Keiko moved through the crowd, a living testament to his power and control. He knew she was completely broken, her spirit extinguished, and her obedience absolute. She was a hollow shell, an obedient servant, her past and identity erased by the relentless conditioning. She was Hartmann’s trophy, his obedient servant, and she would remain so until he decided otherwise.
Keiko knew that, like Lyria, she would eventually be sold once Hartmann grew tired of her. It was a fate she had already accepted. She understood that she was nothing more than an object to be traded, her value measured by her submission. The story of the diadem had come full circle—just as Lyria was passed from master to master, so too would Keiko be.
And so she served, silent and obedient, her cage always in view. It stood as a constant reminder of what she had become, her fate sealed by the very thing she had once sought to steal—the Diadem of Lyria.

title: Chapter 10: Sonia packs and flies to Shanghai
content:
Sonia packs and flies to Shanghai# Arriving at GAIA, Sonia did not go straight upstairs. She said goodbye to Anna, who continued up to her office and stopped in the GAIA lobby and decided to do some science: Changed vs. Unchanged numbers.
Changed women were the easiest to spot: gloves, fitted skirts, high collars, scarves or hats, the same contained economy of movement she had already started to recognize. Changed men took longer. Their clothes varied less, but the posture gave them away sooner or later. A new stillness. More attention to the women with them. An altered kind of ease in taking up space.
Fifteen minutes gave her enough for a working sample.
Roughly one person in six.
Sick leave reports would push the real number higher. She caught fragments as people crossed the lobby in pairs and threes: another lab down three staff, someone still feverish, someone else’s wife suddenly refusing trousers, a senior researcher “not herself at all” and therefore, in the speaker’s opinion, doing wonderfully.
The virus was already everywhere inside the institute, not an isolated incident, and it would not simply stop. Even the Unchanged would be turned soon.
Sonia closed the notebook and went upstairs.
Her office felt smaller in the blouse and skirt. The gloves had to come off before she could type properly, which meant working the cuffs loose and swearing under her breath at tiny buttons meant for more patient hands. The Yoyah Sheengzoh kept asserting itself even seated. It did not let her spread out. It organized her knees, her hips, the angle of her back.
Useful to know. Infuriating to experience.
She started with the data she trusted most: spread curves, outbreak timing, internal reports from partner hospitals, early sample metadata, shipping records tied to the first clusters. That work she understood. The other line she built next was messier and stranger.
Boutiques.
She pinned dates to a wall timeline until the pattern stopped looking like coincidence. Outbreak, then Maylee Shufoo. Another outbreak, another boutique. Not always the same week or the same district, but close enough to stop being funny.
The boutiques were not a side effect.
They were part of the same machine.
Sonia sat back and rubbed at one temple.
Viruses did not sign leases or register shell companies. People did.
She went hunting for the people.
Maylee Shufoo in Geneva led to a registration. The registration led to Veridis Quo. Veridis Quo led to Maximilian Grothe, who existed on paper and almost nowhere else. Drexel and Saigne LLC appeared in the margins through consulting records, asset-protection language, restructuring filings, boring corporate language wrapped around something rotten. Sonia could follow enough of it to know she was out of depth and still nowhere near the actual hand on the wheel.
She reached for her phone.
Mara Delacroix picked up on the second ring.
“Tell me this is billable.”
“Almost certainly,” Sonia said.
“Good. Then I can still like you. What happened?”
“I need ownership tracing on a retail chain with layered shell structures and probably offshore nonsense. Fast.”
There was a brief silence.
“That does sound like me,” Mara said. “How fast?”
“Yesterday.”
“Lunch. Twenty minutes. Bring whatever you’ve got.”
The line went dead.
That was why Sonia called her.
Mara arrived two minutes late and made lateness look intentional. Small, sharp, dark suit, no wasted motion, no softness anywhere that had not been selected for effect. She slid into the chair opposite Sonia, set down her phone, and looked once at the folder Sonia had brought.
“You look absurd,” Mara said.
“Thank you.”
“You know I mean the clothes.”
“I assumed so.”
Mara’s mouth twitched.
“Good. I was worried Geneva had finally bullied you into participating.”
Sonia pushed the papers across the table.
“Not yet.”
Mara scanned the first page and stilled.
“Maylee Shufoo.”
“You know them?”
“Everyone knows them. The retro-submission boutique for women who want to dress like a Stepford wives cosplay.”
Sonia almost smiled despite herself.
“Useful. Keep going.”
Mara flipped through the registrations, slower now.
“Veridis Quo is real enough. Grothe is probably a mask. Drexel and Saigne I’ve seen before, not on anything clean. They’re the kind of consultants people hire when they want three extra walls between themselves and liability.”
“Can you break it open?”
Mara looked up.
“Of course I can break it open. The question is how much crime you want me to imply while I do it.”
“Only the amount that’s already there.”
“Reasonable.”
She kept reading.
“Why do you care?”
Sonia took a sip of the terrible coffee and gave her the version that was mostly true.
“We’re tracking unusual overlap between the boutiques and a viral event. I want the ownership map before I decide whether that overlap is coincidence, opportunism, or design.”
Mara glanced again at Sonia’s collar, gloves, skirt.
“And you are wearing their product because?”
“Field camouflage.”
“You hate it.”
“Deeply.”
“Good,” Mara said. “I’d worry otherwise.”
She stacked the papers into a neater pile than Sonia had managed.
“I’ll send you corporate trees, registrations, beneficial ownership if I can get it, and anything interesting buried under the consultant layer. If someone in this chain is trying to stay invisible, I want to know what they were afraid of before they had the good sense to be afraid.”
“Mara.”
“Yes?”
“Thank you.”
That earned Sonia a dismissive wave.
“Buy me something expensive when this turns into a disaster.”
By the next morning Mara had sent thirty-seven files and a message with no greeting.
You were right to ask. Start with folders 3, 5, and 9. Someone is hiding on purpose.
Sonia read standing up.
Mara had pulled the whole structure into the light. Veridis Quo fed into overseas entities. Drexel and Saigne sat between clusters of holdings like reactor shielding. Maylee Shufoo linked outward to another chain Sonia had never heard of before seeing the documents:
迷人的景象
“Mirende Ginciao”, if read aloud from what the virus had installed in her. “A Captivating Sight.”
The American-facing name, buried in a market report, was Mirren’s.
Same product logic. Same aesthetics with regional tweaks. Same timing near infection zones. Same corporate fog.
And all the cleanest lines led back to Shanghai.
Sonia’s pulse steadied instead of jumping. Good. A city. A direction. Something you could board a plane toward.
She sent messages into the contacts she still had from prior China trips. Journalist. Founder. One old research liaison. Most answers came back thin or useless. People had heard rumors. People knew someone who knew someone. People asked why she cared.
The useful response came late and without charm from Jiang Han, who called himself a broker because any more specific noun would have sounded criminal.
You want the man behind Cheng Biotech Industries. I can get you enough to justify a visit. Not enough to keep you safe.
Sonia wrote back at once.
Send it.
The dossier landed twenty minutes later.
Dr. Mingyu Cheng. “ABC”, American-born Chinese. Family money. Neurological biotech. CBI founded in the nineties, respectable in exactly the way that meant dangerous if the respectability ever cracked. He had patents, board memberships, old press, vanished collaborators, and a private residence in Shanghai straight out of a Bond film.
Sonia read the file twice.
Neurological disorders.
Of course.
If half the world had not already started dressing its women like managed relics, the whole thing would have sounded melodramatic. As it was, she only felt grimly confirmed.
Shanghai was no longer a hypothesis. It was the next step.
That part required Clara.
Sonia drafted the field-trip request with careful restraint. Sample tracing. Early cluster analysis. Origin mapping. Existing contacts on the ground. Shenzhen precedent. No mention of boutiques, shell companies, or the possibility that a biotech magnate was underwriting social engineering through couture.
She sent it, then carried the same controlled version of herself into her one-on-one with Clara Dumont.
Clara was Changed.
Sonia knew that before she consciously registered the details. Then the details arrived all at once: the gray skirt too narrow for a natural stride, the blouse buttoned high and closed at the back, the hijab, the satin gloves resting on the desk as if they belonged there. Clara had always been authoritative. Now the authority had been rerouted through a version of femininity that should have weakened it and somehow did not.
Sonia sat carefully.
“You wanted to discuss Shanghai,” Clara said.
Her tone was efficient. Calm. Helpful.
Too helpful.
“Yes,” Sonia said. “I want to trace early infection clusters through existing research contacts and collect additional samples. The Shenzhen trip gave us enough structure to justify a second field pass.”
Clara opened the proposal and read more quickly than Sonia expected.
“This makes sense.”
That was it. No resistance. No budget objection. No concern about timeline, exposure, biohazard transport, duplicated effort, or Sonia’s suddenly corrected clothes.
Sonia waited for the harder part.
It did not come.
“You should go,” Clara said. “Sooner rather than later.”
Sonia kept her face neutral.
“You agree?”
Clara looked up, and for one strange second she seemed almost warmly pleased.
“Of course. If there is useful data to gather, you should gather it.”
The answer was reasonable. That was what made it wrong.
Sonia had worked under Clara for years. Pre-Change Clara would have asked six harder questions before offering support, then three more while pretending she had already decided. This Clara approved the trip as if helping Sonia do difficult work gave her genuine satisfaction.
Eerie.
It was not blank obedience or mindless enthusiasm, but something smoother, cooperative at the root.
“I can authorize travel this afternoon,” Clara said. “Do you need anything else?”
There it was again. Readiness. Support. No visible defensiveness even though the research Sonia was proposing might eventually circle back to the thing that had remade her.
“No,” Sonia said. “That should be enough.”
“Good. Keep me informed.”
Sonia left with the approval in hand and a fresh problem she could not yet name.
Why were the Changed so willing to help?
Not just Anna. Clara too. Not eager to be changed back, not horrified, not pleading for a cure, and still cooperative with an investigation that might threaten the system that now held them.
She did not have time to solve that before boarding a plane.
So she packed.
Passport. Existing Chinese paperwork. Biohazard handling documents. Work visa still valid. Chinese phone, active SIM, spare battery pack, encrypted drive, sample tubes, laptop, chargers, hard copies of the Cheng file, harder copies of Mara’s ownership maps. One small medical kit. One knife she would not be allowed to keep past security and packed anyway before remembering herself.
Then clothes.
That part stopped her.
She could fly in jeans and draw eyes the moment she landed, or she could travel as the city now expected women to travel, not because she had yielded, but because she needed to move.
Tactical. Temporary. Useful.
The lie was getting more efficient every time she used it.
She went back to Maylee Shufoo before leaving for the airport.
Now that she knew the chain belonged in the same file as the virus, she saw the place differently: infrastructure, public-facing doctrine, a showroom for the society the virus was building inside people.
The new stock had shifted again.
Corsets now, more than before. Stiffer skirts. Narrower sleeves. High-necked blouses that looked severe even on mannequins. One new line caught her at once:
高抱佑护
“Gowbao Yoohoo,” the installed Chinese offered. “Embrace and Protect.”
The blouse was a beautiful trap. Pale fabric, severe line, immaculate finish. Inside the collar sat a reinforced leather structure that would hold the neck high and still once fastened. The sleeves buttoned along the outer forearm in a way that made self-dressing clumsy at best. Gloves would make it worse. The whole design implied assistance, supervision, hands other than the wearer’s.
The name pretended tenderness.
Protect. Embrace.
It really meant “hold still.”
Sonia touched the collar once with two fingertips and imagined it closed around a woman’s throat, posture corrected, gaze managed, dependence built directly into dress.
The boutiques were teaching the same lesson as the virus, not through genes, but through ritual, inconvenience, beauty, public expectation, and the slow conversion of care into control.
She bought nothing else.
At the airport she moved with the same shortened stride she despised, documents in order, her anger folded back so tightly it almost passed for calm.
Shanghai next.
That was good enough.
Clara Dumont at her desk at GAIA.

title: Chapter 11: Anna and Julien
Chapter 12: Lakeside Proposal
content:
Lakeside Proposal# Julien chose the Lakeside Cafe for Saturday dinner.
Anna understood the choice at once and did not ask about it. The place carried several meanings now. It was where Sonia had tried to drag her backward by force and failed. It was where Changed Geneva liked to display itself in polished glass and careful posture. It was also simply beautiful at dusk, which made everything worse.
She dressed with unusual care.
The corset first, because it now had to go on before the rest and because she still felt a strange thrill each time she chose it willingly. It tightened her into the line Lily had promised, waist drawn in, shoulders encouraged back, lower spine curved. Over that came the Gowbao Yoohoo blouse, all pale silk and patient cruelty. The collar fixed her head in its flattering compromise: chin lifted enough for dignity, gaze lowered enough for obedience. Her skirt followed, with the hidden underlayer that kept her steps short and exact. Gloves. Shoes. Hijab pinned smooth.
By the time she was ready, her body had become an elegant request for assistance.
Julien met her outside. His eyes moved over her once, carefully, and then returned to her face.
“Very nice,” he said.
The words sank into her at once.
“Thank you, Sir.”
He offered his arm. She took it and enjoyed the contact through the cloth of her gloves.
The walk from the tram stop to the cafe was short, but the clothes made her work even for short distances. She had to watch the pavement, manage the steps, keep her posture, accept his steadying hand when the curb came too quickly. None of it was theatrical. That was what made it intimate. Her dependence no longer lived in theory. It lived in curbs, chair backs, doorframes, and the pressure of a hand at her elbow.
Inside, the room was all low light, lake reflections, glass, and soft conversation. People noticed them properly rather than rudely: a well-dressed pair, a woman arranged with obvious care and a man attentive enough to deserve her polish.
Julien guided her to the table more slowly than usual because he knew what the blouse and corset changed. When he pulled out her chair, she had to turn, gather her skirt, back carefully into position, and lower herself in stages. The corset decided how far she could bend. The collar corrected every attempt to look down too much. The underlayer kept her knees together and her footing precise. By the time she was seated, she was upright, composed, and only a little trapped.
Julien’s hand came down briefly to settle the fall of her skirt over her knees.
That simple, competent touch made her flush.
“Comfortable?” he asked.
She nearly laughed at the question and did not dare.
“I am well, Sir.”
He took the answer for what it was.
Julien ordered for both of them. He did it without asking, but not carelessly. He knew what she liked. Fish instead of beef. The white wine she would not have chosen in public anymore but still enjoyed if he decided on it. Dessert, because he knew she would want it and pretend not to.
Being known that way felt almost extravagant.
Dinner unfolded slowly. Julien spoke more than she did, but not to dominate the room. He had begun to like explaining things to her, checking her reactions, making sure she followed the shape of his thoughts. Work. The city. The strange calm settling over people. The way routines were changing faster than anyone would admit. When he asked her a question, she answered. When he did not, she let the silence sit between them without trying to rescue it. The clothes helped with that too. They made stillness easier to hold.
More than once she caught him watching not just her face, but the effects of the outfit on the rest of her: the way she had to lift a gloved hand carefully to drink, the way the blouse guided her chin, the way every movement had become measured by design.
She wanted him to watch. By now she was able to admit that to herself, was comfortable with her new look and her new role.
By dessert the lake beyond the windows had gone silver-blue. Candlelight reflected in the glass. The room had not emptied, but it seemed to recede. Anna felt exposed and private at once, a sensation the outfit seemed built to produce.
Julien set down his fork.
“Anna.”
The use of her first name without the “Miss” caught her attention more sharply than any formal preface could have.
“Yes, Sir?”
He looked at her directly, and for once she did not drop her eyes at once.
“This last week has been very strange.”
“Yes, Sir.”
His mouth moved, almost a smile.
“You have made it easier to bear.”
The sentence entered her body like warmth.
He reached across the table and turned one of her gloved hands palm-up under his. The touch was almost formal. It still made her heart kick.
“When I was ill,” he said, “I woke into a world that expected things of me before I understood the rules. You were the first part of it that felt ordered instead of absurd.”
Anna held her breath.
“You were kind to me before either of us knew what we were becoming. You have been patient with me while I learned how to stand in the place this world now gives me. And I find that I do not want a future in which you are not part of my household.”
Household.
The word landed with quiet force.
“Sir…” she began, and stopped, because too many feelings pressed at once against her.
Julien did not let her pull away into generality.
“I want to ask your father for permission to take responsibility for you,” he said. “To become your guardian in due course. I want you under my care. Openly. Properly.”
The words were calm. The structure inside them was not.
Guardian. Responsibility. Under my care. Properly.
Each one struck against the changed parts of her until pleasure and fear became almost impossible to separate.
For one clear second she saw the shape of it with clarity. She would be his, through care, ritual, approval, legal transfer, and the promise that being possessed would feel like safety with him.
She looked at Julien and saw not an abstract system but the man who had fed her, steadied her, remembered her preferences, watched her struggle in difficult clothes without mocking her for it, and taken obvious satisfaction in making room for her in his life.
She had to make a choice, and she welcomed it.
“If I say yes,” she said quietly, “I will belong to you.”
“Yes.”
“And you will ask my father to give me to you.”
“Yes.”
She wanted him.
She liked being cared for by him.
She liked belonging somewhere.
She liked what his approval did to her.
She liked the future he was naming.
She answered, and it was not even a decision, but simple alignment.
“Yes, Sir.”
Julien closed his eyes briefly, as if relief itself had weight. When he opened them again, something in him had settled into commitment rather than triumph.
“Thank you, Anna.”
He lifted her gloved hand and pressed his lips to the fabric above her knuckles. The gesture was old-fashioned enough to be almost absurd. Instead it sent a clean bolt of want through her.
“Good girl,” he said softly.
The reward that followed was so fierce she had to bite the inside of her cheek to keep from making a sound in the middle of the cafe. Obedience is pleasure, she remembered her mother explaining, and under the table her thighs pressed together helplessly around the literal truth of it.
Julien saw it. His eyes sharpened, then softened again.
“Steady,” he murmured.
The care in it only made the sensation spread.
When the meal was done, he rose and came around to help her up. One hand at her elbow, one waiting in case the chair, skirt, corset, and collar conspired against her balance. She leaned into the help because refusing it would have been both foolish and dishonest.
Outside, the air off the lake was cool.
Julien settled her on his arm again and covered her gloved hand with his own for a moment before guiding her toward the car.
The city had not changed further in the last hour. The same lights burned. The same women crossed the pavement in disciplined skirts. The same men opened doors, guided elbows, chose restaurant tables, set the pace of shared movement.
What had changed were the terms on which this world meant to keep her.
And she was not sorry.

title: Chapter 13: A Giving-Away Ceremony
Chapter 14: In Shanghai
content:
In Shanghai# Sonia stepped off the plane into damp Shanghai heat and understood at once that Geneva had only been a beginning.
The airport was bright, crowded, and so disciplined it made her skin tighten. Women moved through it in restrictive elegance so consistent it no longer looked like fashion. Fitted jackets over corseted waists. High collars. Gloves. Narrow skirts or local variants that forced the same short, careful gait. Men beside them varied more in age, build, and dress, but not in bearing. They all carried the same settled authority Sonia had started noticing back home, only here it looked older, deeper, fully at home in itself.
More complete, she thought.
No one here looked as if they had been talked into any of it last month.
By the time she reached the outer concourse, she knew her Geneva wardrobe would not be enough. It had worked there as camouflage, enough to blunt attention and let her move. Shanghai was further along. She needed a local version if she wanted the city to stop reading her as a visitor.
A Mirende Ginciao storefront solved that problem for her.
The boutique stood just beyond the airport flow, all lacquered wood, quiet light, and polished self-possession. The mannequins in the window were dressed for a world that had stopped pretending functionality was neutral. Severe collars. Controlled waists. Skirts that asked for help without ever admitting the need aloud.
Sonia stood outside for one breath too long, then went in.
The saleswoman who greeted her wore a fitted jacket over a narrow dress with long cuffed sleeves and a soft head covering pinned close along the jaw. She bowed slightly.
“Welcome, miss. How may we help you?”
Sonia hated how quickly the answer came.
“I need something suitable for business.”
The woman nodded as if the request contained more than the words.
“Of course.”
What she brought was not Geneva’s language copied directly, but a local dialect of the same coercion. A deep blue corset. A Gowbao Yoohoo blouse designed to close without assistance but still cut to keep the shoulders back and the head properly placed. A narrow overskirt to hide the Yoyah Sheengzoh beneath it. Gloves. Heels chosen to alter the body all day, practical enough for walking, but only just.
“This will travel well,” the saleswoman said. “Respectable. Restrained. Serious.”
Sonia took the stack and went into the fitting room before she could argue with herself.
She stripped down to her base layer and stared at the garments hanging from their hooks.
Camouflage, she reminded herself.
Then she put the corset on.
She knew enough now to manage it. Busk first. Laces next. Tighten from top and bottom toward the waist, then again, then once more after the body has accepted the first lie about what counts as comfortable. The pressure settled around her ribs with a familiarity she resented. Her posture changed. Her breathing changed. Sweat gathered under her breasts in the humid air and stayed there, trapped. Her thoughts narrowed toward the body instead of staying above it.
The Yoyah Sheengzoh followed, and with it the immediate correction lower down: shorter steps, closer knees, a different relationship to balance. Then the blouse. Shoulder closures first, then the collar. By the time she fastened the top, her head no longer belonged entirely to her. Looking up took effort. Turning meant the whole body had to agree.
She stepped into the overskirt and then the heels.
The gloves came last.
The woman in the mirror had become legible to Shanghai in a way Sonia no longer was.
It worked.
That was the first humiliating truth.
The second came a beat later and landed lower in her body: part of her liked how coherent it felt. Not morally. Not politically. In the body. Every piece spoke to every other piece. Upright here, narrowed there, guided above, limited below. The whole system made sensual sense once it closed around her.
She hated that almost as much as she believed it.
When she stepped out, the saleswoman’s eyes flicked over her once, not lingering, only confirming.
“Yes,” she said softly. “Much better.”
Approval moved through Sonia with a small, ugly force.
She paid too much, took her luggage, and entered the city dressed in obedience she did not believe in.
The subway ride to Jing’an gave her too much time to look.
Women around her wore versions of the same life in different fabrics: neat jackets, shaped waists, narrow sleeves, gloves, controlled hair, every public movement already edited down to something composed and modest. A young woman stood when an older man approached and lowered her gaze before he touched her elbow to steady her back into her seat at the next stop. A businessman shifted aside to make room for an older woman, then took her shopping bag without discussion and carried it for her until she left the train. Near the door, a girl no older than twenty waited with her hands folded while the man beside her checked the route on his phone and told her when to move.
None of it drew stares.
That was what made it worse.
By the time she reached the hotel, the collar had started to feel like a hand at the back of her neck. The corset held her in one exact shape. The humidity had turned the blouse tacky under her arms. She checked in, got to her room, closed the door, and began pulling the clothes off in the first wave of private relief.
The blouse first. Then gloves. Then heels. The overskirt. The underlayer. Last, carefully, the corset.
When the pressure released, she had to sit on the edge of the bed and wait for herself to come back fully.
Underneath the relief sat a faint disappointment.
She swore at herself under her breath, showered, changed into a hotel T-shirt, ordered bad noodles, and spread Mara’s files and Jiang Han’s material across the desk.
Dr. Mingyu Cheng emerged from the documents piece by piece rather than all at once. American-born Chinese. Family money sharpened by personal brilliance. Neurological biotech. Cheng Biotech Industries. Rich. Respectable. Untouchable in his villa in Xuhui. Sonia read old interviews, board notes, clipped profiles, and the careful little public myths wealthy men accumulated around themselves. Visionary. Modernizer. Philanthropist. The vanished collaborators sat at the edge of all that polished material like missing teeth. Nothing linked cleanly enough to force a door open. Everything suggested a perimeter built to absorb curiosity and redirect it into admiration.
She read until the lines blurred.
The city glowed beyond the window. Somewhere out there lived the man who had either built the virus or stood close enough to its making to matter. Somewhere between him, the boutiques, and the women on the subway, the same lesson kept repeating itself in different forms. Structure women beautifully. Teach dependence through grace, inconvenience, praise, relief. The rest followed faster than anyone liked admitting.
By morning she had reduced her options to three, then to one.
Business contact would fail.
Journalistic pressure would fail.
Scientific inquiry would be blocked, redirected, delayed, watched.
The one kind of person who moved through households and private rooms without being important enough to remember was the one kind of person Sonia had spent her whole life being determined never to become.
A maid.
She sat with that for a long time, elbows on knees, one hand against her mouth.
The logic was simple enough. The recoil was not.
Service fit the world Cheng had built. Service fit the boutiques, the subway, the men who guided without asking and the women who made that guidance look natural. Service fit the shape the clothes kept trying to teach her body even when her mind rejected the lesson.
And under the disgust waited another feeling she did not want to examine too closely: the suspicion that she could do it.
Worse, that she might do it well.
She reached for Jiang Han’s card.
“I need placement,” she said when he answered. “Domestic staff. High-level household. Close to Cheng if possible.”
He was quiet just long enough to make her wonder what expression he was wearing.
“That can be arranged,” he said. “Not cheaply.”
“Nothing about this has been cheap.”

title: Chapter 15: Maid in Training
content:
Maid in Training# Harmony Household Staffing occupied two upper floors over a quiet commercial street, respectable enough from the outside that Sonia might have walked past it if Jiang Han had not sent the address to her phone.
He met her in a back office with Mei Lin standing at his shoulder.
“Ten thousand more,” he said, as if they had paused a conversation ten minutes earlier instead of the previous day. “We will provide references, history, interview shaping, training, and the bribes you need to succeed in household placement.”
Sonia did not argue.
“Fine.”
Jiang glanced at Mei Lin.
“You were right. She learns fast.”
Mei Lin let her eyes travel once over Sonia in her fitted Shanghai business dress and gave nothing away.
“Fast is not the same as useful.”
That seemed to be her answer to everything.
The cover identity came together by evening. Prior placements in homes Sonia had never seen. Skills she could already perform badly enough to need instruction and well enough to pass after two weeks of it. A narrowed life on paper. Domestic work. Service standards. Discretion. Obedience.
When Jiang finished explaining how the butler at Cheng’s house would be nudged toward the right file, Mei Lin took over without transition.
“From now on,” she said, “you train exactly as you will serve.”
She did not smile. Sonia had the impression smiling would have weakened whatever method she believed in.
Mei Lin used her own apartment first, then a rented service flat attached to the agency, both arranged with the same intention: nowhere for Sonia to relax into herself. Every room taught or corrected something. Doors to open the right way. Trays to balance. Tables to lay. Floors to cross without noise. Mirrors placed where posture would betray her.
The first morning began at six.
By six-ten Sonia was in uniform.
The maid dress was not theatrical. It was a working dress, strict enough to demand attention every minute it stayed on her body. Black, modest, and closely controlled. White apron. Long sleeves. Cuffs that reminded her not to spread. Proper shoes. Gloves for certain tasks. Hair pinned up and covered. A corset under it because the line mattered. A restricting underlayer beneath the skirt because gait mattered too.
The fabric at the back of her knees caught whenever she tried to take a full stride.
Mei Lin walked around her once in silence.
“Again,” she said.
“Again what?”
Mei Lin’s eyes hardened by a fraction.
“Everything.”
So Sonia undressed, dressed, laced, buttoned, pinned, tied, stepped into shoes, arranged the apron, lowered her gaze, and stood for inspection again.
“Better,” Mei Lin said. “You look less like a scientist playing maid.”
It was not praise.
Sonia took it like praise anyway.
The days turned into drill so quickly she could not point to the hour it happened.
A maid either worked or stood ready to work. There was no third state. If Sonia finished polishing silver, there was floor wax to check. If the floor was right, flowers needed cutting. If flowers were done, laundry folds could still be improved. If no task presented itself at once, she stood at attention with her hands arranged properly, posture exact, listening for the next instruction.
Mei Lin corrected everything.
Too much shoulder. Too much stride. Too much voice. Too much self.
“You enter a room already apologizing for the space you take up,” she said on the third day. “That is western guilt, not service. Service is cleaner. It waits. It notices. It moves only when needed.”
Sonia hated how true that was.
The flowers were worst at first. Mei Lin made her re-cut stems, rebuild arrangements, start again because the asymmetry leaned too far to one side or because Sonia had missed the shape entirely. Then tea. Then folded linen. Then tray work. Then kneeling to present. Rising without bracing on a chair. Turning in a skirt that allowed very little turning at all.
At meals Mei Lin was not generous, but she was practical.
“Eat.” “Faster.” “Not like that.” “Again.”
No comfort.
No cruelty for sport either.
Only method.
On the fifth day Sonia dropped a spoon from the tray because her fingers had started shaking from exhaustion.
The sound on the floor was small.
The shame was not.
Mei Lin looked at the spoon, then at Sonia.
“Pick it up properly.”
Sonia bent, corset resisting, skirt narrowing, and had to think through the mechanics before her hand reached the floor.
When she rose, Mei Lin tipped the tray and let more spoons fall.
“Again.”
Sonia wanted to throw the whole tray into the wall.
Instead she did as told.
Something in that choice stayed with her.
By the end of the first week, the uniform no longer felt like a disguise she put on for a job. It felt like a narrowing passage she entered every morning and only partly emerged from at night.
She did not notice the danger at first because it did not arrive as panic.
It arrived as ease.
Mei Lin never explained what she was doing. She did not have the language Sonia would have used, and probably would not have wanted it. She was producing a service personality the only way she knew how: repetition, fatigue, posture, correction, approval withheld until it mattered, and a schedule that left no room for interior rebellion.
One Sunday morning Sonia was polishing silver in a shaft of pale light while the flat stayed quiet around her. The work had stopped feeling like separate motions. Cloth, turn, inspect. Cloth, turn, inspect. Her corset held her. The dress contained her. Somewhere in the building a pipe clicked once, then again. The room made no demands beyond the next piece and the one after that. Behind her, Mei Lin moved from shelf to shelf checking dust she would certainly find.
“More shine,” Mei Lin said.
“Yes, Mistress Mei Lin. This humble maid will improve.”
The words came out before Sonia had time to stop them.
She should have flinched.
Instead the phrase moved through her with a low, almost soothing inevitability. This humble maid, not I, not Sonia, but a narrower self that fit the room better. She kept polishing. Cloth, turn, inspect. The pressure in her ribs and waist, the constrained line of her legs, the cool weight of the spoon in her hand, all of it folded together into something smooth enough to rest inside.
For a while she stopped measuring time.
She only worked.
The next task replaced the last without any seam she could feel. Silver to flowers. Flowers to dusting. Dusting to tea tray. She did not choose the movement from one to the next. She answered it. The uniform rustled. Her shoes clicked softly. Her hands stayed small and efficient in front of her body when they were not actively serving.
At some point Mei Lin tasted the tea and nodded once.
“Better.”
The single word went into Sonia so deeply she almost swayed.
Pride flared, but not the kind she knew from publications, fieldwork, or being right in public. This one sat lower. Stranger. Quieter. It made her want to kneel and stay useful.
The response did not pass through thought first. It landed in her body and spread from there.
Late that afternoon Mei Lin sent her to the small maid room off the kitchen that had become her home during training.
“Rest for thirty minutes. Then change and begin again.”
Sonia closed the door behind her, sat on the edge of the narrow bed, and felt the whole day come apart at once.
The room looked wrong. Too still. Too empty. Her own name did not fit inside it for a few seconds. She knew it was her room. She knew what city she was in. She knew why she was there. None of that stopped the hollow drop in her stomach when the service rhythm fell away and left her alone with herself again.
She covered her face with both hands and breathed.
The tears came for a reason she could not have explained.
Not many. Enough to humiliate her.
She had not been drugged. She had not been hypnotized. Mei Lin had barely touched her except to correct a shoulder, a wrist, the angle of her chin. Even so, something had happened to her in that long morning of labor and correction. Some part of her had gone quiet in a way that was not entirely unpleasant and had returned only roughly when the work stopped.
The work had comforted her.
Not the scolding or the ache. Not the humiliation either. The narrowing. The relief of not having to carry herself as a person with a hundred possible directions to move in. The clarity of expectations. The simplicity of being told what came next and doing it well.
She came from women who would have called that weakness.
She had called it weakness herself.
She still wanted to call it that.
But sitting there with her face hot and her chest uneven, she could not make the word hold.
That evening, when Mei Lin corrected her posture again and told her to hold the tray lower, Sonia obeyed with a flush already rising under her skin.
The next morning she woke before the call and lay still for several seconds, one hand on the blanket, knowing two things at once.
She was here on a mission she had chosen for herself.
And part of her was looking forward to disappearing into the maid again.
By the second week, the phrase “this humble maid” came more easily, and that frightened her too. Mei Lin never encouraged it directly, but she did not interrupt when Sonia used it correctly. That was enough. The self kept thinning at the edges during long runs of work, and returning to ordinary speech afterward felt like putting on a face she had misplaced for a few hours.
Mei Lin watched the process without discussing it.
One evening, after Sonia had re-laid the same breakfast table three times to correct the spacing of a spoon, Mei Lin finally spoke while adjusting the fall of Sonia’s apron.
“You are nearly ready,” she said.
Sonia kept her eyes lowered.
“For Cheng?”
“For service.”
The distinction stayed with her long after the lesson ended.
She lay awake that night in the little room off the kitchen, sore, corseted, and unable to think her way cleanly out of what was happening to her. She told herself it was cover, adaptation, necessity. She told herself the comfort meant nothing. She told herself the strange peace she found in being corrected into usefulness was only another danger to manage.
None of those explanations changed what she felt the next morning when the uniform closed around her body and the day narrowed down to tasks, posture, and the relief of being told what came next.

title: Chapter 16: A Maid's work
Chapter 17: Return from Shanghai
Chapter 18: Immune to the Virus, but not to Social Pressure
content:
Immune To The Virus, But Not To Social Pressure# The virus had not rewritten Sonia’s mind the way it had rewritten Anna’s.
That did not mean she was untouched.
Geneva kept pressing on her from the outside.
Two days after her return, she stepped onto a tram in a soft blouse and an ordinary skirt and knew almost immediately she had made a mistake. Not a moral mistake. A practical one. The carriage was full enough that everyone had time to look and not so crowded that anyone had to pretend not to.
More fitted jackets now. More corsets. More narrow skirts forcing shorter steps and a different way of turning in place. The women around her looked composed in the new rules, even the younger ones who could not have been living under them for very long. That was what kept catching at her. Not theatricality. Ease.
She found a seat and opened the book she had brought for cover, but the line of women opposite her stayed in the edge of her vision. Three of them, all Changed, all tidy in the same legible way. One in dark green with gloves buttoned at the wrist. One in gray with a high collar and a hat pinned close to soft blond hair. One in navy, younger than the others, with the bright attentive face of someone still proud to be getting it right.
They looked at Sonia once, then again.
The youngest leaned toward the woman in gray and said something too low for most of the tram to hear.
Not too low for Sonia.
“She came out like that?”
The woman in gray did not quite smile.
“Perhaps no one corrected her before she left home.”
The one in green glanced down at Sonia’s ungloved hands.
“Poor thing.”
That was worse than open contempt would have been. Sonia kept her eyes on the page in front of her and felt heat rise into her face anyway.
At the next stop a man got on, broad-shouldered, middle-aged, carrying a leather briefcase. He paused beside the women, took in the row, and then looked at Sonia. Not with desire. Not even with much curiosity. Assessment, then polite disappointment, as if she had arrived underdressed to a formal lunch and made the whole carriage fractionally less orderly to look at.
He moved on without offering his seat to anyone.
The woman in navy followed him with her eyes, then let them return to Sonia with almost pitying composure.
“A little structure helps,” she said after a moment, not quite addressing Sonia directly and not quite avoiding it either. “One feels so much better.”
Sonia raised her eyes at last.
“I’m comfortable, thank you.”
The answer came out cooler than she had intended.
The woman in gray answered for the group.
“Comfort is not really the point.”
No one around them reacted. A year earlier the exchange would have drawn stares. Now it dissolved into the ordinary sound of the tram, the rails underfoot, the stop bell, the rustle of tailored skirts and coats.
Sonia looked back at her book and did not turn the page for three stops.
By the time she got off, she felt strangely unfinished. As if she had gone out of the house missing an obvious layer and only discovered it when everyone else politely chose to notice.
That evening Anna said nothing sharp about Sonia’s clothes.
That made it worse.
They met for coffee after Anna had spent several hours with the first batch of data from Cheng’s files. Anna arrived in a fitted cream jacket over a pale blouse with fine pintucks at the throat and a dark skirt cut narrow enough to keep every step small and exact. Julien had clearly been involved somewhere in the result. Not because the outfit was flamboyant. Because it was thoughtful. It arranged her.
Anna kissed Sonia’s cheek, sat carefully, and gave her one quick glance that lingered just long enough to register the soft blouse, the uncorseted line, the careless ease.
Then she said only, “You look tired.”
Sonia almost laughed.
“I was underdressed on the tram this morning, if that’s what you mean.”
Anna’s expression changed in the smallest way.
“Ah.”
“Ah?”
Anna lowered her eyes briefly to her cup.
“People can be unkind when they think they are helping.”
That should have been comforting. Instead it put Sonia right back on the tram, feeling those three women’s attention pass over her like fingertips checking a hem for flaws.
“You think they were helping.”
Anna looked up.
“I think they believed they were.”
The distinction irritated Sonia because it was fair.
She blew on her coffee and watched a woman near the window settle into her chair while the man beside her adjusted the fall of her scarf without being asked. The woman thanked him under her breath and leaned into the correction as if it had relieved a small strain she had not wanted to manage alone.
“It keeps happening,” Sonia said.
“What does?”
“I keep waiting for people to look oppressed.”
Anna went very still.
Sonia hated herself a little for saying it out loud, but there it was now.
“And they don’t,” she said. “They look… settled. Supported. Annoyingly well put together.”
Anna’s mouth softened.
“Sometimes they are.”
Sonia looked at her sharply.
“That’s not a defense.”
“No,” Anna said quietly. “It isn’t.”
For a second they sat with that.
Outside, a tram slid past in a wash of reflected light.
Anna rested her fingertips against her saucer.
“You can hate what was done and still notice what people build inside it,” she said. “Those things are not mutually exclusive.”
The sentence stayed with Sonia long after they parted.
The next morning she dragged the Shanghai purchases out from the back of her wardrobe.
The Gowbao Yoohoo blouse looked even more ridiculous in her hands than it had in the boutique. The corset looked worse. An instrument. An argument made in fabric and boning. She stood in her underwear staring at both for so long that the room cooled around her.
This is tactical, she told herself.
It was tactical. She had work to do. She needed freedom to move through the city without inviting comment every time she stepped onto a tram or into a café. Conformity was camouflage. She already knew that.
That did not explain why her pulse had begun to quicken.
The corset closed around her with humiliating familiarity. Busk. Laces. Tighten. Adjust. The blouse followed, then the underskirt, then the outer layer that made the whole thing legible instead of merely restrictive. By the time she pinned her hair and stepped into shoes with just enough heel to alter her center of gravity, the mirror had stopped reflecting a woman making a compromise and started reflecting a woman who looked as if she understood the city again.
She hated the relief first.
Then she hated how incomplete hatred felt.
On the tram no one looked twice at her.
That was its own kind of narcotic.
The same middle space opened around her that she had seen granted to other women: not exactly respect, not exactly protection, but a willing social ease. A man rose almost at once when she stepped into the aisle near him.
“Please, miss.”
He said it with a nod that carried expectation inside the courtesy. Sonia felt the old training come up through her body before she had time to resist it. She lowered her gaze, bent in the smallest curtsy, and thanked him properly.
“Thank you, Sir.”
There.
Done.
She sat with her knees pressed neatly together because the underskirt required it and because it was easier not to fight the clothing once she was already inside it. The carriage moved. The corset held her upright. She could feel the fabric under her arms, the pressure at her waist, the tiny careful balance required every time the tram shifted over a curve. A woman across from her gave her a faint approving smile and went back to her own thoughts.
Sonia stared out the window.
The exchange had taken seconds. It should have meant nothing. Instead it sat warm and ugly under her ribs. Not the seat itself. The little current of recognition that ran through the moment. You are dressed properly. You are behaving properly. You may belong here.
That calm did not look fake on other women.
That was the problem.
By the time she stepped off near the lakeside, the movements had come back fully. The smaller stride. The hand checking the skirt before sitting. The slight turn of the shoulders when making room for someone to pass. Nothing dramatic. Nothing she had to think through. Shanghai had settled into her body deeper than she wanted to admit.
The café had added more privacy cabins along one side since her return. Women used them casually now, slipping in and out with the matter-of-fact rhythm of people adapting to infrastructure rather than ritual. Sonia watched one woman disappear into a cabin with a paper cup and emerge a minute later smoothing her gloves back into place. No spectacle. No shame. Just process.
Inside, the room carried the same pressure as the tram but in a softer register. Women sat straighter. Men ordered more often. Little courtesies accumulated until they began to look like a whole social system instead of separate choices. Sonia ordered coffee and took a seat near the window.
At the next table two women about her age were discussing a friend who had apparently refused to start dressing properly for work.
“She keeps saying she wants to be taken seriously for her mind,” one said.
The other stirred her drink.
“Then she should stop insisting on looking unfinished.”
Neither woman sounded cruel. That was what made the line stay with Sonia.
Unfinished.
The word hooked somewhere deep. She looked down at her own gloved hands around the cup. Finished, then. Correctly assembled. Socially legible. The thought should have revolted her. It did, a little. It also reached something more embarrassing than revolt. A private slackening. The tired pleasure of not having to argue with the room.
Later, in the market, the same sensation sharpened.
The vendors were mostly women. Not masked, not silent, just brisk and competent behind orderly displays of produce, flowers, household goods, and bread. Sonia bought pears from an older woman in a navy jacket with reinforced stays visible under the front seam.
“Beautiful blouse,” the vendor said while weighing the fruit. “Shanghai cut?”
“Yes.”
“I thought so. It suits you.”
Sonia should have brushed it off.
Instead she said, “Thank you.”
The answer came out small. Almost pleased.
She took the pears and moved on annoyed with herself, more annoyed when she caught her reflection in a shop window and saw exactly what the woman had meant. The clothes suited her. Not in spite of what they did to her body. Because of it. The straightened posture. The disciplined line. The way the blouse and skirt turned every movement deliberate.
She stopped in front of the glass longer than she meant to.
This was not conversion. It was worse, in some ways. Conversion would have been a clean story, virus and surrender and altered values. What she had instead was friction. Resistance in the head. Appetite elsewhere. A growing suspicion that belonging, restraint, and the quiet choreography of feminine dependence might answer some need she had spent half her life pretending not to have.
She went home with the pears in one hand and the city’s approval still clinging to her skin like scent.
By evening the corset had left shallow marks at her waist.
She stood in front of the mirror after undressing and touched them lightly.
The apartment was quiet. No one was there to praise her. No one to correct her. No one to tell her how much better she looked when properly arranged.
She thought of the tram seat offered with that little nod. Of the approving glance from the woman opposite. Of the vendor saying it suits you. Of Anna speaking about settlement in a voice so calm it was almost impossible to call delusion.
Then she thought of taking the corset back out tomorrow morning instead of shoving it away again.
That thought did not feel like defeat.
It felt dangerous for subtler reasons.

title: Chapter 19: Masking up
content:
Masking Up# Anna asked Julien for permission in the sitting room after breakfast, when the apartment was still quiet and the light off the lake had not yet turned harsh.
He was reading. She stood beside his chair with her hands folded and waited until he looked up.
“Sir, may I speak?”
“Of course.”
Anna lowered her eyes, not from fear but from the sweetness of wanting something she hoped would please him.
“I would like to change my outdoor presentation. If you permit it, I would like to begin wearing a Jurenmuse in public, and to exchange my hats for headscarves.”
Julien set the paper down.
“Tell me why.”
“It feels right,” she said softly. “More modest. More complete. And…” She smiled, a little embarrassed by her own eagerness. “I think it would reflect well on us.”
His attention warmed.
“On us.”
“Yes, Sir.”
He held her gaze for a moment, then reached out and touched two fingers lightly to the inside of her wrist.
“You may.”
The permission went through her like a pulse.
“Thank you, Sir.”
“If you’re going to do it, do it properly,” he said. “Take your time choosing.”
Anna’s smile widened before she could school it smaller.
“Yes, Sir.”
“And come back to me in it.”
That did more to her than the permission itself.
“I will.”
When she reached Maylee Shufoo’s an hour later, the boutique had already rearranged itself around the new fashion. Headscarves hung in softened gradients of cream, blue, and deep green. The mask display occupied the far wall under careful lighting, porcelain and lacquer gleaming against dark fabric as if silence had always belonged to luxury.
Lily Chen came forward in a fitted qipao with no walking slit and a Jinshuwan covering the lower half of her face. The mask had been chosen to match the dress so precisely that it looked less like an addition than the last necessary line in the composition.
Her eyes brightened when she saw Anna.
Anna smiled back and answered Lily’s graceful hand-dancing with her own. She was still not as fluent as women who had been using it daily for longer, but she understood enough now to keep the exchange easy, warm, and precise.
Lily led her toward the Jurenmuse display with the pleased authority of a woman showing a client something she already knew would be desired.
A high-end Jurenmuse presented at Maylee Shufoo’s.
Up close, the masks were more beautiful than Anna had expected and more frightening only if she let herself name the fear too plainly. Some were left nearly bare, all smooth white porcelain and disciplined lines. Others were painted with delicate mouths, floral work, softened cheeks, or the faint suggestion of an idealized doll’s face. They were elegant. Finished. Inhuman in a way that felt almost tender.
Lily placed one in Anna’s hands.
The porcelain was cool.
Anna looked at the painted mouth, small and perfect and permanently composed.
She imagined stepping into the street with her own lowered face hidden behind that serenity. No accidental expression. No careless mouth. No visible uncertainty. Only stillness, posture, grace, and whatever could be read through the eyes.
The thought settled low in her body with unmistakable force.
Lily showed her two mouthpieces next, one smaller, one slightly fuller. She handled them matter-of-factly, not as curiosities but as the practical interiors of a garment.
Anna hesitated with one in her hand.
Lily did not rush to fill the silence. When she signed, it was gentle rather than persuasive.
For a first time, something you can wear for hours is better. All day fighting it is no pleasure.
That steadied Anna.
She nodded.
The fitting itself was intimate enough to make her blush. Lily settled the first mouthpiece into place with practiced care, waited for Anna to adjust, then brought the porcelain shell up over it and fastened it beneath a pale headscarf. Her fingers were efficient, respectful, unembarrassed. By the time she stepped back, Anna could not speak even if she had wanted to.
She looked in the mirror.
The transformation was immediate.
Her blouse and corset already shaped her into the woman she had been becoming for months. The mask finished the thought. It quieted her. Drew the eye upward. Made every small movement of the head feel deliberate and composed. The woman in the glass looked more modest than Anna usually managed to feel and somehow more exposed at the same time, as if the mask had stripped away the last untidy piece of private self she still carried into public.
Lily touched her elbow and signed, Walk for me a little.
Anna obeyed.
The heels kept her measured. The corset held her upright. The covered mouth made her aware of every breath, every swallow, every impulse to part her lips and find she no longer could. It should have felt claustrophobic. Instead it felt like the world had narrowed to one polished line and asked her to inhabit it beautifully.
When she turned back toward the mirror, her pulse had quickened.
Lily signed again. On you, this is beautiful.
Praise while masked went through Anna differently. Sharper. More private. As if the approval had been sent under her skin.
She tried the plainer white one next and felt the difference at once. The painted version was elegance. This one was surrender. It left her less decorated, more abstract, almost severe. The woman in the mirror no longer looked like Anna dressed beautifully. She looked like a ward already halfway absorbed into a role.
That was the one that frightened her.
That was also the one she could not stop looking at.
In the end she bought both.
A beautifully painted Jurenmuse from Maylee Shufoo’s.
The painted one for ordinary public use. The white one for days when she wanted the greater discipline of it.
When Lily wrapped one, and Anna kept the other on. She felt light and solemn at once. Not because she believed she had crossed into some entirely new life. She was already living that life. This only made it visible.
Outside, she put the painted mask back on before going home.
The city looked different through it. Not literally. Her vision remained clear. But the act of moving through the street unable to speak shifted her attention elsewhere: posture, pace, eye line, hands, the management of space. Men looked at her and saw what she intended them to see. Women looked and understood immediately. A few gave her the smallest nods of recognition.
By the time she reached Julien’s building, the mask no longer felt like an object resting against her face.
It felt like conduct.
Julien was in the front room when she returned. He rose the moment he saw her.
Anna stopped inside the doorway and lowered her gaze.
He crossed the room slowly, taking her in. The headscarf. The painted porcelain. The strict line of her blouse and waist. The silence.
“Turn for me.”
She turned.
“Come here.”
When she stopped in front of him, his hand came up and touched the edge of the mask with surprising gentleness, not to remove it, only to confirm it was really there.
“Do you like it?”
Anna answered in hand-dancing because speaking was impossible and because it felt right to answer him in the mode the mask required.
Yes, Sir.
He watched her hands.
“You look very pretty,” he said. “Very well behaved.”
The praise dropped through her so fast her knees nearly softened.
He noticed.
“Steady.”
She breathed through her nose, swallowed around the mouthpiece, and signed an embarrassed Sorry, Sir.
His mouth curved.
“No apology. I asked you to come back to me in it.”
Yes, Sir.
That evening she spent too long in front of the mirror after he had gone to his study. She wore the white one then, not because anyone had asked it of her, but because she wanted to see what happened when she gave herself the harder version of the thing.
What happened was simple.
She felt more complete.
That was the word that kept returning, quiet and firm and impossible to improve on.
Sonia arrived at the same boutique later that day with none of Anna’s softness about the matter.
She came because the city had changed again and because she was tired of being marked out the moment she entered a tram, a café, or a market. The masks had spread quickly after Shanghai. Not universal yet. Not even close. But established enough that choosing not to wear one had started reading as a statement. Sonia did not have the energy to make statements every time she bought coffee.
Lily recognized her too and greeted her with the same polished warmth, masked and silent and impossible to dislike.
That almost made things worse.
Sonia’s eyes went first to the cheaper Jinshuwan line. Lighter, easier, less absolute. Then to the Jurenmuse display, which was where Lily was already guiding her.
Of course.
Lily signed toward a pale white piece, then a painted floral one, inviting preference rather than imposing it. She handled Sonia’s reluctance the way a good saleswoman handled any hesitation that could be soothed into purchase: respectfully, with the assumption that the customer would arrive where fashion and common sense already pointed.

Living In A Changed Society# Several weeks into her effort to blend in, Sonia discovered that blending in was not the same thing as pretending.
Pretending had edges. It required attention.
This was becoming easier than attention.
She noticed it first at night.
The day corset came off when she got home, but not into a heap on the floor the way she had stripped it off in Shanghai. Now she changed into the softer night corset almost automatically, fingers moving through the laces with the dull competence of repetition. The first evening she had done it for comfort she had sworn at herself. By the fifth or sixth, she had stopped swearing. By the second week, going to bed uncorseted made her feel oddly unfinished, too loose in the middle, as if her body had been asked to hold its own shape without enough guidance.
That should have humiliated her.
Instead it made her more careful to keep the night corset within easy reach.
Mornings were worse.
Or better. Depending on what exactly was being measured.
She could dress herself now without the process turning into a fight. Gowbao Yoohoo blouse. Corset. Skirt or dress cut narrow enough to manage her stride. Gloves. Shoes. Mask when the day required it. Hair pinned. The sequence no longer felt alien. Not natural, exactly. Fluent. That was closer. The city had become easier to move through once she presented herself in its language, and her body had started treating that ease as reward.
At the tram stop one wet Monday morning, a gust of wind drove cold rain under the shelter roof. Sonia shifted the paper folder in her hands and tried to angle herself so the droplets would not spot the pages. A man beside her, older, umbrella already open, stepped closer without crowding.
“Here, miss.”
He tilted the umbrella just far enough to cover both her and the folder.
Sonia thanked him automatically, with the small lowered head and contained gratitude that no longer had to be invented on the spot. He nodded once as if the exchange had gone exactly as it ought to and turned back toward the tracks.
Nothing in it was dramatic.
That was the thing.
The city kept offering her these tiny arrangements of dependence, each one too minor to protest without sounding absurd. Men moved chairs before she sat. Held doors while her skirt and heels made speed unattractive. Reached the top shelf in a bookshop without asking whether she needed help because the answer, in her clothes, was already visible. Once, in the square outside GAIA, a young man she had never seen before caught her elbow as she stepped off a curb slick with rain and steadied her so neatly that she barely had time to be startled before she was thanking him.
Every single thing could be dismissed on its own.
Taken together, they formed an atmosphere.
At work that atmosphere had become institutional.
GAIA had not turned into Shanghai. It had turned into a place that assumed women like Sonia would be corseted, masked some of the time, gloved most of the time, and not especially well served by ordinary office furniture or casual meeting etiquette. Chairs with higher backs had appeared in conference spaces. Walkways for summer events had been laid with heel-friendly surfaces. Meetings ran more slowly and more deliberately when women were masked, less because anyone claimed to be accommodating than because the men chairing them had quietly started building women’s altered presentation into the structure of professional life.
The first time Sonia admitted that some of it worked better this way, she nearly walked the thought back out of her own head.
It happened during a strategy meeting.
Three men from finance, two from policy, Sonia, and another senior woman from operations. Ten months earlier the room would have filled with people talking over each other and then pretending afterward that the strongest ideas had simply risen to the top. Instead, the discussion moved in set turns. The men spoke aloud. Sonia and the other woman contributed through hand-dancing because both were masked that morning, and the men stopped, watched, translated aloud for the notes, then answered. The signed contributions did not feel lesser or provisional. The language was exact, expressive, and impossible to interrupt in the old way. No interruptions. No one barging through a point because he had found a louder one. No need for Sonia to fight to keep the floor while simultaneously managing how angry or imprecise her own voice might sound.
She hated how much easier it was to think inside that arrangement.
Afterward Henry walked beside her down the corridor with the unforced patience that had become his way.
“You were right about the compliance model,” he said. “I hadn’t accounted for municipal delay.”
Sonia glanced at him.
All that, you understood?
“Not all of it.” He smiled. “You sign faster when you’re annoyed.”
She should have been irritated by how closely he had learned to read her.
Instead the comment warmed her in a place she did not entirely trust.
That, is it a complaint?
“Not remotely.”
He opened a door before she reached it. Not ostentatiously. Just in time.
The small grace of that followed her all the way back to her office.
The office itself had changed too, though less visibly. Sonia had switched to a kneeling stool because it worked better with her skirt than any standard chair. At first that had felt like capitulation. Now it felt like practicality. Typing in gloves, another indignity that had once left her furious, had become manageable after she learned the exact pressure each key required and stopped taking the gloves off every time she needed precision. The first day she worked bare-handed again for half an hour and then had to pause because the exposure felt wrong: skin on keys, skin on communal surfaces, skin on the world.
That bothered her enough that she pulled the gloves back on with a muttered curse and could not decide which part of the reaction she found more embarrassing.
Even lunch had become social in a way she had not chosen but could no longer ignore.
Masked women did not simply eat at their desks anymore. They moved toward the privacy cabins or toward small side rooms and alcoves that everyone now treated as obvious infrastructure. Sonia had resisted at first, resenting the inconvenience and the symbolism both. Then one afternoon she found herself in a cabin with two women from policy, all three of them unmasked in the little hush of the enclosed space, eating soup and sharing the kind of easy professional gossip that never seemed to happen when she was left alone with a tray and a laptop.
One of them mentioned her guardian. The other complained affectionately about her brother reorganizing her bookshelves without asking. They laughed. Sonia laughed with them. For ten minutes the whole thing felt less like social engineering than like belonging to a world with extra rules and better manners.
She left the cabin annoyed by how pleasant it had been.
The city had also become startlingly skilled at smoothing over the practical humiliations of feminine restriction. At a summer reception in the GAIA courtyard, wooden planks had been laid across the grass so that heels would not sink. High-backed chairs stood in clusters where women in narrow skirts could perch without struggling. Men moved around the edges of those arrangements adjusting, assisting, anticipating, never quite making a performance of it. Sonia watched one young intern in a severe dark dress step toward a chair after an hour on her feet, only for a man from legal to appear, set the chair exactly where she needed it, and disappear again before thanks could become a scene.
The intern sat with a look of relieved dignity Sonia understood too well.
Convenience was becoming inseparable from submission.
Not philosophically.
Practically.
That distinction mattered less every week.
The sharpest version of it struck on a Thursday evening in a crowded bookstore. Sonia was reaching for a volume on a high shelf more out of reflex than realism when Henry appeared beside her.
“Which one?”
She pointed.
He took it down, checked the cover, and handed it to her without comment.
This, you keep doing, she signed.
“Helping?”

His mouth shifted with amusement.
“I work in the same building. I frequent the same tram lines. We shop in the same district. It’s not quite supernatural.”
