Even so.
Henry’s gaze dropped for the briefest moment to the line of her corset under the jacket, then back to her face.
“You notice things more when you need people,” he said.
That was an outrageous sentence. Condescending, maybe. Intimate, certainly.
It was also true enough to leave her without an immediate answer.
He opened the shop door for her on the way out. She passed through it with a quiet thank-you and spent the next block angry at herself for feeling accompanied rather than diminished.
That was the real problem taking shape under all the smaller ones.
She had spent years understanding autonomy as the absence of dependence. The ability to move, speak, choose, and act without waiting on anyone else’s permission, timing, or body. Changed society was making a competing offer, not in slogans but in daily life. What if dependence, arranged correctly, did not feel like weakness from the inside? What if it felt like being anticipated, supported, carried, absorbed into a choreography that prevented the little abrasions of ordinary life before they happened?
On bad days the whole thing still looked like a polished cage.
On other days it looked like care.
One evening she stood in front of the mirror after work, still corseted, still gloved, mask set aside on the dresser, and studied what had become ordinary. The dress held her upright. The shoulder line was clean. Her waist looked smaller than nature had intended. Every visible choice had already been narrowed by the code of the world outside her door.
She should have looked at herself and seen only coercion.
She did see it.
She also saw coherence.
The second recognition was the one that frightened her.
By then she had started asking Anna more pointed questions about daily life. Not ideology. Not whether the system was just. Anna answered those too, with all the sincerity Sonia had come to expect, but that was not what Sonia wanted most. She wanted logistics. Sensation. What it felt like never to move through the world alone, what correction did to the body, what praise did, what happened when a woman stopped fighting the support structures built around her and let them hold.
Those were not academic questions anymore.
She knew that.
At home, alone, the apartment often felt larger than it really was. Too quiet. Too unstructured. Public life had become crowded with little dependencies, and private life answered that by feeling empty rather than free. Sonia would take off the mask, loosen the day corset, change into the softer one for evening, and feel the silence close around her like a missing step.
She was not ready to call that loneliness.
She was getting uncomfortably close.

title: Chapter 22: The Vial
Chapter 23: Sonia does not want to be alone
Chapter 24: Anna's Giving-Away
content:
Anna’s Giving-Away# Anna’s bridal suite overlooked the inner garden at Jade Garden, though little of the view was visible once Claudette began dressing her properly.
The morning had the hushed seriousness of a ritual everyone in the room already understood. Nothing felt hurried. That made it more intense. Each piece arrived in order, each fastening narrowing the day toward its true purpose.
Claudette started with Anna’s underlayers, then the corset.
The first tightening only gathered the garment around her. The second brought posture. The third brought the familiar changed breath, shallower and more careful, her ribs held, her waist drawn into line. Claudette adjusted the shoulder braces with small competent hands and stepped back for a second to study the result before tightening one side another fraction.
Anna held the dressing screen and breathed through it.
The pressure did not feel punitive this morning.
It felt ceremonial.
The Yoyah Sheengzoh came next under the dress, forcing the day into the body before the outer beauty had even appeared. Claudette lifted the heavy red fabric after that, settling the modernized hanfu over Anna with the kind of care that made dressing feel like consecration. Red with gold. Structured through the waist and shoulders, then falling in rich controlled lines that still allowed almost no heedless movement. The headscarf was pinned last, smooth over the hair Claudette had already braided and rolled away into disciplined neatness.
The white Jurenmuse waited on the vanity.
Anna looked at it while Claudette arranged the final folds of fabric at her wrists.
Today she would wear the severe one.
Not the painted face. Not the softer public prettiness of ordinary afternoons. This was the day she ceased to be her father’s Anna and offered herself formally into Julien’s care. The white porcelain felt right for that. Less decorative. More absolute.
Claudette brought the mouthpiece to her with the same calm professionalism she had brought to the corset laces.
Anna opened for it.
That still carried a pulse of humiliation, even now.
Not shame exactly. More the hot intimate knowledge of cooperation. She had to yield to the fitting. Had to let her own silence be arranged into place by another woman’s careful hands. Once the porcelain shell settled over it and the headscarf hid the fastenings, the mask completed the rest of the dressing in one decisive motion.
Anna looked up into the mirror.
There she was.
The bride, yes. But more than that. A ward prepared for transfer. Face quieted into porcelain stillness. Body held into elegant submission by silk, boning, and weight. No visible mouth. No careless expression. Only eyes, posture, and whatever truth could still move through the hands.
Claudette’s gaze met hers in the mirror.
Beautiful, she signed.
Praise while masked traveled differently. Deeper.
Anna bowed her head in thanks and signed back, For preparing me so well, thank you.
Claudette smiled and finished the last inspection at Anna’s sleeves and hem, then left her alone for a few minutes before Sonia arrived.
Alone, Anna stood before the mirror and let herself feel it fully.
The dress was heavy enough to remind her of every movement. The corset held her upright. The mouthpiece made each swallow a small act of awareness. None of it felt like adornment detached from meaning. The whole ensemble told her what kind of day this was, what kind of woman she had chosen to become inside it.
She sank carefully to her knees before the mirror.
Then she began the private ritual she had taken up in recent weeks, the one she meant to keep after marriage as part of morning discipline. Her hands rose and moved in the bright hush of the suite, the signs precise and almost tender.
Silence, I will honor.
The mask on her face turned the promise from abstraction into practice. Silence no longer meant merely speaking less. It meant accepting that composure, restraint, and visible modesty could be more beautiful than expression left loose.
In obedience, I will be graceful.
The corset pressed at her ribs while she signed it, and the pressure felt right. Not because discomfort was holy on its own, but because the body remembered more faithfully than intention ever did.
Guidance, I will meet with trust.
Julien’s face came into her mind then, not as an authority in the abstract, but as himself. Attentive. Calm. Firm where firmness steadied her. She felt the answer in her body before she finished the line.
Care, I will receive worthily.
That one always moved through her strangely. It contained humility, but not self-erasure. An obligation to receive well, to answer guidance beautifully, to make dependence something he could take pride in giving shape to.
When the sequence ended, Anna stayed kneeling another moment and looked at the bride in the mirror.
Peace was too small a word for what she felt.
The knock came softly.
Anna rose as carefully as the dress required and opened the door for Sonia.
Sonia came in masked as well, already dressed for the ceremony in proper public modesty, though even through the porcelain Anna could read tension in the set of her shoulders. Sonia removed her mask once the door was locked and set it on the dressing table with more force than was strictly necessary.
Then she looked at Anna.
Really looked.
The shock on her face was small and immediate and impossible for Anna to miss.
“You chose the white one.”
Anna signed because she preferred the precision of it while masked.
Yes.
Sonia’s mouth tightened for the fraction of a second it took her to remember herself. She answered in hand-dancing too, less fluid than Anna but still clear.
In this, you look almost ready to disappear.
Anna felt the truth in that and smiled behind the porcelain.
No. In this, I look properly finished.
Sonia flinched at the phrasing as if Anna had meant it as provocation.
She had not.
Anna turned back to the mirror and began rehearsing the key vows again, not because she feared forgetting them, but because the repetition settled her. Sonia stood beside the dressing table and watched.
Anna’s hands moved with ceremony now rather than conversation.
For my father’s care, his guidance, and the house in which he raised me, I give thanks.
Before him, I come in gratitude and obedience, ready to be released from his authority with honor.
To my new guardian, I go willingly, with loyalty, trust, and a clean heart.
Then the second sequence, the one for Julien:
Sir, if willing, take me into your care.
To you, I offer loyalty, obedience, and faithful conduct.
Your guidance, I will honor, and your house, I will uphold with diligence and grace.
The room felt smaller by the time she finished.
Sonia had gone very still.
“You say all that so calmly,” she said. She had reverted to voice in the privacy of the suite, as she often did when emotion made hand-dancing feel too exact for comfort.
Anna turned.
She wanted to answer in hand-dancing because the truth deserved the clean line of it. Sonia made a frustrated little gesture and switched back herself, perhaps because she knew that too.
I am calm.
Sonia’s hands sharpened.
Your father is about to release you, and before guests, tea, flowers, and all this beauty, another man will take you into his care. And you are calm.
Anna held her gaze.
Yes.
Not because she did not understand the imbalance. Because she did.
Sonia looked away first.
On the dressing table beside her mask lay the little ceremonial gifts, hairpins, folded cloth, perfume, and a small lacquer tray Claudette had left ready. Sonia’s eyes moved over all of it and then back to Anna.
Do you ever hear how much of this sounds like surrender?
Anna answered without softening the truth for her.
It is surrender.
That halted Sonia’s next reply.
Anna stepped closer, the dress making the approach slow and stately whether she intended it or not.
But this is not annihilation. Father cared for me and guided me. Today he releases me with honor. After that, Julien will take me in and answer for me. I am not being cast off. I am being transferred with love.
Sonia’s face did something complicated then, grief and disbelief and affection fighting in public for only half a second before discipline covered them.
And that makes you happy.
Anna’s hands softened.
Yes.
Sonia’s gaze dropped to the line of the dress, the severe white mask, the narrow controlled waist, everything in Anna’s appearance designed to make the answer visible before she signed it.
Then, because it was there between them whether they named it or not, Sonia signed:
I still have the vial.
The suite seemed to quiet further around them.
Anna did not look pleased. She did not look disappointed either. Only attentive.
I know.
I haven’t touched it.
I know.
Sonia’s fingers slowed.
And on today of all days, you make giving in look like the easiest thing in the world.
Anna felt that in her throat, behind the mouthpiece, where speech would have failed her anyway.
It is not easy, she signed. It is deep. That is different.
Sonia closed her eyes for a moment.
When she opened them again, she signed more carefully.
For you, I do not know whether to feel horror or jealousy.
Anna moved before thinking too much about it and took Sonia’s hand in both of hers.
The gesture looked strange against gloves and silk and porcelain, but the intimacy of it remained.
Today, you do not have to choose.
Sonia gave a short, silent laugh.
Convenient, since it’s your ceremony.
Anna’s eyes smiled above the mask.
Yes.
There was a knock then, firmer this time. Claudette returning. The ceremony drawing closer.
Sonia released Anna’s hand first and reached for her own mask.
Before she put it on, she looked at Anna one last time with her bare face exposed.
“I do want you to be happy,” she said quietly.
Anna could not answer aloud, so she lifted her hands.
I know. Thank you.
Sonia remasked. The porcelain restored distance at once. She signed a final wish for a beautiful ceremony, then left to join the guests.
Anna stood alone for one last breath in the bridal suite, fully dressed, fully masked, no longer daughter in waiting but not yet Julien Moreau’s Anna.
Then Claudette came in to escort her downstairs.

title: Chapter 25: Giving Anna Away
content:
Giving Anna Away# By noon the Jade Garden had filled with the kind of quiet company Anna had wanted from the beginning.
No crowd. No spectacle for its own sake. Only a small assembly of family, close friends, and the people whose presence mattered to the shape of the vow. The pond reflected pale light through the carved screens. Gravel paths curved between clipped pines and dark wood. Everywhere the garden offered calm, and everywhere the calm sharpened the fact that something irreversible was about to happen.
Sonia stood among the guests in proper dress and mask and watched the place take on ceremony.
Women stood or sat with the particular composure formal clothes and formal expectation drew out of them. Men occupied space more openly, greeting one another, adjusting details, guiding older relatives into place. A low platform had been arranged near the water with a tea table already set behind it, cups waiting under linen covers for later.
Julien arrived before Anna.
He wore dark formal dress with Chinese details worked into the cut, the result restrained enough not to compete with the bride but deliberate enough to show that he understood exactly what this day meant. He greeted the guests, spoke quietly with staff, exchanged a few final words with Marc Lefevre, and then, for a brief interval before the formal beginning, withdrew with Anna into one of the garden’s side rooms.
Sonia did not follow. She saw enough through the half-open screen before it slid shut to understand the shape of it.
Anna in white porcelain and red silk. Julien bending his head to see what she signed. His hand resting once at her waist, not possessive for display, only steadying. Her body answering that touch with visible ease.
The screen closed.
The guests turned their attention toward the platform.
When Anna emerged at last, led by her father, the entire garden seemed to settle around the sight of her.
The white Jurenmuse erased her mouth and left only her eyes to speak. The red and gold of the dress moved richly around the severe calm of the mask. Her corseted waist and constrained stride made every step measured enough that Marc naturally moderated his own pace to match hers. He did not look burdened by that. He looked proud.
Sonia felt a strange hollow open in her chest as she watched them approach.
Not because the beauty disguised the patriarchy.
Because the beauty made the patriarchy feel emotionally legible from the inside.
Marc brought Anna to the center of the platform and turned to face her first, before facing Julien.
That detail mattered. Sonia saw it at once. The ceremony was not only transfer. It was release.
Julien stepped forward and stopped at the appropriate distance. The guests fell into complete silence. Even the water at the pond edge seemed to lower its voice.
Marc lifted one hand.
“Anna.”
His voice was formal, but tenderness moved beneath it plainly enough for everyone to hear.
“You come before me as my daughter and ward, raised under my house and my authority. Do you come in gratitude and good conduct, ready to be released honorably from my care?”
Anna’s gloved hands rose.
Yes, Sir. In gratitude I come. For your care, your guidance, and the honor of your house, I give thanks. I ask to be released from your authority with your blessing.
The sight of the white porcelain while those signs moved in the air gave the moment an eerie kind of purity Sonia would have despised more easily if it had not also been beautiful.
Marc watched every sign.
“You have honored my house well,” he said. “I release you freely and with pride.”
That was the first severing.
Sonia felt it like a thread cut in public.
Marc stepped aside half a pace then, not abandoning Anna but no longer standing as the man who defined her. He turned toward Julien.
“Julien Moreau, do you come prepared to take this woman into your care and answer for her before your house, your family, and your society?”
“I do.”
Julien’s voice carried cleanly across the platform. He did not raise it. He did not need to.
Marc looked back to Anna.
“Then go to him.”
Anna moved.
The dress made it a glide rather than a walk. Short steps, composed balance, hands gathered before her until she reached Julien and lowered herself into a kneel that the clothing turned into something difficult enough to be meaningful. Sonia saw one of the older women in the guest row lower her eyes at the sight, moved almost to tears.
Anna lifted her hands.
Sir, if willing, take me into your care.
The signs were flawless.
To you, I offer loyalty, obedience, and faithful conduct.
Your guidance, I will honor, and your house, I will uphold with diligence and grace.
Julien looked down at her for one suspended heartbeat, and Sonia saw what the scene would feel like from Anna’s side. Exposure. Relief. Completion. The erotic danger of asking and waiting to be accepted.
Then he extended his hand.
“I will have you.”
He did not lift her immediately. He gave the words their full shape first.
“I take you into my care before these witnesses. I promise you protection, guidance, and faithful regard. I will answer for your well-being, honor your trust, and keep you under my protection as befits my ward and wife.”
Only then did he take her hand and bring her to her feet.
When Anna rose, it was no longer as Marc Lefevre’s Anna.
Marc spoke the change aloud for everyone.
“Then let it be known that this woman leaves my authority with blessing and enters yours with honor. She is no longer of my name. She stands before us now as Julien Moreau’s Anna.”
The phrase moved through the gathering like a physical thing.
Sonia hated how much power it had.
She hated, more, that Anna visibly loved hearing it.
Even behind the mask, that was clear. In the way her body settled. In the tiny softening of her shoulders under the braces. In the almost imperceptible lean toward Julien as if the naming itself had given her somewhere to rest.
The guests bowed their heads or murmured polite assent. A few of the women signed blessings too quickly and lightly for the men to read in detail. Marc stepped back completely then, his role concluded.
Julien and Anna turned together toward the tea table.
This was where the ritual became domestic, and therefore more intimate.
They took their places on opposite sides of the low table. Anna had to lower herself carefully again, the dress and underskirt making even that one act a small public display of constraint. Julien watched without helping because the ceremony required the effort to be visible. Only once she was settled did he sit opposite her.
The tea set had been chosen with almost absurd care. White porcelain edged in deep green. Small cups. Narrow pot. A lacquer tray beneath it all reflecting sleeve, hand, silk, and sky in dark blurred shapes.
Anna began with the cleansing.
She lifted the pot and cups, rinsed them, poured out the first water, then warmed the porcelain with steady gloved hands. Nothing in the sequence was rushed. Sonia had expected more abstraction from a public tea ritual. Instead it was bodily and exact. The turn of Anna’s wrist. The drag of the sleeve. The slight pause required when the corset limited her lean and forced her to redistribute effort through shoulders and forearms.
Constraint made the ritual more visible.
Not less.
When she measured the leaves, Anna’s hands were so steady they looked serene.
The water followed. The wait. The pour.
Julien watched her with the full attention of a man being publicly served by a woman who had just asked to be governed by him, and the concentration in his face kept the scene from slipping into pretty pageantry. He understood that the tea was not decorative. She was giving him her discipline, her composure, her readiness to serve in a form everyone present could witness and read.
Anna lifted the first cup and offered it across the table.
Both hands. Lowered gaze. Perfect stillness.
Julien received it the same way a man might receive an oath.
“Thank you.”
The words were quiet. They landed like praise anyway.
He drank.
Sonia watched Anna feel it.
The reaction was small, private, unmistakable. The little bodily yielding that came whenever male approval reached the place the virus had prepared for it. This was not theory anymore. It was in front of her, in silk and porcelain and sunlight.
Anna prepared the second cup after that and drank from it herself, completing the exchange. Then the sequence continued in smaller formal movements: the arrangement of the cups, the shared pour, the symbolic joining not through a kiss or a modern declaration of equality but through service accepted and protection implied in that acceptance.
Somewhere behind Sonia, someone sniffed softly.
When the formal sequence ended, applause came not as a roar but as a swelling of contained approval through the garden. Gloves touching lightly. Men nodding. Women signing blessings to one another. Staff moving in silent competence at the edges. The whole setting seemed to breathe out.
Julien rose first and offered Anna his hand.
She took it.
This time when she stood, he did help. He steadied the difficult upward movement her dress demanded, and that simple assistance, coming after the public transfer and the tea, seemed to seal the whole thing more deeply than any speech still could have.
Marc approached them once more, no longer as Anna’s authority, but as family.
Julien bowed his head respectfully. Anna lowered hers.
“You have both done honor to the day,” Marc said.
Anna signed her thanks. Julien answered aloud.
Around them the guests began to loosen into post-ceremony life. Tea for others. Soft conversation. The relief of people who had witnessed something emotionally satisfying and morally unquestioned by the culture around them.
Sonia stood among them and felt more apart than she had inside the bridal suite.
Before the ceremony, Anna had still been split between names, between houses, between male authorities. That intermediate state had left room for Sonia’s disbelief to catch on something human and unfinished. Now the ritual had done its work. Marc had set her free. Julien had taken her in. The old name had fallen away in public. The new one had been spoken aloud and answered by Anna’s whole body.
Julien Moreau’s Anna.
It should have sounded grotesque.
Instead, in that garden, with that woman, it sounded cherished.
That was the part Sonia could not forgive the world for making true.

title: Chapter 26: Fashionista
content:
Fashionista# Anna’s giving-away stayed with Sonia longer than she wanted to admit.
It was not the ceremony itself, though that had been hard enough to watch, or even the moment Marc and Julien settled things over Anna as if a woman could be passed from one set of hands to another without the world stopping in protest. What stayed with Sonia was Anna’s face: calm, fulfilled, deeply, sincerely pleased by a structure Sonia had been raised to call degrading.
It should have made the whole system easier to hate.
Instead it had left Sonia with a worse problem.
She wanted to know why it worked.
Monday morning, she decided to stop pretending that question was theoretical.
She arrived at GAIA in a new lace-covered mask and clothes chosen with more intention than usual: a fitted skirt, a cream blouse, tight gloves, heels just impractical enough to alter the way she moved all day. Nothing outrageous by the standards Geneva had settled into. Enough, however, that a man who cared about such things would notice.
Henry noticed.
He let her finish her first tasks before crossing the corridor toward her desk. Sonia saw him coming and made herself remain seated until he reached her. When she rose, his gaze had already taken in the mask, the blouse, the line of her posture, and the fact that she was waiting for him to speak first.
“Good morning, Sonia.”
Good morning, Sir.
The title came easily now. That still irritated some older part of her. It no longer stopped her.
Henry tilted his head slightly as he studied the mask.
“New.”
Yes, Sir.
“Maylee Shufoo?”
She nodded.
“I thought so.”
He did not touch it. The restraint of that pleased her more than touching would have.
“You wear it well,” he said. “More severe than your usual choices.”
Sonia let the praise settle before answering.
Less apologetic, yes.
His mouth shifted at that.
“And is that what this is? Less apology?”
Partly that. Partly curiosity.
“About what.”
The question was too direct to dodge gracefully.
How far form can go before practicality must give way.
Henry glanced once at the collar of her blouse, then back to her eyes.
“That is not a neutral question.”
No, Sir.
They stood in the corridor while people moved past in the normal Changed choreography of workday Geneva: women with shortened steps and careful posture, men carrying coffee, opening doors, pausing to let a woman settle herself before passing through a narrow space. It would have been easy to turn the conversation theoretical. The building offered endless excuses for theory.
Henry did not take them.
“You are dressing further in,” he said.
Sonia felt the accuracy of it in her stomach.
Perhaps.
“No,” he said quietly. “You are.”
The certainty in his tone did more to expose her than the words themselves.
He should have left then. Instead he looked once more at the buttons of her cuffs, at the close line of the mask, and said, “If you are going to ask a question like that, you should ask it properly.”
Then he went back to his office.
Sonia stood very still for several seconds after he was gone.
Ask it properly.
The sentence stayed with her all morning.
By lunch she had turned it over enough times to understand what it required. He did not want an essay or another polished conversation about aesthetics and the Changed world and what clothing meant. He wanted a demonstration, or perhaps he wanted to see whether she was serious enough to make one.
The idea should have embarrassed her out of it.
Instead it followed her back to Anna’s apartment after work with the clean persistence of hunger.
Anna opened the door wearing the settled contentment of a woman who had stopped fighting her own life. Sonia still did not know whether that sight comforted or infuriated her more.
Anna’s gaze dropped once over Sonia’s work outfit and came back up with immediate interest.
That mask is new.
Sonia removed her shoes by the door.
Henry noticed.
Anna smiled.
Of course he did.
Sonia followed her into the sitting room and stood there for a moment without taking off the mask. The request she was about to make felt stupid enough that she almost abandoned it.
Anna waited.
Need help dressing tomorrow.
Anna’s expression changed very slightly, not into surprise but recognition.
For work.
Yes.
For Henry.
Sonia gave her a look.
Anna’s smile deepened.
That was not a question.
It was easier to admit things to Anna now that Sonia no longer pretended the world ought to be otherwise.
He said if question is to be asked, it must be asked properly.
And what question are you asking?
Sonia looked away toward the window.
Whether dependence is part of what I want.
Anna did not pounce on the answer. She simply stood and went to the wardrobe where some of Sonia’s things still hung from older practical arrangements between them.
Show me what you had in mind.
They chose the pieces together. Tight corset with shoulder braces. Narrow skirt with the kick pleat that could be buttoned down further once Sonia no longer had to walk far. A Gowbao Yoohoo blouse that would need another person’s hands to close fully and would not come off again without help. Gloves fixed under the cuffs. A niqab that allowed speech and would therefore sharpen the dependence instead of hiding it behind silence.
Sonia watched the outfit gather across Anna’s bed and felt something between dread and relief.
This is too much for the office, she signed.
Yes, Anna signed back. That is why it will work.
The next morning Sonia arrived early enough to finish most of her tasks before making the rest of the day impossible. Anna dressed her in the guest room first, fastening the blouse, closing the collar, fixing the gloves, and finally asking, Arms or skirt first?
Sonia’s mouth had gone dry.
Arms.
Anna closed the inner sleeve zips and fixed the press-studs that held Sonia’s upper arms in close to her sides. The effect was immediate. Her forearms remained free enough for small motions, but proper signing was gone. So was any illusion of self-sufficiency.
Last chance, Anna signed lightly.
Sonia met her eyes in the mirror.
No.
Anna nodded, then buttoned the kick pleat down only slightly so that Sonia’s steps shortened into a careful walk.
The niqab came last.
Sonia looked at herself in the mirror and knew she had crossed from workwear into statement. She was not dressed to get through the day efficiently. She was dressed to make dependence visible and then ask a particular man to touch it.
That realization should have sent her home.
Instead it steadied her.
Anna rode up with her to GAIA and left her near Henry’s office with a look that contained too much amusement to be charitable.
Try not to fall over.
Sonia gave her what dignity the niqab and the posture brace would allow.
Thank you.
You are welcome.
Then Anna went on, and Sonia was left with the corridor, her restricted steps, the pressure of the blouse, and the absurd fact that she was waiting for Henry like a woman in a fairy tale waiting for the man with the key.
He arrived late enough to make her earn the waiting.
Sonia heard him before she saw him. Male voices, footsteps, the lift doors, then Henry turning the corner and stopping cleanly when he found her beside his desk.
His eyes moved over her in one measured pass.
The look was so intent that she forgot, for one dangerous second, how to breathe under the corset.
She curtsied.
“Sir, might I request your assistance with my attire?” she said through the niqab.
That made the moment explicit. No theory left to hide in.
Henry set the folder in his hand on the desk without taking his eyes off her.
“What do you need.”
“The kick pleat may be closed further for office propriety, if you find that appropriate. In return, if it pleases you, my arms may be released enough for work.”
The bargain sat between them with all its intended meanings.
Henry stepped close enough to inspect the blouse, the skirt, the niqab, the press-studs at her sleeves. Sonia kept still because any movement would have looked like fidgeting and because his nearness was already doing enough to her pulse.
“You came in like this on purpose.”
“Yes, Sir.”
“To make a point.”
“Yes, Sir.”
His gaze lifted to hers.
“And what point is that.”
Sonia could still have lied. She did not.
“That I would like to know how it feels to let someone else decide the practical terms.”
Something warm and dangerous entered Henry’s expression.
“Very well,” he said.
Then he went down on one knee in the corridor and buttoned the kick pleat another two increments closed.
The intimacy of that act nearly undid her, not because he touched her legs, but because he did it calmly, as if a woman presenting herself for adjustment in a work corridor were something he was entirely prepared to handle.
He rose and moved behind her to release the sleeve fastenings enough that she could work.
“Not all the way,” he said. “You asked for functionality, not comfort.”
“Yes, Sir.”
She could feel people noticing. That should have made her furious. Instead it made the moment sharper. Public. Legible. Real.
“Can you manage the rest of the day?”
“Yes, Sir.”
“Come see me before you leave.”
“Yes, Sir.”
She worked like that for hours.
Everything took longer. Sitting, standing, turning, typing, going down the corridor, dealing with doors. Henry did not hover, but he checked on her often enough that she could feel the shape of his attention around the whole experiment. Once he brought her coffee without asking. Once he paused at her desk only to say, “Shoulders back.” Once, when she had nearly forgotten the new limits of the skirt and turned too fast, he caught her elbow and set her straight without comment.
By late afternoon Sonia was exhausted, sore, and so aware of him that her nerves felt flayed open.
She returned to his office as instructed.
“Sir, may I ask for your assistance to release my attire so I may return home?” she asked.
Henry stood from his desk immediately.
“Come here.”
He re-pinned her upper sleeves, because way home required less gesture and more containment, then adjusted the kick pleat back to a level she could manage safely. The reversal should have felt like rescue. Instead it felt almost disappointingly temporary.
He noticed that too.
“You liked more of this than you expected.”
Sonia kept her eyes lowered.
“Yes, Sir.”
“So did I.”
He did not let her go immediately after that. He stepped back, studied her once more in the altered outfit, and said, “Saturday evening. Champel. I would like to show you part of my collection.”
Sonia waited.
Her pulse quickened at once.
Only me, Sir?
“Bring Anna and Julien if you like. I am not hiding the invitation. I am giving it through you.”
That distinction mattered more than it should have.
I would like that, Sir.
“I thought you might.”
She made it home with Anna’s help, because the outfit still required another woman’s hands to undo completely and because Sonia was too tired by then to be vain about it. Later, alone, with the blouse opened and the corset still marking her ribs, she sat on the edge of the bed and replayed the day in hard bright pieces: Henry kneeling in the corridor, Henry refusing full release, Henry bringing coffee, Henry inviting her to Champel as if he had already seen enough to decide the next move.
She had meant the office stunt as a test.
It had been that.
It had also been an admission.
Sonia was no longer merely studying Changed femininity from the outside. She was beginning to use it as a language for desire, and Henry had answered her in the same language at once.
Saturday evening brought the second part of the answer.
Anna and Julien arrived with Sonia at Henry’s villa just after dusk. Anna was radiant in the settled way that still disturbed Sonia when she looked at it too directly. Julien carried himself with the calm certainty of a man well settled. Henry received all three graciously, but Sonia noticed at once that his attention divided unevenly. The collection mattered to him. Anna’s responses mattered because they were informed and sincere. Julien’s mattered because he understood construction. Sonia’s mattered because he expected them to.
That expectation made her stand a little straighter in the entry hall.
Henry led them first into the long room he used for storage and display. Cases opened one after another under his hands: Maylee Shufoo evening pieces severe enough to turn femininity into architecture, Mirende Ginciao work more overtly ritualistic, experimental latex translations of traditional forms, collars, cuffs, understructures, visible attachment systems, and more technical items laid out with the same exact care as the decorative ones.
Anna took to it immediately.
She moved from piece to piece with the pleased fascination of a woman who had already stopped drawing a moral line between beauty and dependence. Julien asked better questions than Sonia had expected about closures, weight distribution, maintenance, and how certain garments were intended to be managed in daily use rather than simply admired on a body at rest.
That opened the conversation Henry had clearly wanted.
“I hear you’re going to London with Anna to take posession of her. London will take some adjustment,” he said to Julien, lifting a fitted cape from its stand and turning it so the concealed hardware became visible. “The British are less interested in hiding support systems. Geneva still prefers the fiction that a properly guided woman is simply very disciplined. London likes visible solutions.”
Julien examined the cape with real interest.
“And you think Anna will like that.”
Henry glanced at Anna, who was already studying a lockable muff with thinly disguised delight.
“I think Anna will adore it.”
Julien smiled in a way that said the answer had not surprised him.
“So do I.”
Anna turned to Sonia then and signed with bright quick hands, Visible dependence. Weatherproof. Publicly normal. I cannot decide whether it sounds practical or shameless.
Both, Sonia signed back.
Henry watched the exchange, then said, “That is the British specialty.”
The talk moved naturally from there into the trip itself. Train compartments designed for guardians and wards. Accomodation with integrated rails and domestic dock points. Outdoor systems built for rain, mud, and long walking distances without forcing women into masculine practicality. Anna listened as if Henry were describing a city made specifically to flatter her new instincts. Julien listened like a man quietly preparing himself to be competent in another country’s version of care.
Sonia listened too, but with divided attention. She cared about the London discussion. She also cared, more than she wanted to admit, about the case Henry had not opened yet, the flat white one on the far worktable.
He noticed that she had noticed.
Later, after wine for the men and tea for the women, when the conversation had softened enough to leave room for play, Henry crossed to that table and opened the case.
The room quieted almost at once.
Inside lay a restrictive blouse with a high collar and integrated half-mask, a severe underskirt, a long hobble design with no concession to stride, gloves meant to be fixed in place, and the more technical pieces needed to make the whole thing livable once closed. Nothing in the arrangement called attention to itself. That was part of the effect. The obscenity of it was hidden under craftsmanship, etiquette, and practical finish.
“One of my experiments,” Henry said. “Not for daily wear. Too much management. But the line interests me.”
Anna stepped closer.
It is beautiful, she signed.
“Yes,” Henry said. “And inconvenient enough to become honest.”
Sonia felt the line in her stomach.
Julien, who had been looking over the hardware with professional interest, asked, “Can it actually be worn for an evening?”
“With help,” Henry said.
His gaze moved to Sonia.
Not a command. Not yet.
An opening.
Sonia could have left it there. Let Anna admire, let Julien ask technical questions, let the evening remain civilized and observational.
Instead she signed, Would you show us?
Anna’s eyes shifted to her at once. Julien looked from Sonia to Henry and understood enough not to interrupt. Henry held Sonia’s gaze for one second longer than politeness required.
“Yes,” he said.
There was no audience-performance in the way he said it. Only acceptance of the terms she had just set.
Anna helped at first, because some of the underlayers still required another woman’s practical touch before a man could make the final decisions. The technicality of that helped Sonia keep her balance. Stockings. Corset. The first skirt. Gloves. Collar. Each step had an order. An objective. A reason.
Then Henry took over.
He closed what Anna had left open, fixed what needed fixing, and drew the whole arrangement into its final shape under the quiet watch of the others. Sonia became aware of herself in layers: posture brace, narrowed gait, fixed gloves, the high set of the collar, the half-mask changing the meaning of her mouth, the long skirt deciding distance in advance. It was neither convenient nor practical, but none of it hurt. It simply removed options one by one until every remaining motion became legible as dependence.
When he was done, she could stand beautifully.
Everything else required management.
Anna looked delighted. Julien looked fascinated in the way of a man cataloguing both elegance and liability. Henry looked exactly as he had in the office corridor when he had adjusted her skirt: calm, attentive, already accounting for the implications.
“Walk,” he said.
Sonia did.
The room had become longer. She knew it had not, but the outfit made distance feel instructional. She reached the far table, turned with care, and came back.
“Well?” Julien asked, not of Sonia but of Henry.
“Wearable,” Henry said. “Not independent.”
The phrase settled over the room with a warmth Sonia did not trust.
Anna signed, That is the point.
Sonia could not disagree.
The feeding apparatus was introduced as if it were the most technical part of the demonstration, which in one sense it was. Henry explained it in exactly those terms: if a garment rendered mouth access impractical, or if the line of the mask had to remain undisturbed, then hydration and light nourishment had to be solved cleanly. He spoke about valves, cleanliness, flow control, not staining fabric, not interrupting the visual line. Julien responded in the same register, asking about maintenance and failure points. Anna, standing beside Sonia, watched with that bright disturbing attentiveness fully Changed women brought to systems that made dependence cleaner.
No one named the atmosphere that formed around the demonstration.
No one needed to.
Henry fitted the attachment with grave concentration and checked it twice before using it. Sonia stood between Anna and Julien in the middle of the room and let him handle her in front of them all. The technicality made it possible. The technicality made it impossible too. His fingers at the side of her face, the brief adjustment at her jaw, the careful angle of the vessel, the pause while he made sure she was ready: every part of it could be defended as proper procedure.
None of it felt procedural from the inside.
The first cool mouthful was so controlled, so cleanly measured, that Sonia had time to register each part separately: the pressure, the swallow, the awareness of being watched, the helplessness of needing it given. Nothing overt happened. No one said anything indecent. Julien only observed. Anna only watched. Henry only repeated the process with the same exact, unhurried attention he had given the closures.
And the room still changed.
Sonia could feel the allusion in it without wanting it named.
An earlier Sonia would have hated it, but she felt herself going soft around the edges.
When Henry finally withdrew the apparatus and checked the line of her mask once more, his thumb rested briefly under her jaw as if the whole point of the evening were not the garment, nor even the collection, but the fact that she had let him manage something so intimate in front of others and remained standing afterward.
“Good,” he said.
Only that.
Anna’s eyes met Sonia’s for one brief charged second and then moved away with tact Sonia had not expected from her old friend and did expect, now, from the woman she had become.
The demonstration ended there. Henry and Anna helped Sonia out of the more final pieces afterward, Julien standing back now because the practical intimacy had shifted again into women’s work. They returned instead to talk of London routes, British rain, and which collection pieces would travel well under supervised conditions.
But for Sonia the evening had already divided itself into before and after.
Before, restrictive fashion had been a language she was learning to speak for Henry.
After, it had become something else: a way to stand inside managed helplessness under his hands and discover that even public technicality could carry a private charge strong enough to alter the whole shape of a room.
At the door, while Anna and Julien made their slower, more encumbered way down the front steps, Henry kept Sonia back for one last second under the excuse of seeing them out properly.
“Lunch tomorrow,” he said. “Les Petits Chats. Just you.”
The invitation landed differently now than it would have in the office corridor. It no longer felt like a speculative next step. It felt selected.
Yes, Sir.
“Good.”

title: Chapter 27: Anna and Julien's departure for London
Chapter 28: A Photography Project
content:
A Photography Project# The day after Henry invited her to lunch, and while Anna and Julien traveled north, Sonia met him at Les Petits Chats and tried to treat it like an ordinary invitation.
It was not ordinary. She knew that before she sat down.
The café had small iron tables under plane trees, striped awnings, and the kind of polished quiet that made every gesture visible. Sonia had chosen one of the outside tables because she needed air and because being seen with Henry in public no longer felt like a risk she should avoid. It felt like a line she was walking toward on purpose.
Sonia waits for Henry at the “Les Petits Chats.”
She wore a teal pencil skirt, a cream blouse, and long leather gloves. The lace-covered mask she had ordered recently sat beautifully on her face, less blank than the smooth porcelain styles that had become popular and somehow more intimate for that. By the time Henry arrived she had already eaten. She preferred not to perform the gag and veil ritual in front of him until she knew exactly why he had asked to see her.
Then he appeared at the corner of the terrace and all that caution felt a little thin.
He came toward her in a dark suit, not overdressed, just exact. Sonia rose. He took in the mask, the gloves, the line of her waist, and the fact that she had stood for him before he said a word. The look lasted only a second. It still altered something in her.
“Sonia.”
Sir.
She curtsied. It had started as irony weeks ago. She no longer lied to herself about that.
He seated her, sat opposite, and waited until coffee had been brought before saying why he had asked her there.
“I want to photograph you.”
Sonia set down her cup and signed.
As a favor, Sir?
“As a collaboration.” He stirred his coffee once, then set the spoon down. “And not the polite kind where nothing is risked. I have pieces that need a body, a temperament, and someone who understands what restrictive dress does when it is doing its work properly.”
She should have laughed at the seriousness of that.
Instead she signed, Why me, Sir?
Henry’s expression hardly changed. “Because you don’t disappear in these clothes. Even when you are covered, you make choices inside the restriction. You push back, then use it. That reads.”
The answer went through her more cleanly than praise should have.
She leaned back slightly, trying not to show that it had landed.
And what exactly would I be agreeing to, Sir?
He did not rush. That was one of the things she had begun to trust about him.
“A real shoot. Proper location. Proper styling. Time to do it well.” He watched her face, not the mask. “You would be dressed, posed, adjusted, and directed. Some of the pieces are severe. One or two are severe enough that you would need to surrender most of the practical control.”
That could have been a warning.
It did not sound like one.
Sonia felt the old split appear in her almost automatically. The part of her raised to hear danger first. The part that had knelt on tiled floors in Shanghai, had taken instruction, had found something in obedience she had not wanted to name. Henry’s phrasing reached both parts at once.
What sort of pieces, Sir?
His mouth shifted, just enough.
“A midnight-blue Maylee Shufoo gown with a brutal collar and the kind of corset that decides your breathing for you. A brocade piece with integrated restraint through the sleeves. And one look we can build together, if you want it, around overt bondage and ceremonial dress.”
She held his gaze.
Overt.
“Yes.”
How overt?
“Enough that you would have to trust me.”
That was the first truly honest thing either of them had said.
Sonia lowered her eyes for a moment, not as surrender exactly, but to think inside her own body. The thought of being costumed for Henry was exciting. The thought of being arranged by him was worse. Worse in the way that meant better, if she were being honest. She did not yet like how easily those categories had begun to collapse.
Photographs shown afterward?
“Only if you consent after you have seen them.”
If panic comes in the middle?
“Then we stop.” He took a sip of coffee. “I am not asking for endurance. I am asking whether you want to make something with me.”
Sonia let out a breath she had not realized she was holding.
That answer mattered.
It mattered because he could have asked for display. He could have asked for obedience. Instead he had asked for trust and had left her room to give it.
You already have ideas, she signed.
“Of course.”
Then tell me, Sir.
That pleased him. She saw it.
He began with the location: an abandoned villa above the lake, half reclaimed by weather and vines, enough ruined elegance to hold strong shapes without looking theatrical. Then he moved to light, timing, fabric behavior outdoors, how dull stone made brocade look more severe, how a hood changed the relationship between posture and presence, how a woman locked into a silhouette she could not negotiate herself became legible in a different register.
When he spoke about clothes in this mode he did not sound like a collector showing off. He sounded like a man building circumstances.
Sonia listened and asked sharper questions than he expected. About balance. About whether latex should read as futurity or ceremonial gloss. About the difference between a woman who looked trapped and a woman who looked given over. About how far the line could be pushed before a photograph stopped reading as fashion and turned into simple cruelty.
Henry answered each question seriously.
“A woman who looks merely trapped is boring,” he said. “The interesting image is the one where the viewer can tell she is held and still complicit.”
The sentence sat between them.
Sonia should have disliked it. It was too close to home.
Instead she felt heat rise slowly through her chest.
Complicit, she signed back.
“Not cheerfully or simplistically, but present in it.” He rested his forearms lightly on the table. “You do that already.”
She looked away toward the street.
Women passed in Changed dress: gloves, skirts, masks, one with her gait shortened so much by the underlayer that crossing the street became a quiet little performance of dependence. Men guided, carried, watched, opened, waited. Geneva had stopped feeling theoretical months ago. Henry’s project did not invent any of this. It only promised to isolate it and make her stand inside it on purpose.
That was part of what tempted her.
I have an idea too, she signed.
“I assumed you would.”
Latex. Not modern intrusion. Obedience made glossy. Traditional shapes with no softness left to hide in.
Henry smiled properly then.
“Go on.”
She did. Once she started, she could not quite stop. A long latex skirt held out by petticoats. A Changed blouse severe enough to turn the shine ceremonial. Hidden attachment points. Possibly a feed adapter, but only if the image justified the dependence rather than using it as a cheap shock. She heard herself talking and knew two things at once: she was excited, and he was looking at her in a way that made excitement dangerous.
“You have better taste than most people who think they have opinions about fashion,” he said.
That should have sounded dry.
It landed as praise.
Sonia had worn enough masks with gags by now to know what happened in her body when approval struck in the right place. The sensation was not as automatic as it was in Anna. It still had to pass through resistance. But once it got through, it stayed.
Henry noticed the delay before she answered.
“Too much?”
No, Sir. Useful only.
He looked amused by that.
“Good. Then let me be clearer.”
He leaned in slightly, not enough to draw attention from the other tables, only enough that she could hear him without the terrace hearing back.
“One setup will require very little from you but poise. One will require trust. One will require submission.”
Her pulse stepped once, hard.
And you think I am ready for all three?
“I think you want to find out.”
The answer hit too close to the bone to dodge.
She could have refused then. Could have turned the lunch back into banter and logistics and left with the gentler version of him intact. Instead she looked at him through the lace of her mask and recognized something she had been circling for weeks: she wanted to be seen by him in the condition of surrender, not despite the surrender but through it.
If we do this, I do not want glass handling.
“I had not planned to.”
And afterward, no polite lies.
“Then do not ask for them.”
That settled it more than reassurance would have.
Sonia lowered her gaze, not out of compulsion but because saying yes required passing through a point of shame she could feel in her throat.
All right.
Henry waited.
She lifted her eyes again.
Yes, Sir. I want to do it.
He did not pounce on the answer. He let it stand.
“Good.”
One word. Enough.
They spent the rest of lunch on practicalities: timing, transport, what he would bring, what she should wear to arrive in, what level of privacy they could expect. Yet even the logistics carried a charge now, not because either of them spoke crudely, but because the underlying shape had been accepted. Sonia had agreed to let Henry build circumstances around her body and direct her inside them. That was the fact under everything else.
By the time they stood to leave, the afternoon had softened into a pale gold that made the street look briefly less exhausted than it was.
Henry waited for her to rise, then said, “One more thing.”
Sonia paused.
“When I tell you to hold still during the shoot, hold still.”
There was no threat in it. No performance.
Only expectation.
Sonia felt her stomach tighten around the words in a way she knew better than to dismiss.
Yes, Sir.
He nodded once, satisfied.
They left in opposite directions. Sonia lasted half a block before she had to stop under a tree and stand very still, because she had just agreed to far more than a photography project and both of them knew it.

title: Chapter 29: Anna and Julien in London
content:
Anna and Julien in London# London began with rain on brick and the feeling that the city had been designed by people who regarded weather as a moral fact.
The B&B on Great Titchfield Street was narrower than Anna had imagined and more ingenious. Brick exterior, polished brass, a small ground-floor boutique, a pair of upper rooms given over to guests, and everywhere little systems of accommodation shaped specifically around the Changed life. Nothing announced itself as spectacular. That was the point. The city did not think restraint was exotic. It thought it was infrastructure.
Mike Smith greeted them first, broad-shouldered, dryly cheerful, already reaching for the luggage. His Wendy followed a step later, practical and warm in the distinctly British way that made efficiency sound like kindness. She wore a belted rain cape over a structured dress, gloves, a hat with layered veils, and the visible rail attachment at the back of her corseted waist as casually as a woman elsewhere might wear a handbag strap.
Anna noticed all of it at once.
Wendy noticed that she noticed.
“First time in London?” she asked.
Julien answered for both of them.
“Yes.”
Wendy smiled at Anna through the veil.
“You’ll either find it absurd or wonderfully sensible by tomorrow.”
Anna smiled behind her veil.
“Perhaps both.”
Wendy laughed softly.
“That is usually the correct answer.”
Their suite occupied the upper floor and looked out over wet rooftops, chimney pots, and a surprising amount of green. The rooftop garden Wendy had mentioned in her message was real, not decorative, and still visible even in the rain: raised beds, herbs, a small water catchment system, careful use of every piece of space.
Inside, the more revealing details emerged.
The rail system ran along the ceiling of the bedroom and sitting room both, with a clean exterior track visible outside the window, linking the domestic interior to the street below. Dock points had been built into furniture, not as curiosities but as expected conveniences. There were hooks placed exactly where hats, veils, muffs, and capes would need to be managed. A standing support near the dressing mirror suggested that no one in the house considered female dressing entirely independent work.
Anna stood in the middle of the room and turned slowly, looking upward.
Julien watched her take it in.
“Overwhelmed?”
“Interested.”
That answer pleased him too much to hide.
They unpacked, and then Julien told her to change for the boutique downstairs because he wanted their first outing to be simple. Shopping. Looking. Learning local standards before they tried to perform them in public.
The boutique beneath the B&B sold weather, modesty, and dependence with remarkable elegance.
Latex catsuits in varying weights hung beside walking skirts, structured capes, fitted rain hoods, veiled hats, lockable muffs, and rainproof oversleeves that narrowed the arms into decorative helplessness while still claiming practicality. The colors were more disciplined than Geneva’s. Black, cream, storm blue, muted teal, signal orange used almost clinically. British taste seemed less interested in prettiness than in surface, polish, and visible engineering.
Anna loved it immediately.
Julien put her through the process methodically.
The thin black catsuit first, because it would show him the cut. Then a thicker muted teal one, slick against her skin and just resistant enough at the joints to make every movement seem already supervised. Then the orange one, more aggressively restrictive, which made her laugh softly behind the veil when she tried to bend and discovered how much of the decision had already been made for her by the material.
Julien’s eyes darkened in a way she recognized.
“That one later,” he said.
Anna lowered her gaze.
“Yes, Sir.”
They chose three in total, each for a different weather and visibility problem. Then came the real British refinements.
The tailor downstairs examined Anna’s existing corsets and proposed rail adaptations that could be fixed discreetly into them: attach points between the shoulder blades and at the small of the back, depending on outerwear and destination. He discussed them with Julien the way one might discuss luggage handles or boot soles.
Anna listened with growing fascination while locked to the small fitting dais with her hands arranged and her veils still in place.
This was what London seemed to do best. It took female dependence and moved it out of the realm of embarrassment. It treated it as a design category.
Wendy joined them midway through the fitting with a tray of tea, as if she had wandered in by chance and not because British hospitality required a competent woman to appear at exactly the useful moment.
“If you’re going to be out in weather,” she said, setting the tray down, “get the proper capes and don’t be silly about it. Tourists always try to compromise. Then their women end up cold, wet, or badly guided.”
Anna looked at her.
“Badly guided?”
Wendy nodded as if the phrase were entirely ordinary.
“Of course. Rain makes everyone hurry. That is when systems matter most.”
She tapped one of the lockable muffs with one gloved finger.
“These seem severe until you’ve crossed Regent Street in weather and realized your hands would only have been useless outside anyway.”
Anna adored her a little for saying it that way.
They left the boutique with capes, muffs, adapted corsets, and the first beginnings of an English wardrobe. By then the rain had thickened into a steady silver fall over the street outside.
Julien fastened her into one of the lighter setups before they went up: catsuit, walking skirt, fitted cape, veiled hat, and one of the muffs belted at her waist. He did it without hurry, right there in the private fitting space behind the shop, as if the process itself were part of introducing her properly to the city.
When he finished and stepped back, Anna could feel what had changed immediately.
Geneva had arranged her into correctness. London arranged her into managed weatherproof display.
She could walk. She could not hurry. She could see. She could not see widely. She could travel. She would not travel unassisted.
Julien looked her over once and then asked the only question that mattered.
“Well?”
Anna answered with a satisfaction so deep it almost felt like gratitude.
“It is practical in a way that admits exactly what it is.”
Wendy, who had been pretending not to watch, gave a small approving sound.
“Yes,” she said. “You’ve understood us already.”
That evening, after supper and after the rain had deepened the city into reflected gold and black outside their window, Anna stood beneath the ceiling rail in the suite and let Julien attach the newly adapted corset point into the indoor system just to feel how the house wanted her.
The connection was light, almost gentle.
The meaning of it was not.
She looked out over wet London and felt, not fear, but excitement sharpen into something calmer and more enduring. This city had not invented what she already was. It had simply externalized it, built it into walls, weather, clothing, and movement until dependence could travel openly as care.

title: Bitche (Amelie 2)
content:
Storycodes F/f, BDSM, D/s, Bondage, Gags, Blindfold, Sensory-deprivation, Caning, Spanking, Electro, Exhibitionism, Voyeurism, Humiliation, Chastity-belt, Petplay, Ownership, Praise/Degradation, Aftercare, Objectification, Collaring, TPE, Orgasm-from-pain, Heels, Obedience-training, Endurance, Consensual
A guided tour becomes surrender, training, and the moment Sonia chooses to belong Sonia’s first visit to the medieval citadel opens a door she never expected, when Amelie turns a simple tour into an intimate lesson in restraint and exposure that leaves Sonia shaken with desire. Drawn back to her, Sonia steps willingly into silence, darkness and strict control in Amelie’s private rooms, where the bite of the cane and the tenderness that follows teach her how deeply she wants to yield. At Amelie’s private gathering she becomes a living display of skill and obedience, held upright in elegant torment while guests witness her strength. Electricity, patience and pain pull her to a clarity she embraces without hesitation, and by morning the collar at her throat marks a truth she can no longer hide: she belongs, and she chooses to be kept.
EPUB# Read below, or click on the image for the EPUB download:
The Citadel# Sonia and her colleagues trailed Amelie through the winding corridors of the old citadel, surrounded by the cold, damp stone walls that seemed to breathe the shadows of history. The citadel in Bitche, burrowed deep into the rock, felt far from the castles they’d toured earlier that week. This place was no grand hall of royalty but a citadel designed to survive siege after siege, and as they descended further, Sonia could feel the air grow heavier.
As they entered a low-lit chamber, Amelie paused and gestured around. The room was packed with chains, stocks, and various iron restraints, all displayed with an eerie sort of pride. “This is one of the more… unique parts of our exhibit,” she explained with a smile. “Though it isn’t part of the original citadel, we’re hosting a collection of medieval restraint devices. Quite rare to see them all together like this.”
Sonia’s eyes widened as she took in the collection, her gaze landing on a particularly sinister-looking contraption that resembled an iron mask. It was heavy and primitive, with a jagged collar attached. Amelie noticed her staring and lifted the object, holding it up to the group.
“This, ladies, is a brank,” Amelie said. “Sometimes called a scold’s bridle. Used in certain cases to control unruly behavior. Care for a demonstration?” She glanced around the group, her gaze settling on Sonia.
Without waiting for an answer, Amelie positioned herself behind Sonia, holding the brank up to her face. The others watched with mixed reactions of intrigue and discomfort as Amelie carefully fit the front and back halves around Sonia’s head, snapping it shut with a click. The collar encircled her neck, its high metal rim holding her chin up, pressing slightly into her jawline. A cold metal tongue piece rested inside her mouth, keeping her tongue firmly in place.
Sonia’s eyes darted around the room, now limited in what she could see as the mask blocked most of her view. She could still hear Amelie’s voice, though the brank muffled it slightly.
“Not the most comfortable, is it?” Amelie’s voice held a light tone as she inspected Sonia. “It would’ve kept one quite obedient, I think. Speech was out of the question, and, well, movement was severely limited.”
Sonia tried to nod but found she couldn’t move her head more than an inch in any direction. She let out a muffled sound, earning a chuckle from one of her colleagues.
Amelie gave her a small pat on the shoulder, almost reassuringly. “Now, if you’ll follow me…” She took a step back, waiting for Sonia to shuffle along as best she could. With each awkward step, the collar dug slightly into her neck.
The tour group moved on, Sonia struggling to keep up, hindered by both the weight and restrictiveness of the brank. Amelie led them to a massive wooden contraption near the far wall, her eyes gleaming as she gestured towards it.
“This, ladies, are the stocks. Used to hold someone firmly in place, hands and head, so they couldn’t escape or resist,” Amelie explained.
Amelie took Sonia firmly by the arm and guided her toward the stocks, her fingers pressing gently but insistently into Sonia’s elbow. Sonia’s heart thumped as she looked down at the ancient wood, worn smooth from use. She hardly had a moment to take a breath before Amelie positioned her neck and arms into place, lowering the heavy top bar until it clicked shut with an unforgiving clank. Sonia’s arms were forced outward, shoulders straining, and the stocks held her body forward, her breasts exposed, hanging unprotected.
Then Amelie adjusted a T-shaped bar, positioning it firmly against Sonia’s pelvis, leaving her no choice but to tilt her hips back and press her legs apart. Amelie locked her ankles to each side of the bar’s base with iron manacles, the cold metal biting into her skin. The pose forced her into a stance that felt both unnatural and humiliatingly vulnerable. She tried to move, even shift her weight, but the stocks held her absolutely still.
Amelie stepped back, admiring her handiwork with a slight smile. “The stocks weren’t just for punishment. They were meant to humble someone, often an unruly woman,” she said with a glance back at the group of wide-eyed colleagues. “Like this, she couldn’t protect herself. She had to accept whatever happened next—anyone passing by could touch her, scold her, or worse.”
Sonia’s skin prickled as Amelie walked over to a large wooden bucket filled with slender, flexible hazel and willow canes, each soaked in water to keep them supple. She selected one, swishing it experimentally through the air, producing a fierce, hissing sound that made Sonia’s stomach twist. Amelie turned back toward the group, holding the cane in her hand with a casual expertise.
“These,” Amelie said, lifting the cane for everyone to see, “are nasty little things. They sting, they bruise, and, if used hard enough, they leave marks that last. People could step up and have their way with her, physically or otherwise. It was a kind of public justice, as well as a very clear message to others. This could be anyone, it could be you, if you stepped out of line.”
Sonia’s heart raced faster as the cane swished past her ear. She tried to look up, but the stocks and the stiff collar of the brak held her in place, offering only the limited view down. Her pulse pounded in her ears as she realized just how helpless she was. Mute, unable to move, exposed to everyone, she couldn’t prevent anything that might happen.
Despite her fear, another feeling crept up inside her, foreign and insistent. Her helplessness and vulnerability in this archaic device, her exposure, and the strict restraints made something in her pulse with strange excitement. Henry picked Sonia up just after noon in a shared electric car already packed with garment bags, cases, stands, and one flat black box she knew without asking contained things he did not want sliding around loose. The drive up toward the old villa above the Salève took less than an hour. They spoke little. Sonia was too aware of him beside her, of what they had agreed to, and of how much the quiet felt like preparation rather than awkwardness.
The villa was exactly the kind of place Henry would choose: ruined without collapsing, theatrical without needing decoration, expensive once and now surrendered to weather. Broken windows looked out over the lake. Vines climbed the stone as if the house had been waiting to be redressed by something patient.
Henry walked the grounds with her first. He showed her the overlook, the upper room with the broken balcony doors, the interior wall where afternoon light still struck cleanly, the marble column half strangled by growth near the garden edge. He did not explain every shot. He only let her see how he saw.
That was enough to make her nervous.
They carried the equipment in together. Henry worked with efficient concentration, checking light, placing cases where he would need them, laying garments out in the order he intended to use them. Sonia stood beside the open cases and watched midnight blue, deep green, black leather, polished metal, chain, and layered white petticoat emerge one after another into the old room.
“Still in?” he asked without looking up.
“Yes, Sir.”
He looked up then.
“Good.”
The first look was the midnight-blue gown from lunch, and it was less romantic in the hands than it had been in description. The silk was beautiful. The construction was merciless.
Henry told her to undress behind a screen in the adjoining room, then came in when she said she was ready. Sonia stood in stockings and underwear, arms folded across herself for half a second before she made herself lower them. She had agreed to be looked at. The least she could do was stop pretending otherwise.
Henry’s professionalism did not soften the exposure. It sharpened it.
He fastened the corset first, drawing her waist in slowly enough that she could adjust but not slowly enough to forget what he was doing. Then came the gown, the severe collar, the cuffs, the weight of the skirt distributing itself around her until her body no longer belonged to spontaneity. Every practical motion narrowed. Breathing changed. Turning changed. Standing itself became a managed posture.
“How bad?” he asked.
Sonia tested the new limits, then answered honestly.
“Strict enough to matter.”
“Good.”
She almost smiled.
At the overlook he positioned her between the vine-covered statue and the broken balustrade. The lake sat below in hard silver. Wind worried the outer layers of the dress but could not persuade the heavy structure to move far.
“Chin up.”
She obeyed.
“Eyes past me.”
She obeyed again.
“Do not pose for the camera. Let the dress pose you.”
That was the first instruction that got under her skin.
He was right. The gown did not need interpretation. It had already decided what kind of woman it wanted. Sonia only had to stop interrupting it.
Henry moved around her in arcs, camera rising and lowering, his voice reaching her between shutter clicks.
“Hold there.”
“Turn from the waist, not the shoulders.”
“Again.”
“Yes. Keep that.”
The rhythm became its own enclosure. Sonia had expected embarrassment. Instead what unsettled her was how quickly she began to value each correction. His direction made the posture intelligible. When she got it right, she knew before he said so only because the line of his silence changed.
Then he asked for the veil to come off.
The request landed harder than the corset had.
She unfastened it with gloved fingers and gave it to him. Cool air touched her mouth. Her face felt naked at once, not because strangers could see it but because Henry could. The gown still held her in conquered grandeur. Without the veil, the grandeur had to share space with her actual expression.
“There,” he said quietly, and lifted the camera again.
The exposed-face shots were the first point where the day changed for her.
She stopped acting regal and started being watched.
Henry came close only when he needed to adjust a shoulder seam or the angle of her wrist. Every time he stepped back, she felt the loss of him and hated that he could probably see it. He gave her no room to hide in performance.
“Do not harden your mouth.”
She had done exactly that.
“I’m not.”
“You are. Stop defending yourself from the lens.”
The correction was so accurate it stung.
She let the stiffness go. The next set of frames felt worse and better at once.
When they finished the first look, Henry showed her a handful of images on the camera screen. Sonia saw immediately what he had seen. Masked, veiled, or rigid, she had always assumed she could hide some private reserve from the world. In the photographs, the reserve was visible only as tension. The better images were the ones where she had stopped trying to keep that part of herself intact.
“You see it,” Henry said.
“Yes.”
“Then we can do the second look properly.”
The green brocade piece held her differently. It was less grand and more intimate in its cruelty. The sleeves drew her arms in and down, the hidden attachments turning simple elegance into managed helplessness. Henry dressed her into it in the upper room with the broken balcony doors while light came in through cracked glass and strips of ivy.
By then she trusted his hands.
That was new enough to frighten her.
He fastened the sleeve points one after another and stepped back to study the effect.
“Walk to the window.”
She did.
The gown allowed only a measured glide. The restraint did not merely reduce movement. It eroticized every reduced motion by making it visible. Sonia felt it with embarrassing clarity. She could not adjust the dress herself, could not free her own arms, could not even brush a strand of hair off her cheek when it came loose. Henry noticed, came over, and tucked it back into place with two fingers.
The touch was brief.
Her body answered it anyway.
“Stay with that,” he said.
She did not ask whether he meant the posture or the reaction.
He shot her against the broken doors, beside the interior wall, then in the center of the room where the ruined architecture and the bound sleeves did their work together without needing to be explained. At one point he told her to try to pull free once, not theatrically, just enough to show that the dress would not allow it.
She obeyed. The resistance failed almost before it began.
Heat moved through her in a low, humiliating wave.
Henry lowered the camera.
“Again,” he said, softer this time. “But do not act disappointed. Let yourself like that it holds.”
That instruction almost undid her.
She did as told.
When the shutter clicked after that, something in her attention dropped away. The room was not literally quieter, but less crowded. Henry’s voice stood out from everything else with impossible clarity. The vines at the window, the cold light, the pressure of the gown, the ache in her shoulders, all of it remained present and yet somehow less demanding than the next word from him.
He noticed before she did.
“Good,” he said. “Stay there.”
She stayed.
“Breathe.”
She breathed.
“Look at me.”
She did.
The world had not vanished. She had simply stopped needing to hold all of it at once.
By the time he undid the sleeves, Sonia was not gone exactly, but she was thinner at the edges. She stood while he unfastened her with the passive steadiness of a person who had handed some useful amount of herself to someone else and was not yet ready to take it back.
“Water,” he said, offering the bottle.
She drank because he had told her to.
That fact landed a few seconds later and made her flush under the corset.
The last look was the one he had warned her about.
He set the black box on a stone bench and opened it. Inside lay the leather hood, chains, cuffs, and a gag. The gag was clinical in its construction and intimate in its purpose, filling the inside of her mouth. It made dependence impossible to misunderstand.
Sonia looked at it for a long moment.
“You can still refuse this one,” Henry said.
She appreciated that he offered.
She hated that she wanted him to stop offering.
“No,” she said. “Do it properly.”
Something in his face settled at that.
He dressed her slowly: severe corset, high blouse, long skirt lifted and shaped by petticoats, then the harder pieces. The hood closed out the villa and left her in leather-scented dark with only filtered breath and the warmth of his hands to orient by. The gag under the hood. Once fixed, it changed the meaning of her mouth instantly. Then the chains, heavy enough that she could feel their decisions before he finished placing them.
It wasn’t really rough, but it was severe enough.
By the time he guided her to the marble column and secured the last length of chain, Sonia’s body had crossed from arousal into something cleaner and stranger. A submission too complete for performance. She could no longer maintain herself for an audience because there was no audience she could feel, only Henry and the structure he had built around her.
“Listen to me,” he said.
The words came through the hood as if they had been made for her alone.
“You are safe.”
The chain at her waist was adjusted.
“You are held.”
His hand checked the line of her shoulder.
“You do not need to manage anything now.”
That was the moment she dropped.
It was not symbolic or poetic. The effort of being Sonia Becker in full, continuous possession of herself simply ceased to be the most urgent task in the room. Henry’s voice took its place. The leather, the gag, the chain, the column at her back, the fixed set of her body inside the clothes, all of it pressed in until resistance stopped being a principle and became a waste of energy.
She gave it up.
The release was so deep it felt almost holy.
He photographed her for a long time after that. She knew because the shutter kept moving around her, because his steps changed positions, because now and then he touched her to alter the angle of her head or settle a chain more beautifully across the blouse. But those things happened at a distance from the place where she now floated. She followed instruction. She held still. She existed inside the shape he had chosen for her and found, to her own shock, that the state was not empty. It was peaceful. More than peaceful. Intimate in a way sex had almost never been for her because intimacy usually required too much negotiation.
Here there was only this:
be still
be held
be his for the frame
That last thought should have frightened her.
Instead it loosened something deeper.
