Sonia remembers# Sonia smiled softly as memories of her early days with Henry came back to her. She recalled the corrections, the intense training, and how her behavior gradually changed. Henry had guided her carefully, with each correction aimed at helping her improve. As she embraced submission, she realized it didn’t take away from who she was. This was striking, considering her progressive upbringing, where female submission was seen as betraying her “sisters.”
Growing up, Sonia had been taught to value autonomy and equality above everything else. Submission was viewed as weakness, something her family could never accept. But her time in Shanghai showed her a different side of herself. Working and training as a maid allowed her to let go of her ego, quiet her sense of self, and find joy in serving others. At first, she felt guilty and confused, worried that she was betraying the values she’d grown up with.
But with Henry, Sonia learned that submission didn’t make her less of a person. Instead, it was freeing to give herself fully to someone she trusted, someone who saw her submission as a gift, not a flaw. Henry’s guidance helped her understand that choosing to submit wasn’t a denial of her worth but a way of affirming it. Her submission didn’t diminish her—it enhanced who she was.
At GAIA, Sonia maintained a professional image. But at home, she became Henry’s maid, with no personal identity. She stopped referring to herself in the first person, even in her thoughts. She was just “this humble maid.” Her entire focus shifted to Henry—his needs, his desires. She found peace in shedding her individual identity and becoming fully absorbed in her role.
Balancing her public and private lives had been hard at first. After long days at GAIA, she would come home, change into her maid uniform, and try to leave “Sonia” behind. But with Henry’s firm guidance, she learned to make the transition smoother. “Your value is in your service. Be precise and disciplined; be the perfect maid. That’s what defines you,” he told her. His words resonated deeply, bringing her back to her time in Shanghai. Under his direction, she fell into those familiar habits with ease.
Sonia repeated Henry’s words like a mantra. Her service was her gift to him, and she gave herself completely. In doing so, she found her true self—a self hidden beneath her upbringing and education.
Henry accepted her gift gracefully, correcting her when needed and offering rewards sparingly. He used her fully but always stopped just short, the unyielding metal of her chastity belt remained a constant reminder of her unfulfilled desire, a silent echo of her commitment. Sometimes she regretted agreeing to wear it, but she knew she was bound by her promise, both by the belt and by her unfulfilled desire. It kept her from touching herself, and kept Henry out. Though the longing remained, she eventually understood that her own desires were unimportant. She was a maid, meant to serve, to fulfill the desires of her betters, and to bring them joy. It took months for her to fully grasp this lesson.
At night, Sonia repeated her mantras, just as she had in Shanghai—a thousand repetitions to make one truth. Her thoughts focused on Henry—his touch, his voice, his commands. She remembered the look in his eyes when she presented herself perfectly, and the rare smile of approval that made her heart swell with pride.
The chastity belt, once a source of discomfort, became a symbol of her commitment. Her gloved fingers traced its edges, feeling the cool, unbreakable metal that both protected and confined her. Its pressure against her skin provided a constant reminder of her devotion. The knowledge that she couldn’t touch herself, even if she wanted to, gave her a new sense of restraint, making her feel both safe and vulnerable.
As the weeks turned into months, Sonia found comfort in her routine. Her world narrowed to Henry, the villa, and her duties. Her work at GAIA became secondary, an interruption of her time as a maid, where she could fully lose herself in service. She found satisfaction in the simplicity of her tasks, in the structure of her role. The chastity belt became a badge of honor, symbolizing her dedication.
She learned to treasure moments of approval, rare rewards, and the sense of belonging she felt. Her own desires faded, replaced by the desire to serve Henry and make his life better. Her submission didn’t take away from her—it completed her. It made her Henry’s. In that, she found true fulfillment.
Sonia still had the vial Anna had made for her, the so-called “cure” for her incomplete infection. Anna had handed it to her with a simple message: “If you’re ready to accept the peace of the Changed, this will ‘fix’ you. Swallow it, and in two hours, you’ll be healed.”
Sonia kept the vial as a reminder of the path she could have chosen. But now, in her modest maid’s chamber next to Henry’s room, she realized she had found her own peace. She no longer needed the vial. She had found harmony within herself, discovering fulfillment and purpose in her submission to Henry.
The next day, Sonia met Anna at the Lakeside Café. Anna was dressed simply but stylishly—a flowing skirt, a tailored blouse, and a hijab covering her hair. They sat with their backs to the room, removed their masks, and donned veils that allowed them to share a coffee together. Anna’s eyes sparkled with curiosity.
Anna signed warmly. Sonia, it is so good to see you again.
Sonia signed back as she pulled out the small vial and placed it on the table. It is wonderful to see you too, Anna. Anna’s eyes widened.
Anna signed, clearly surprised. You still have it.
Sonia nodded. “I kept it, just in case. But I don’t need it anymore. The serum is probably too old to work, but even if it wasn’t, I don’t need it.”
Anna looked at her with understanding. “What changed?”
Sonia took a deep breath. “When you gave me the vial, I was lost. I didn’t know how to navigate this new world. But then Henry came into my life, and everything changed.”
Anna listened closely.
“Henry taught me to understand myself and embrace my nature. I thought submission made me weak, but he showed me it was the greatest gift I could offer. He guided me, corrected me, and helped me find my place in this world.”
Sonia’s signs became more confident. Eventually this one realized she had fixed herself. She found harmony within.
Anna took Sonia’s hand and squeezed it gently. “I’m so proud of you, Sonia. You’ve found your path, your peace.”
Tears welled up in Sonia’s eyes. “Thank you, Anna. You’ve always been there for me. I don’t need the vial anymore because I’ve found what I was looking for.”
Anna smiled, her eyes moist as well. “We’ve both found our places in this world. That’s something to celebrate.”
Sonia nodded, feeling deep gratitude and love for her friend. “Yes, we have. And I’m grateful for every step of the journey that brought us here.”
Sonia knew she had found her place, her purpose, and her peace. A deep sense of contentment settled within her.

At first it binds only her girlfriend Marion, whose devotion blooms into need, but soon the other relics stir—belts, bands, shackles, even towering heels. The Atlantean Slave Collar# The Dig# Sonia crouched by the edge of the trench, brushing sand off what looked like the base of a carved column. The Canary sun burned overhead, but she barely noticed. Her focus was on the intricate patterns emerging beneath her careful work—geometric shapes interspersed with flowing, almost organic lines. None of it matched anything she had seen in the textbooks. It wasn’t Roman or Phoenician. It wasn’t even the vaguely familiar motifs of indigenous Guanche culture.
“Hey, Sonia!” Her colleague, Nate, called from the other end of the dig. “You gotta see this.”
Reluctantly, Sonia set her brush down and stood, brushing dirt from her gloves. She adjusted the wide-brimmed straw hat tied under her chin. Crossing the uneven ground, she dodged around half-excavated walls and trenches. The site sprawled across the rugged hillside like a forgotten puzzle, half-buried under centuries of volcanic ash.
“What is it?” she asked as she reached Nate.
He pointed to a slab of stone they had uncovered the day before, now resting on a makeshift frame of wooden beams. It had been cleaned enough to reveal a series of carvings, arranged in rows and columns like a bizarre form of text. But it wasn’t the carvings that drew her attention—it was the inlay. Metallic streaks ran through the stone, glinting faintly in the sun, as if liquid metal had been poured into the grooves.
“Does that look… technological to you?” Nate asked, his voice laced with unease.
Sonia frowned, leaning in closer. The inlays formed a network of patterns that might have been decorative, but there was a symmetry to them that felt almost purposeful. She traced a gloved finger over the lines, the metal cool under the canvas. “I don’t know,” she admitted. “It’s too precise for something ornamental.”
“It gets weirder,” Nate said. He gestured toward another section of the site, where a group of workers was uncovering a set of wide, shallow steps leading down into the ground. “That’s the entrance to the main complex. Just got a glimpse inside—there’s something down there you should see.”
Sonia followed him, her boots crunching over the gritty soil. The staircase descended into shadow, flanked by walls carved with more of the strange patterns. Lanterns had already been set up below, their light flickering against the rough-hewn stone.
As they stepped into the chamber, Sonia’s breath caught. The air felt… different here. Heavy, almost oppressive, with a faint metallic tang that reminded her of storms. The room was circular, its walls lined with niches that held cracked and broken objects—ceramic bowls, glass vials, things that might once have been tools. At the center of the room stood a dais, its surface smooth and black, as if carved from obsidian.
“This,” Nate said, “is what I wanted you to see.”
He pointed to a panel set into the wall near the dais. Unlike the rest of the carvings, this panel was clean, almost pristine, its surface glowing faintly with a blue-green hue. It was divided into squares, each one etched with more of the strange symbols. As Sonia approached, she felt a faint hum beneath her feet, like the vibration of a running machine.
“This isn’t possible,” she murmured. “This has to be some kind of hoax.”
“Keep telling yourself that,” Nate said. “But if this is fake, it’s the most convincing one I’ve ever seen.”
Sonia reached out, hesitating before her fingers touched the glowing panel. The air around it seemed warmer, buzzing faintly against her skin. “If this is Atlantean…” she started, but the words died in her throat. If this was Atlantean, then everything they knew about ancient history was about to be turned upside down.
The glowing panel wasn’t the only thing drawing her attention. Around the edges of the dais were shallow depressions, arranged in a precise circle. They reminded her of something, though she couldn’t place what. Almost like… placements for standing or kneeling.
“What do you think this was for?” she asked, her voice low.
Nate shrugged, his unease evident in his expression. “Doesn’t feel like a temple, does it?”
“No,” Sonia agreed. “It doesn’t.”
Her gaze drifted to the carvings on the walls, the faintly glowing lines running like veins through the stone. The patterns seemed to shift subtly in the flickering light, as if alive. There was something here—something they didn’t understand yet. But it wasn’t worship, and it wasn’t art. Whatever this place had been, it had a purpose. And Sonia couldn’t shake the feeling that it wasn’t meant for anything benevolent.
The following day, Sonia crouched in the shade of the tarpaulin, brushing sand off another piece of metal that had emerged from the soil. The delicate curves and hollows of the object made it clear it was no random scrap—this was crafted. She tilted it in the sunlight, revealing a faint seam along one edge. It could have been a hinge, though it was so corroded that even calling it that felt speculative. The blackened surface glinted faintly under her brush, but any detail had been worn away by time and exposure.
The area she’d chosen to explore was set a little apart from the main excavation. The others were too focused on the inscriptions in proto-Linear A to pay much attention to her quiet work. She didn’t mind. She wasn’t a linguist. And if she was right about what she’d found, this could be just as significant.
Her tray was already filling with fragments—mostly round or half-round, with sharp edges and smooth curves that suggested some kind of intricate assembly. A few had empty sockets where stones might once have been set. She imagined them colorful and polished, though now they were as blackened as everything else.
Her brush stilled as she uncovered something different. It was larger than the others, split cleanly into two pieces. Unlike most of the fragments, this one had clearly once formed a complete unit. She tilted her head, fitting the two halves together in her mind. A collar, she realized. Or something like it. The curve was unmistakable.
Sonia’s lips tightened. A sense of unease prickled at the back of her neck. What kind of society used things like this? Jewelry? Restraints? Some hybrid of both? The designs were elaborate, but the purpose… She wasn’t ready to speculate yet.
She should document it. The team would want to see it—would need to see it. But as she stared at the pieces in her hand, a strange sense of possessiveness crept over her. This one was different. Intact, or nearly so. A single artifact she could hold in her hands. Something about it felt personal, almost intimate.
She glanced over her shoulder. Nate was still in the main dig site, debating with one of the linguists about the implications of the proto-Linear A inscriptions. The workers nearby were preoccupied with sifting through soil for smaller finds. No one was watching her.
Her gloved fingers slid the pieces into her satchel, tucking them carefully between layers of cloth to keep them from clinking. Her heart thudded against her ribs as she straightened up. It wasn’t like her to do this—she prided herself on her professionalism, her methodical approach. But this was different. She told herself it wasn’t theft. Not really. There were so many other fragments like it. This one didn’t even seem special.
Still, her hands trembled slightly as she turned back to her tray. She brushed more sand away, working more slowly now, her mind distracted. If someone found out… No. No one would find out. It was just a souvenir. Something to remember the dig by. Something to prove to herself, years from now, that she had been here.
When the time came to package the rest of her finds, Sonia worked with precision, cataloging each piece, noting every detail in her notebook. She even lingered a little longer over the fragments with empty sockets, their jewel settings blackened and unrecognizable. She recorded it all, as thoroughly as always.
Except for one.
The artifacts piled up day after day, each new discovery stranger than the last. Sonia sat cross-legged on the tarp-covered ground near her section of the dig, her gloves dusty as she examined the latest batch of finds. The pieces were baffling—everywhere she turned, she saw designs that were alien to anything she had studied before. The team had started calling them Atlantean as a shorthand, a placeholder for something they couldn’t yet define.
“This is insane,” muttered Carla, one of the field techs, holding up what looked like a small, delicate frame. It was made of metal, twisted into looping curves that seemed decorative but had clearly been shaped with purpose. “It’s like someone tried to combine a chastity belt with a circuit board.”
Sonia glanced over, suppressing a smile. Carla wasn’t entirely wrong. There was something bizarrely modern about the artifacts they were pulling out of the ground—an almost technological precision in the designs, though they were clearly ancient. They found arm bands that looked more like restraints, rings with mechanisms no one could figure out, and strange structures with grooves that might have been meant to lock something in place.
One of the strangest items was uncovered by Nate. He held it up triumphantly as Sonia approached, her curiosity piqued. The object resembled a collar, not unlike the fragments Sonia had found earlier, but this one was almost intact. It had a sleek, curved design, and inset into its surface were dull black stones. They looked like they might have been gemstones once, but now they were lifeless and opaque.
“Check this out,” Nate said, handing it over. “Doesn’t it look… I don’t know… too functional to be just jewelry?”
Sonia turned it over in her hands, her brow furrowing. The inside of the collar had faint ridges, almost like contact points. She ran her thumb over them, her gloved hand catching on something that might once have been a hinge. “It’s not just decorative,” she said finally. “This had a purpose. Something practical.”
“Or sinister,” Carla quipped, tossing a shard of glass into a labeled bag. “I mean, half of this stuff looks like it came from some kind of ancient BDSM dungeon.”
“You’re not wrong,” Nate said, crossing his arms. “There’s definitely a… theme here. Restraints, collars, these weird cuffs we found yesterday. And it’s all so… deliberate.”
“It doesn’t fit any of the cultures we know,” Sonia added. She set the collar down carefully and gestured toward the growing collection of artifacts. “The designs are too advanced for Mycenaean or Minoan, but the aesthetic isn’t like anything else. It’s almost—”
“Alien?” Nate offered, grinning.
Sonia rolled her eyes. “Not alien. Just different. These people—whoever they were—they weren’t like anyone else. They must have had a completely unique way of thinking. A different worldview.”
“Yeah, one where bondage chic was all the rage,” Carla said, smirking.
Sonia ignored her, though a faint unease prickled at the back of her mind. She had been trying to avoid thinking about the implications of the artifacts—the collars, the restraints, the way so many of the designs seemed to straddle the line between function and fetish. It was easier to focus on cataloging, documenting, analyzing. But the mystery was impossible to ignore.
As the dig progressed, more of the complex came into focus. They uncovered what appeared to be a market square, with rows of stalls marked by low stone walls. Many of the stalls had been buried under volcanic ash, their contents preserved in eerie detail. Sonia found herself staring at the remnants of what looked like display racks—metal and stone constructions that might once have held goods, or perhaps something more unsettling.
The temple itself revealed even stranger secrets. The carvings inside depicted scenes that were difficult to interpret—figures in elaborate headpieces surrounded by glowing objects, others kneeling or bound in strange devices. The designs were sensual, almost overtly sexual, but they also hinted at something else. Power. Control. Submission.
The team argued endlessly over the meaning of it all. Some thought it was a religious site, others a center for trade or governance. Sonia wasn’t sure. The artifacts didn’t just suggest utility—they suggested intent. Whoever these people were, they had a vision, a purpose. But it was a purpose that felt alien, even after all these centuries.
She couldn’t shake the feeling that the place wasn’t just about worship or trade. It was about control. But control of what—or who—remained a mystery.
Back at Home# Sonia sighed as she walked out of the airport into the crisp Parisian air, her carry-on slung over her shoulder and a heavy sense of relief settling over her. The two-month dig on the Canary Islands had been equal parts exhilarating and exhausting. The discoveries—the intricate carvings, the mysterious artifacts—had consumed her thoughts day and night, pulling her into a world long buried under volcanic ash. But now, standing on familiar ground, she realized how much she had missed home. And Marion.
The cab ride through the city was surreal. Paris’s familiar rhythm felt almost alien after the isolated, windswept island. The muted sounds of the dig—shovels scraping, the low hum of voices—had been replaced by the bustle of urban life. She had kept in touch with Marion, of course, but calls and texts weren’t the same. She missed her girlfriend’s warmth, her presence, the way Marion made the world feel solid even when Sonia was chasing mysteries older than history itself.
She set her suitcase down with a thud in the cramped entryway of the apartment, the air cool and faintly scented with Marion’s favorite lavender diffuser. The faint rustle of movement came from the kitchen, followed by Marion’s warm voice calling out, “You’re home! Finally!”
Sonia didn’t have time to reply before Marion appeared, her short curls slightly damp from a shower. She wore a simple black tank top and faded jeans, but the grin on her face was enough to make Sonia drop everything and wrap her arms around her. The kiss they shared was long, deep and slow, after the whirlwind of travel. Marion pulled back, her hands resting on Sonia’s waist.
“You look exhausted,” Marion said, brushing a strand of Sonia’s hair back under her still-dusty hat. “But you’re here, and that’s what matters.”
Sonia smiled, already feeling the weight of the dig slipping away. “I missed you. And I’m starving. What’s for dinner?”
“Something edible, I promise,” Marion said with a wink, leading Sonia into the tiny kitchen, swaying her back. “Sit down, and I’ll grab it.”
Dinner was simple—pasta with a light tomato sauce and a bottle of cheap red wine—but it was perfect. They sat at the small, wobbly table, catching up on the mundane details of life. Sonia filled Marion in on the dig, starting with the heat, the long hours, and the frustrating logistics. But as the wine flowed, her recounting turned to the more intriguing details.
“The artifacts were… bizarre,” Sonia said, swirling her glass of wine. “We’re calling them Atlantean, but they’re nothing like the Atlantis people imagine. No shiny domes or lost cities under the sea. Just strange, advanced designs that feel… wrong, somehow.”
“Wrong how?” Marion asked, her chin resting on her palm as she leaned forward.
Sonia’s lips quirked into a mischievous smile. “Well, take this theory of mine. Imagine a society—a really old one, five or six millennia back—that’s obsessed with control. Not just the kind of control you need to run a city or a religion. Personal control. Physical control. Over people.”
Marion raised an eyebrow, intrigued. “Like slavery?”
“Exactly,” Sonia said. “But not in the way we think of it today. Their artifacts, their designs… it’s like they were blending technology and ritual. Restraints that look ceremonial but are so precise they could have been functional. Collars with sockets for what might have been jewels—or something else entirely. It’s like a mix of high-tech and ancient BDSM.” She paused, grinning. “I’m telling you, the team was in denial. Too academic. Too vanilla. But you and I? It’s obvious.”
Marion laughed, the sound warm and unguarded. “You’re saying Atlantis was a bondage cult?”
Sonia shrugged, her grin widening. “Why not? If you look at the carvings, the structures—it all points to obsession. Control. Submission. They didn’t just rule; they owned. Bodies, minds, everything. It was their identity. And they made it beautiful, in a way.”
Marion leaned back in her chair, studying Sonia. “And what do you make of it? Really?”
Sonia hesitated, her fingers tracing the rim of her glass. “It’s fascinating. And unsettling. It’s like they were so advanced in some ways but so… regressive in others. But I can’t stop thinking about it. About what kind of people they were, how they lived. It’s haunting.”
After dinner, they moved to the couch, a cozy nest of mismatched cushions and throws. Marion poured them each another glass of wine while Sonia rummaged through her bag. She returned with the collar fragments, carefully wrapped in cloth. Unfolding them, she placed the pieces on the coffee table.
“These,” Sonia said, her voice quieter now, “are what I brought back. Probably shouldn’t have, but… I couldn’t resist.”
Marion picked up one of the fragments, her fingers brushing over the corroded surface. The blackened metal was smooth in some places, pitted in others, but the craftsmanship was undeniable. “This was a collar?” she asked, tilting the piece to see where it might fit with the other half.
Sonia nodded. “I’m almost sure of it. Look at the curve, the hinge. It’s not just decorative—it’s functional. A slave collar, I think. A sign of ownership and control.”
Marion’s lips curled into a smirk as she set the piece down. “And you thought this would make a good souvenir?”
Sonia laughed, leaning against her. “What can I say? It’s too fascinating to leave behind. And maybe a little sexy, in a dark, twisted kind of way.”
Marion wrapped an arm around Sonia’s shoulders, pressing a kiss to her temple. “Well, it’s definitely unique. And very you.”
They sat in silence for a moment, the fragments gleaming faintly in the lamplight, as if holding secrets they would never fully uncover.
The following days Sonia spent hunched over her workdesk at home, the evening light filtering through the lace curtain and casting soft shadows over her meticulous setup. The collar fragments rested in the center of the table, propped on a soft cloth. Next to them were her tools: fine brushes, a loupe, a small container of solvent, and tweezers. She worked with a steady hand, brushing away layers of petrified grime that had hidden the true nature of the material beneath.
As the grime came away, what emerged was breathtaking. The “metal” at the core of the collar wasn’t metal at all, or at least not any metal Sonia recognized. It was black and pristine, gleaming faintly in the light. Despite millennia of burial, the material showed no sign of damage. Its surface was impossibly smooth, as if untouched by time.
The jewels—if that’s what they were—were even stranger. They remained set firmly into the collar’s outer surface, their dull sheen giving way to hints of color as Sonia worked at them with a delicate pick. She was their ruler, their guide, their idol. The power she wielded was immense, intoxicating, and yet it came with an equally immense responsibility. These people weren’t just her slaves—they were her subjects, her charges, and they depended on her for direction, for structure, for meaning.
And this, Sonia felt, was the way forward. She’d not be an Atlantean Slaver, wielding power without consideration. She’d be a Queen, ruling over her subjects – her power just as absolute, but her rule entirely different, compassionate, merciful, and looking out for those that were hers.
Sonia took a deep breath, letting her hand fall to her side as she looked down at Marion. “Thank you,” she said softly.
Marion opened her eyes, her smile gentle. “For what, my Queen?”
“For being here,” Sonia replied. “For being you. And for teaching me.”
Marion’s smile widened. “Always,” she said simply.

title: Chapter 50: Intermission
Chapter 51: The Conference
content:
The Conference# The next morning, the group gathered for brunch at Henry’s place. Anna wore a 1950s flower-print dress with large petticoats, a cinched waist, and long sleeves. She had on short blue leather gloves and a matching headscarf, with a mask concealing her face, completing the vintage look. Sonia was dressed in a floor-length gray pencil skirt and a white blouse buttoned at the back. Her elbow-length leather gloves tucked under the cuffs, and she wore a straw hat pinned to her bun. She was masked as well. Mara, in her usual attire, had on a bonnet and a mask fixed to the collar of her iGuardian, keeping her head still. She wore a white blouse locked in the back, an Edwardian walking skirt in deep navy blue, and her usual ballet knee-boots under the Yoyah Sheengzoh.
The women, locked to their chairs, signed to each other while the men talked outside on the terrace, their conversation taking on a more serious tone.
Anna glanced around before signing to Mara. The leather of her tight gloves creaked softly. This one heard there was an attack during intermission. What happened?
Mara’s fingers moved gracefully. Yes. A group of Freeborn tried to free us. It was chaotic, but the Grenadiers stopped them quickly.
Sonia added, Apparently one woman noticed them beforehand. The women in the group were obviously underdressed and uncorseted, and the men behaved rudely. They tried to blend in, but badly. Because of the attack on Zendaya, she grew suspicious and called the police helpline. The Grenadiers were already on the way when it began.
Anna’s eyes widened with interest. That is fascinating. How did the Freeborn stay uninfected by something as contagious as LASS-VASH-2024? Why form a terrorist group only now, three years after the Change? And where did they get money for their equipment?
Mara’s fingers paused before she signed. This one will use her contacts. More information is needed. That group cannot be allowed to cause serious harm.
The women exchanged nods, understanding the seriousness of the situation. Mara’s vague response suggested she had ways of gathering information, and they would discuss it more once she had news.
The conversation then shifted to other topics.
Mara mentioned that she had received the agenda for the upcoming conference on viruses and pandemic control.
Sonia signed with curiosity. What is the conference focused on?
Mara signed. The conference will cover the medical and legal aspects of pandemic control. It is a major event for all of us. There will be sessions on antiviral development, vaccine distribution strategy, and the legal side of pandemic response.
Anna nodded. It sounds very informative. Who is speaking?
Mara’s hands showed a hint of amusement. One of the keynote speakers is Dr. Cheng, CEO of CBI. She turned to Anna. And did Anna know he is also CEO of Maylee Shufoo? This one found that out for Sonia a long time ago. He will speak on neuroactive viral disease and future pandemic preparedness. There are several other well-known experts from medicine and law as well.
Sonia’s hands froze mid-sign. She signed quickly, anxiously. Dr. Cheng? Are you sure?
Mara nodded, noticing Sonia’s reaction. Yes. Why? Is something wrong?
Sonia’s hands shook slightly as she signed. When this one met him in Shanghai three years ago… the situation was not favorable. From her signs, it was clear there was more to the story. Anna knew the details, but Mara did not, and Sonia wasn’t ready to share. It has been three years, but this one worries he might recognize her.
Anna reached over, gently touching Sonia’s arm to calm her. Sonia, that was a long time ago. Now you are masked or veiled, and even if he sees your bare face, he probably will not recognize you. You have changed, and so has the world.
Sonia took a deep breath, trying to steady her hands. This one knows. Still, the thought makes her nervous. He was involved… Her hands paused, then she started again. What if somehow he realizes who she is?
Mara’s eyes softened with understanding. Sonia has come a long way since then. Dr. Cheng may not remember her at all. Besides, we are going to the conference to learn and to make a difference. If she feels uncomfortable, she need not attend his session.
Sonia nodded, her fingers moving more slowly. Thank you, Mara. This one appreciates that. She will try to focus on the positive side of the conference.
Anna signed. Feeling nervous is normal, but we are in this together. We will support one another.
Later that week, the conference at the International Conference Center began with a quiet sense of anticipation. The venue, designed to accommodate thousands, had most of its space unused, except for a small section set up for the 200 attendees. The main auditorium had been thoughtfully divided: one half was arranged with locking fempads for unattended women, while the other half was set up for men and their wards. The seating was cleverly designed, allowing the chairs to convert easily from standard seats to secure women’s seats with locking arms and modified beds.
Anna, Sonia, and Mara arrived without their guardians. Philippe had programmed Mara’s iGuardian to guide her to the center and had set a geofence to keep her within the conference area. Dressed formally, Mara wore a sleek, dark navy suit with a high-collared blouse that locked at the back. The blouse, made from smooth, matte silk, had delicate lace detailing at the cuffs. Her long skirt fell just above her ballet boots, with a traditional Yoyah Sheengzoh underneath. She also wore matching leather gloves, and a tight bonnet held her mask securely in place, fixed to the collar of her iGuardian.
Sonia chose a more balanced look. She wore a fitted gray pencil skirt with a lavender blouse featuring puffed sleeves and a ruffled collar. Her light gray gloves matched her stylish mask, which had subtle embroidered patterns complementing her outfit. A matching headscarf kept her hair neatly tucked away.
Anna, opting for a more casual style, wore a pale blue dress with a flared skirt and short sleeves that covered her elbow-length gloves. The dress had a playful polka-dot pattern, giving it a relaxed “casual Friday” vibe. Her mask was simple and plain white, without any embellishments, and she wore a light summer hat pinned to her bun.
The three women made their way to the women’s section and locked themselves into the fempads. They felt the firm grip of the restraints as they settled into place, a reassuring pressure that anchored them in the midst of the growing crowd. The atmosphere was thick with anticipation, though the room was eerily silent, save for the soft clicking of heels and the rustling of fabric as other women took their places. The subdued murmur of male voices drifted from the other side of the room, adding to the quiet tension.
As the lights dimmed, Dr. Cheng stepped onto the stage, ready to deliver his keynote on neuroactive diseases. Sonia, already anxious, felt her heart race as she realized she was now locked into a fempad for a talk given by the very man she had been avoiding. The mask she wore, along with her complete coverage in Changed attire, meant there was little chance of being recognized, yet the anxiety gnawed at her. She had to consciously breathe deeply, forcing herself to stay calm, knowing there was no real danger, though the memories of Shanghai made it hard to relax.
Dr. Cheng began his lecture, titled “Neuroactive Parasites and Viruses: Common Pathways from Toxoplasma Gondii to Emerging Human Influences,” speaking with the calm authority of someone deeply knowledgeable in his field. Sonia and Anna, both familiar with the LASS-VASH-2024 virus, quickly noticed that Dr. Cheng was only scratching the surface of the virus’s true nature. For them, his presentation was interesting but lacked the depth they knew was possible. However, for most of the audience, his revelations were groundbreaking. He spoke about how a hypothetical virus could influence behavior, and the audience hung on every word.
As the lecture ended, the women were automatically released from their fempads, and they filed out in an orderly manner. The silence was only broken by the sound of their heels and the soft swish of their skirts. The stillness of the event was almost unnerving, with only the occasional murmur of male voices breaking through the quiet.
In the main hall, the space was divided again. The unattended women had their own section, where they could switch from masks to veils modestly for refreshments. Or, in Mara’s case, she had the option to be locked into a women’s chair with a feed bag if she wished to take a break. The wards accompanied by their guardians mingled in the other half, quietly discussing the topics of the day.
Sonia and Mara walked over to the refreshment bar, eyeing the options laid out on the table. Anna, unimpressed by the usual conference fare, stayed back, making a quiet joke about the poor quality of the coffee. Mara picked up a feed bag, reading the label with mild interest.
Suddenly, the kitchen door beside them burst open with a loud crash. A group of armed intruders, their strange breathing masks identifying them as Freeborn, stormed into the room: The door slammed into Mara with brutal force, hitting her body and face. The titanium shell of her iGuardian and her fixed mask absorbed most of the blow and protected her from harm, but the impact still knocked her off her feet. She lost her balance, and fell hard onto her back, her narrow skirt preventing her from getting up. She tried to turn her head to find Sonia, but her locked-on mask held her head rigid. She lay there, trapped and helpless, like an overturned bug unable to right itself.
Around her, muffled cries filled the air—panicked sounds from gagged women who couldn’t scream. The clicking of heels echoed as others tried to flee, their movements frantic and chaotic. Then, a gunshot rang out, loud and terrifying, freezing everyone in place. Mara felt a rough hand grab her, flipping her onto her stomach. She felt the cold edge of a knife scrape against the back of her iGuardian, followed by the harsh buzz of a taser.
A powerful shock jolted through her body, sent from her fried iGuardian through all electrodes at once. The pain was overwhelming, blurring her vision as she slipped into unconsciousness.
The intruders worked quickly, rounding up several Changed women, including Sonia and Mara. Within moments, they retreated, leaving behind a scene of chaos and fear. Sonia and Mara, along with the others, were gone, taken by the Freeborn, their fate uncertain.

title: Chapter 52: Out of the Shell
content:
Out of the Shell# Mara slowly opened her eyes, squinting against the harsh artificial light flooding the room. The brightness stung, piercing her eyes, which were unaccustomed to such intensity after so long in controlled environments. She instinctively closed them again as a wave of disorientation and pain washed over her.
Everything hurt.
Panic rose inside her as she realized how vulnerable she was. Her protective shell, the iGuardian that had encased her for years, was gone. Her mouth felt strangely empty, her face bare and exposed, with nothing to shield her from the world. Her hands, once always gloved, were now uncovered, as were her feet. With a jolt, she realized she was completely naked, covered only by a rough blanket that did little to protect her from the cold or the shame of her exposed state. She felt dirty, as if something essential had been stripped away.
A rough, cracking sound escaped her throat as she tried to speak, but her vocal cords, unused for years, failed her. The sound was more a groan than a word, raw and primal. Whoever had done this had removed her iGuardian and everything else that had defined her existence, leaving her in a strange, cold bed. Her body betrayed her further, leaking uncontrollably now that the inserts that had regulated her were gone. The muscles that had once held her in perfect posture now screamed in agony, unable to perform even the simplest tasks without the support they had grown used to.
Through the haze of pain and fear, she heard a voice—Sonia’s voice, soft and close.
“Mara, are you awake?” Sonia’s voice was barely above a whisper, sending a shiver through Mara. Sonia, too, must have been unmasked, vulnerable like Mara.
Mara managed a low, guttural moan in response, the sound rough and barely intelligible. She couldn’t move much, every attempt to do so sending sharp pains through her body. But she was used to pain; it had been a constant companion in her life, and now it served as a motivator. She began to systematically test her body, trying to regain some control. Fingers twitched, arms moved slightly, and her legs responded sluggishly. Every motion was a struggle, but she pushed through it, forcing her body to obey her will.
Slowly, with immense effort, Mara tried to lift her upper body, using her weakened arms to prop herself up. The world around her swam in and out of focus, but she was determined to see where she was. She looked around, taking in her surroundings: a shiny, new army cot beneath her, stark and cold. The room was a featureless concrete box, with no windows, just a single metal door, and two harsh fluorescent lights buzzing above.
Sonia knelt beside her, her presence both comforting and unsettling. Sonia was dressed in a bathrobe, her face bare and vulnerable, her hands and feet exposed as well. Her hair was pulled back into a makeshift braid, a far cry from the elegant styles she usually wore. In her hands, Sonia held another bathrobe, clearly meant for Mara.
“We’ve been kidnapped,” Sonia said quietly, her voice steady but laced with fear. There was no need for further explanation; the stark reality was all too clear.
With painstaking care, Mara tried to sit up, her body trembling from the effort. Every muscle protested, but she fought through the pain, her determination stronger than the agony she felt. She needed to understand what had happened, where they were, and how they could possibly escape this nightmare. The rough texture of the army cot pressed into her skin as she pushed herself upright, her body shaking with the exertion.
Sonia moved closer, ready to help if needed, but also aware of Mara’s fierce independence. Mara managed to sit, her breath coming in shallow gasps. The pain was overwhelming, but she refused to give in to it. Her head drooped, her neck muscles too weak to hold it upright. Her back ached with every breath, the absence of her supportive shell making every movement a struggle. Sonia moved quickly to help, guiding Mara with gentle hands toward the metal toilet mounted against the side of their cell. Mara could barely walk, her feet refusing to flatten after years spent in an en-pointe position, her body refusing to cooperate with even the simplest actions.
When they reached the toilet, Mara collapsed onto it, all pretense of dignity gone. She felt utterly exposed and helpless, her body betraying her as she fought to regain control over her leaking bowels. The effort was agonizing, each movement sending fresh waves of pain through her already weakened muscles. Sitting there, she tried to clean herself as best she could, the rough washcloths and cold water a poor substitute for the cleanliness she was used to. But she couldn’t stand, so she did everything from where she sat, her mind reeling from the indignity of it all.
Sonia, also struggling with her own weakened body, handed Mara a bathrobe. Mara accepted it gratefully, covering her bare, vulnerable body with the soft fabric. It was the first bit of comfort she’d felt since waking up in this nightmare, and she couldn’t stop the tears that began to fall silently down her cheeks. She had been stripped of everything that made her feel safe, and now she was left with nothing but pain and despair.
A small flap in the metal door opened with a harsh clang, and a steel tray was pushed into the room. On it was a simple meal and a bottle of water for each of them. The sight of solid food filled Mara with dread. She had lived on liquid nourishment for so long that the idea of chewing and swallowing real food was almost alien to her. The smells, the textures—everything was overwhelming, and she felt a wave of nausea rise up as she forced herself to take a bite. She gagged, barely able to keep the food down, and stayed close to the toilet in case she lost the battle.
Along with the meal, there were fresh linens for the cots. Sonia, moving with the same cautious steps as Mara, managed to change the bedding. The task took longer than it should have, both women struggling with their weakened bodies. But eventually, Sonia succeeded, making the beds as comfortable as possible in the cold, sterile room.
Mara’s stomach revolted against the unfamiliar food, and she spent what felt like hours on the toilet, her body purging itself violently. Sonia stayed by her side, offering comfort where she could, even as Mara managed to whisper a few strained words that were a poor imitation of speech. Her hair hung in greasy strands down to her waist, but she was too weak to care for it, too weak to even leave the toilet. Sonia moved Mara’s cot closer so she could rest within reach of the toilet in case of another emergency.
That night was unbearable. Exhaustion weighed heavily on Mara, but sleep was out of reach. Pain pulsed through every inch of her body, and each movement reminded her of her weakness. Despite it all, she forced herself to keep going, to push through the agony. She did simple exercises, flexing her fingers, toes, and limbs, trying to regain some strength. She took small bites of food, determined to keep something down, to give her body the energy it desperately needed.
The days blurred together in a fog of pain, sleep, and boredom. Time lost meaning as Mara struggled to adjust to her new, terrifying reality. At some point, Sonia made a ruckus, shouting at their unseen captors through the door, demanding assistance, clothing, and shoes. Her voice echoed in the small, featureless cell, filled with frustration and desperation. She explained that they couldn’t walk properly without some kind of heel, emphasizing their physical limitations. For days, they had been left with little more than the bare essentials for survival, and their situation was becoming unbearable.
To their surprise, food continued to arrive regularly, pushed through the flap in the door. After one particularly loud outburst from Sonia, something else was delivered. The next tray included two bright orange ballet leotards and a pair of medium-heeled pumps for each of them. The shoes weren’t a perfect fit, but they were better than going barefoot. Despite the pain, Mara’s memory of her ballet training pushed her forward. She put on the leotard and shoes, feeling the unfamiliar fabric against her skin, and forced herself to move. The pain was intense, every step a reminder of how weak she had become. Her shortened tendons protested, and the weight of her body on unfamiliar points in her feet was excruciating. But she pressed on, determined to regain some control over her body.
The food, though still unappealing, became easier to tolerate. Mara forced herself to eat her share and keep it down, knowing she needed the strength. Each day, she pushed herself a little harder, trying to rebuild the endurance she had once taken for granted.
Mara trained her voice, which she had not used for several years. She pushed herself to move from a whisper to modulated, if quiet, speech, even though she hated every second of it. She supplemented her speech with hand-dancing the way little girls do before receiving their first mask, using the familiar motions to convey the nuances and emotions that her voice couldn’t carry. Sonia supported her through it all, sensing how close Mara was to breaking under the weight of her trauma. She knew that Mara needed to feel some semblance of control, and speaking was one way to reclaim that.
While exploring the cell early on, Sonia and Mara found a pile of objects in the corner, covered by a rough blanket. Beneath it, they discovered the broken remains of Mara’s iGuardian, Sonia’s chastity belt, and the shredded remains of the clothing they had worn to the conference. Mara did not understand why their unseen captors left the pieces here with them. In a hoarse, barely understandable voice, and at the same time with clumsy, half-remembered hand-dancing, she asked Sonia, “Are they trying to mock us with that? It’s depressing, seeing my iGuardian destroyed. I feel so exposed and helpless.” The device had been her shield, her prison, and now it lay in ruins before her.
As they sifted through the debris of their past lives, Sonia found some salvageable electronics and batteries among the wreckage of Mara’s iGuardian. With quiet determination, she began to wire something together, working with whatever scraps she could find. Mara watched her with disbelief, clinging to the idea that Sonia might be able to get them out of this nightmare.
At night, when the harsh fluorescent lights finally dimmed, Sonia put her plan into action. Using the makeshift tools she had fashioned from the remnants of their gear, she tampered with the electronic lock on their cell door. The process was slow and nerve-wracking, every small sound amplified in the stillness of the night. The final piece, a shard of titanium from Mara’s vaginal shield, proved to be the key. With a quiet click, the door’s lock disengaged.
Dressed in their tattered white bathrobes, bright orange leotards, and ill-fitting heels, the two women slipped out of their cell and into the concrete hallway beyond. The corridor was silent, cold, and unforgiving, but it was a form of freedom.
Sonia hadn’t really expected them to make it out. Her main goal was to get as close to the open sky as possible, just in case they could send out a signal. Tucked away in the pocket of her bathrobe was the GPS transmitter from Mara’s iGuardian, now wired to some salvaged batteries. The small device was put together in a makeshift way, and its “GPS lock” LED blinked with a slow red pulse, indicating it had no idea where it was, while the “net” LED flashed similarly, unable to connect to any base station to update its location.
With their hard heels clicking on the concrete, the women moved as quietly as they could through the maze of corridors, passing several numbered metal doors identical to their own cell. The dim lighting made the space feel even more oppressive, and every sound seemed to echo in the silence.
At the end of the corridor, a metal-barred door blocked their way to a set of concrete stairs leading upwards. Sonia crouched down and started working on the lock with her improvised titanium tool, her breath slow and steady as she concentrated. Mara, meanwhile, explored the small area around them, her eyes scanning for anything that might help.
In a nearby guard room, she found a desk and a cot. Her hands felt along the underside of the desk, searching the drawers and crevices for anything hidden. When she reached up to the underside of the second-lowest drawer, her fingers brushed against something sticky—tape. She carefully peeled it back and found a key attached. With a small, silent gasp of excitement, she slipped it free and hurried back to Sonia, holding it out to her with a hopeful look.
Sonia took the key with a silent nod and inserted it into the lock. The metal door swung open with a quiet creak, and the two women slowly ascended the stairs, each step taking them closer to the unknown.
At the top of the stairs, they found a final door, unlocked. When they pushed it open, they were met with the cold, crisp air of the high Alps. The night sky stretched above them, the stars glimmering like scattered diamonds. They were standing in the inner yard of a lone mountain farmstead, far from any sign of civilization. The chill wind bit at their skin, and they huddled closer together, their thin bathrobes and leotards offering little protection from the cold.
Mara asked with her hands in the cold air, What now? We cannot stay here.
Sonia didn’t answer right away. She focused on the LEDs on the GPS device, hoping they would turn green. One by one, the red blinking lights shifted to a steady green, signaling that the device had finally locked onto their position and connected to a network.
Sonia pointed at the LEDs with a small smile, and Mara’s face lit up with relief. She clapped her hands softly, her excitement muted but genuine. They had done it. The signal was out.
But Sonia knew they couldn’t stay. The bitter cold was seeping into their bones, and their thin clothes offered no protection against the alpine night. “Let’s go back,” she whispered. “If we’re lucky, they haven’t noticed we’ve been out. It’s time for our guardians and the grenadiers to take care of us.”
Mara nodded, understanding that they weren’t meant to be the heroes in this story, but literally the damsels in distress. Slowly, they retraced their steps, locking the doors behind them. Mara carefully taped the key back to its hiding place, ensuring nothing was out of place.
Finally, they slipped back into their cell, the concrete walls feeling even more suffocating after their brief taste of freedom. They crept into their hard cots, the cold metal pressing against their skin, and waited in the dark, hoping help would arrive soon.
The rescue was swift and chaotic. Down in their concrete cell, Mara and Sonia listened to the sounds above: the thrum of helicopters, the sharp crack of gunshots, the shouts of men, and the deep, resonating boom of an explosion. The very walls that had imprisoned them now served as a bunker, shielding them from the battle raging above.
Heavy footsteps echoed through the corridor, followed by the shouts of soldiers. “Secured!” “Two here!” “One injured!” The clanging of doors, the sound of crying—it was a chaotic symphony of liberation. Finally, their cell door swung open, and heavily armored grenadiers stormed in. “Secured!” one shouted, and another took stock of the room, “Two more! Uninjured!”
After the grenadiers, medics entered, carrying supplies. Their faces were focused as they moved to care for Sonia and Mara. Mara, too exhausted and overwhelmed to fully process what was happening, was secured to a stretcher and injected with a sedative that quickly dulled her senses.
Her next memory was soft and familiar—lying in her bed at home. The warmth of the blanket, the gentle comfort of the bed—it all felt almost unreal. She was unbound, still naked under the blanket, but there was no cold, no harshness. As her eyes adjusted to the dim light of the room, she saw Philippe sitting beside her, looking exhausted and worn.
Before she could fully wake up, Philippe was at her side, cradling her in his arms. His embrace was firm and desperate, as though he feared letting go might cause her to vanish. Mara felt the trembling in his body, the raw emotion he had been holding back.
They both began to cry, overwhelmed by sadness, relief, fear, and trauma. Mara felt the tightness in her chest loosen just a bit, knowing she was safe, that Philippe was there. The physical pain of the past few days melted away, leaving only the rawness of her emotions.
“I’m here, Mara,” Philippe whispered through his tears. “You’re safe now. You’re home.”
Mara clung to him, her voice still weak but filled with the same depth of emotion. “Philippe, I was so scared. I—”
“Shh,” he soothed, holding her close. “You’re safe. Sonia is safe. Anna wasn’t kidnapped, she escaped with a few scratches. I’m here. I’ll stay with you. We’ll get through this together.”
Mara cuddled into Philippe’s arms, her body still trembling from the overwhelming emotions. She knew she needed to tell him everything, but the words felt foreign on her tongue after so long. “The attack… it happened so fast,” she began, her voice hoarse and barely above a whisper. “One moment I was looking at the feed bag, the next… the door just slammed into me. It was… violent. But the iGuardian, the mask… they protected me from the worst of it.”
She paused, her hands moving with a different rhythm, one that spoke of fear and vulnerability. “But then… when I woke up… I was without my shell, Philippe. I was completely vulnerable. I could feel… everything. My skin, the air, the rough blanket against me. It was too much. I felt… exposed, like I was nothing.”
Philippe’s grip tightened around her, offering silent support as she continued.
“I felt filthy,” she said, her voice cracking as she forced the words out. “The belt… it always kept me clean. I never had to worry about anything like that. But there, without it… I was leaking, I couldn’t control my body… it was disgusting.”
Her hands danced, mirroring the depth of her shame and helplessness. “I felt so dirty, so… lost. I couldn’t even stand properly. My neck, my back… they hurt so much without the support. I couldn’t even hold my head up. I felt… broken.”
She took a shaky breath, trying to steady herself as she moved on to the next part. “And the food… I couldn’t stand it. The feed bags are so smooth, so easy. But this… this was raw, intense. The tastes were overwhelming. I almost couldn’t keep it down. It was like… like I was being forced to go back to something primitive, something… uncivilized.”
Her hands stilled, and she looked up at Philippe, her eyes pleading. “I need the belt, Philippe. I can’t… I don’t want to be without it. I need that shell, that protection. I want to be… civilized again. Please.”
Philippe gently stroked her hair, his voice soft but firm. “We’ll get you back into an iGuardian, Mara. I promise. You won’t have to go through that again. You’re safe now, and I’ll make sure you’re cared for.”
Mara nodded, her hands expressing her relief. “Thank you, Philippe. I just… I want to feel whole again.”
Philippe kissed her forehead, holding her close as they both began to calm.

title: Chapter 53: Whole again
content:
Whole again# Philippe took Mara to the fitting room. Unlike her first fitting three years ago, when she had felt dread, this time she was filled with anticipation. The old passive belt she wore on the way there felt like a relic, a temporary substitute for the real thing. She was dressed in proper clothing again—a soft blouse, a skirt. Underneath, her corset, a Yoyah Sheengzoh and her ballet boots shaped and held her. She was masked and felt comforted by the gag that filled her mouth, but it was the thought of what awaited her that gave her a sense of relief.
The technician began the fitting with practiced skill, guiding Mara through a new 3D scan to update her measurements. The new iGuardian Pro Secure model was sleek, a significant upgrade from the one Mara had worn for years. The hip belt was secured first, circling her waist with a snugness that reassured her. As the inserts settled into place and the crotch strap was fastened, she felt a familiar sense of control returning. When the corset was tightened around her torso, its cups holding her firmly, the tension in her back began to ease. The pull of the shoulder braces and the neck corset corrected her posture, forcing her into the disciplined stance she had known for so long. It was a comfort, a return to something she could rely on.
As the belt activated, tightening to its daytime setting, Mara felt its embrace fully. The structure and discipline that had shaped her life for the last few years were back. The sensors and electrodes began their test patterns, and the belt came alive against her skin. She welcomed the subtle impulses, the ones she hadn’t even realized she missed until they were gone. The barely noticeable pulse in her neck corset that always pointed north—she was no longer feeling lost. The rhythmic signal from the hip belt that told her the direction and distance of Philippe’s cellphone—she was no longer feeling lonely.
The test patterns from the scheduler and guidance mode ran through the belt and her system, each one a reminder of the order that had been missing from her life. Even the sharp pain from the calibration impulses of discipline mode was welcome to her. As the subtle, almost subconscious, reward impulses between her legs activated, the dread and depression that had weighed on her since her kidnapping began to lift. The iGuardian had used these subtle rewards and their withdrawal to guide her behavior, creating a system of discipline that kept her in line long before any overt correction was necessary. Being without it had left her in a state of constant anxiety and slight depression, making her feel as if she was doing something wrong. But now she could finally feel joy again, knowing she was back where she belonged.
Philippe moved closer, fitting her new mask with the care of someone who knew how much this meant to her. The mask, custom-made from the fresh 3D scan, fit perfectly. Angelique# Chapter 1: A Dinner in Ibiza# Angelique checked into the Nobu Hotel Ibiza Bay, just a short drive from the Marina. As she entered her suite, the view of the ocean caught her attention, and she took a moment to unwind after her flight. Then, eager to make the right impression, she chose a bold outfit—a tailored, off-the-shoulder navy dress that hugged her frame and heels with enough height to give her that extra boost of confidence. She added a sleek red lipstick, a subtle nod to her signature look, and a few gold bracelets that caught the light as she moved. It was her way of blending business with just enough flirtation to keep things interesting.
Downstairs in the hotel’s restaurant, she spotted Olivier at a table near the terrace. He looked as reserved as ever in a black blazer, quietly elegant, but there was a hint of surprise in his expression as he saw her approach. Seated beside him was a tall, tanned man with sandy blonde hair, whose relaxed posture hinted at years spent on deck rather than at a desk. Opposite them was a woman with dark, glossy hair and a piercing gaze, already deep in conversation with Olivier.
Olivier stood to greet her, extending a hand with his usual understated charm. “Angelique, welcome to Ibiza. I’d like you to meet my friends. This is Marc Delacroix, the man behind our little gadget venture,” he nodded toward the blonde man, who gave her an easy smile. “And Elise Dubois,” Olivier continued, “she’s writing a feature on Marc’s VC business for The Economist.”
“Pleasure to meet you,” Angelique said, her green eyes sparkling with curiosity as she glanced at Elise, who greeted her warmly.
Dinner began, and soon the conversation flowed as naturally as the wine. Marc leaned forward, eyes twinkling as he explained the gadget: a rugged, solar-powered satellite hotspot designed for sailors, climbers, and travelers who needed to stay connected off the grid. “It’s called the WaveLink,” Marc said, with a faint trace of pride. “Gives you a lifeline anywhere on earth, or at least anywhere with a view of the sky. Angelique, it’s the kind of tech that would do well on your channel.”
Elise chimed in with a laugh, “Well, Marc here would know. He’s had his fair share of off-grid adventures—though not all of them went smoothly. Tell her about your trip to Madagascar, Marc.”
Marc’s face split into a grin. “Ah, that one.” He chuckled, leaning back in his chair. “It was a year ago. I decided to explore the northern coast with a local fishing crew, no fancy tech, no back-up plans, just good old-fashioned seafaring.” He paused, glancing at Olivier with a playful glint. “Let’s just say the boat wasn’t exactly seaworthy. We ended up stranded on a sandbank for two days. No radio, no cell signal. When we finally got rescued, I promised myself I’d never sail without the right tech again.”
Everyone laughed, and Angelique found herself glancing across the table at Elise, who was clearly enjoying the story. Elise then shared one of her own—a harrowing encounter during her time reporting in Beirut.
“It was a tense week,” Elise began, eyes darkening. “I was doing a series on young activists. Just when I thought I was safe, the local police decided otherwise.” She paused, flashing a self-deprecating smile. “They dragged me to the station for ‘questioning,’ convinced I was stirring up trouble. A colleague managed to get the French embassy on the line, but those were some of the longest hours of my life. After that, I learned to tread more carefully.”
Angelique’s respect for Elise deepened as she listened, admiring the other woman’s resilience. “You’re braver than I am,” she murmured, catching Elise’s eye. Elise shrugged, a playful smile returning to her lips.
“And you’re smarter than me, building an entire brand on your own,” Elise replied, tilting her head thoughtfully. “You’ll make this WaveLink look amazing, I can already tell.”
As the conversation wound down over a final glass of wine, Marc leaned forward, his eyes gleaming with that unmistakable spark of adventure.
“You know,” he said, swirling his glass thoughtfully, “the Mediterranean is stunning this time of year, especially on a good boat. Why don’t we take Epicurean out for a sail? Chart a course to Málaga, make a week of it. The weather’s ideal; still warm, but not scorching. And the water is perfect for a swim or two.”
Elise’s eyes lit up. “That sounds incredible,” she agreed, leaning back in her chair with a smile. “I could use a week away from deadlines.”
Angelique’s gaze flicked to Olivier, curious to see his reaction. He held her glance, then looked to Marc with a nod of approval. “Not a bad idea,” he agreed, then turned back to Angelique with a subtle grin. “And I think Angelique would make an excellent addition to our crew. What do you say?”
Her lips curled into a teasing smile. “Well, I can’t say I’ve spent much time sailing, but I’m not one to turn down an adventure. Besides,” she added, arching an eyebrow at Marc, “someone needs to make sure you don’t strand us on a sandbank again.”
Marc let out a hearty laugh, raising his glass to her. “Touché. I promise, this time I’ll have the tech covered. Epicurean has everything we need—navigation equipment, comfortable cabins, and all the essentials. Plus, we’ll stop along the way. Good food, good company.” He grinned, raising his glass to them. “To our journey.”
They clinked glasses, each of them caught up in the excitement of it. As the evening wore on, Angelique felt Olivier’s gaze linger on her now and then, though he seemed content to let the moment breathe without pressing forward. There was energy in the air, an unspoken understanding that they’d soon have all the time and space they’d need aboard the Epicurean.
Once they returned to their rooms, Angelique felt the thrill of anticipation bubbling beneath the surface. She could already picture it—the gentle rocking of the boat, the sparkle of sunlight on the water, the nights spent under starlit skies. And then, the thrill of knowing she’d be in close quarters with Olivier for a week.
Chapter 2: A Departure from Ibiza# The next morning, Angelique arrived at Marina Ibiza, her excitement barely contained as she spotted the Epicurean moored and waiting. Marc was already there, overseeing the final checks and talking to a marina attendant. Elise arrived just behind Angelique, her expression as eager as Angelique’s, and Olivier soon joined, casting a subtle smile her way as he approached.
Once they were all on board, Marc handled the lease paperwork, then turned to his makeshift crew with a grin. “Alright, welcome aboard the Epicurean,” he announced, spreading his arms as if to present the boat in all its glory. “She’s a Beneteau Oceanis 55, a beauty with enough room for us to be comfortable and plenty of power to get us to Málaga. Now, quick orientation so you don’t lose your way in the first hour.”
He led them through the deck and interior, showing them the cockpit, the galley, and the seating area, then down to the cabins. “Two cabins in the back,” he gestured toward the stern, where Elise and he would be staying, “and the two forward cabins for Olivier and Angelique.”
Angelique noted the spaciousness of her cabin, surprised at how the boat managed to blend luxury with functionality. It was smaller than any hotel suite she’d ever stayed in, but there was a coziness to it, an inviting sense of adventure. She shared a knowing glance with Olivier, who seemed equally intrigued.
Before they could settle in, Marc’s voice called them back to the deck. “All right, team, we’ve got supplies here for two weeks—plenty of water, food, and, of course, a respectable stash of wine.” They chuckled as a marina crew began unloading crates and boxes. Together, they formed a line to stow everything efficiently, filling the galley and storage spaces with enough provisions to keep them well-fed and hydrated.
When the last of the supplies were packed away, Marc gathered everyone around for a safety rundown. His usual easygoing manner had sharpened with purpose. “Listen up. Everyone’s a captain in fair weather,” he said, his tone steady but serious, “but here’s what you need to know to make sure we’re all safe if things get rough.”
He went over essential protocols: how to work the life jackets, operate the emergency radio, and the importance of keeping a cool head. “If anything happens,” he said, looking each of them in the eye, “we’ll handle it together. But everyone needs to know the basics.”
Angelique found herself listening intently. While she didn’t imagine they’d encounter anything too dangerous, Marc’s words carried weight. A few minutes later, he gave her shoulder a reassuring pat, as if sensing her thoughts.
By two in the afternoon, they were ready to set off. As the lines were cast and Marc guided the boat out of the marina, the sea stretched out before them, wide and welcoming. The October sun cast a soft glow on the waves, and the Epicurean moved forward smoothly, leaving the marina behind as they began their journey.
With a steady, moderate wind pushing them forward, Marc calculated that the journey to Cartagena could take about two days if they kept a relaxed pace, aiming to cover roughly 80 nautical miles each day. At this rate, they’d arrive late on the second day or early the next morning, giving everyone time to settle into the rhythm of sailing.
After clearing the marina, Marc turned to the crew. “Alright, let’s get the sails up. I’ll keep the engine running at low speed for rudder control, but I want everyone to get a feel for the process. Ready?”
They moved into position, and soon it was clear that the teamwork needed some polishing. Lines tangled, hands slipped, and the mainsail caught awkwardly. Marc shook his head with a wry grin, signaling them to bring everything down. “Again,” he called, encouraging them, insistent that they work together as a team.
On the second attempt, the process went smoother, with each of them more aware of their timing and positioning. The sails caught the wind gracefully, the mainsail filling and the foresail billowing. Satisfied, Marc nodded, though he wasn’t quite finished yet.
“Now, let’s try putting in a couple of reefs on the foresail,” he said, demonstrating how they’d reduce sail in stronger winds. He took them through the steps with patience, showing them where to handle the sheets and where to keep clear of the boom.
He then gave them a taste of maneuvering, tacking and jibing to get them accustomed to the motion of the boat and the swing of the boom. “Remember,” he said, pointing to the mainsail boom, “keep your heads down and be aware of where it’s headed. This thing doesn’t care if you’re watching.”
Finally, with everyone looking a little more confident, Marc adjusted their heading to Cartagena. The sails filled just right, and he cut the engine, letting the wind take over. The quiet hum of the boat against the waves settled in, a calming rhythm.
“Since we’ll be sailing through the night,” Marc began, glancing between Olivier and Angelique, “Elise and I will take the helm until one. Then you two are up. Olivier, if anything feels off—anything—wake me. I don’t expect trouble, but it’s better to be sure.”
Olivier gave a quick nod, and Angelique caught his eye with her apprehension. This was far from her typical environment, but the prospect of taking the helm under the stars sent a thrill through her. Elise squeezed her arm reassuringly. “You’ll get the hang of it,” she said with a warm smile.
As the afternoon stretched on, the Epicurean glided smoothly, the sun lowering over the horizon and the Mediterranean sparkling around them.
The hours on the water introduced Angelique to the curious ebb and flow of life at sea. Whenever Marc called for a maneuver, everyone snapped into action, abandoning books, tablets, and earbuds, letting them clatter down the stairs to the main cabin before hurrying to their posts. At Marc’s commands, they shifted ropes, adjusted the sails, and double-checked their positions, moving in a practiced chaos that ended as quickly as it began.
In between these bursts of activity, though, there was an almost endless stretch of calm—a time for relaxing, sunbathing, and letting the warm Mediterranean breeze wash over them. Angelique made herself comfortable on the foredeck, sprawled out under the sun, knowing Olivier had a front-row view. She shifted, letting her dress catch the light and give him a hint of the bare skin along her back and shoulders. From behind his book, Olivier tried his best to keep a neutral expression, though she noticed how he shifted, repositioning the book a little higher.
Just as she opened her mouth to ask him to handle the sunscreen on her back, Marc’s voice rang out, cutting through the lazy quiet of the afternoon.
“Maneuver up! Large tanker coming up behind us, so lets give her a wide berth.” He gestured to a massive commercial ship in the distance, moving fast and growing larger by the second.
Angelique sighed, rolling to her feet, but there was an undeniable thrill in the sudden switch to action. Marc guided them to shift course, everyone taking their places, Elise moving quickly to secure a line while Olivier tightened a sheet. They held position, watching the tanker surge past with a low rumble, a stark reminder of how small they were on the open water.
Once the tanker was safely past, Marc gave the all-clear, and Angelique made her way back to the foredeck, a teasing smile on her face as she looked over her shoulder at Olivier.
“Now, where were we?” she said, tossing him the bottle of sunscreen.
He hesitated for a moment, then pushed himself up and joined her, letting his hands gently spread the lotion along her shoulders, careful and deliberate as he worked his way down. She glanced back at him, arching an eyebrow, a slight smirk on her lips.
As Olivier’s hands slid over her back, Angelique tilted her body just enough to brush against him, a slight, intentional wiggle that sent a clear message. His hands tensed, his fingers pressing a little harder into her skin, but he kept his composure, moving slowly, methodically—almost torturously so. She let out a faint sigh, expecting him to finally lean in and close the distance, but he remained infuriatingly controlled. Just as she started to wonder what was holding him back, he let out a low, possessive growl and firmly grasped her waist, pulling her close. His voice, rough and teasing, made her pulse quicken.
“Careful what you wake here,” he muttered, his hand slipping lower. “You may have to feed it when it awakes.”
The thrill of his words sent a shiver through her, but just then, Elise’s voice rang out from below decks. “Dinner’s ready!”
Chapter 3: A spicy Dinner# Olivier’s eyes darkened, lingering on hers for a moment longer before he released her with a reluctant grin. She smoothed her dress, and they made their way below, catching Marc’s approving nod as they sat around the compact table. Marc and Elise had whipped up a simple yet delicious meal, fragrant with fresh herbs and seasoned to perfection. Conversation flowed easily as they swapped stories, punctuated by Marc’s occasional checks on the radar to ensure they stayed on course. Elise talked about her travels, and Marc shared tales of his own experiences at sea, each story lending the evening a warm, familiar feel.
As they finished, Marc reminded Olivier and Angelique of their shift in the early hours. “We’ll hold the fort until one,” he said, shooting a quick look at Olivier. “Get some rest. You’ll need it.”
After helping clear the table, Olivier followed Angelique down the narrow corridor. As they stopped before their respective cabin doors, the air between them was thick with the tension left unresolved from earlier. Without a word, Olivier closed the gap, pressing her back against the cabin door and capturing her mouth in a heated kiss. She reached for him, fingers sliding under his polo, but before she could lift it over his head, he grabbed her waist with a firm, steady grip and lifted her effortlessly, laying her down on the bed. She felt the solid strength beneath his lean frame as he held her down, a quiet promise that he wouldn’t be gentle tonight. Though Olivier was no towering figure, there was something in the way he held her that made her feel utterly at his mercy.
He took his time, his hands and mouth exploring her with patience that both taunted and thrilled her. Whenever she tried to pull him closer, to take some measure of control, he thwarted her with a gentle but unyielding pressure, his lips and fingers finding sensitive spots that left her breathless. The more she tried to regain control, the more he seemed to revel in keeping her pinned beneath his touch, guiding her to surrender completely.
Her breaths came faster, each one mingling with soft gasps as he worked his way across her skin, touching and teasing her in ways that left her powerless. She’d thought she was the one tempting him, yet here she was, helpless under his gaze and his touch, feeling herself unraveling as he took her further than she’d anticipated.
Olivier held Angelique’s gaze, his smirk dangerously playful as he leaned closer. His voice dropped to a low growl, the question lingering between them. “Would you offer your throat to the wolf with the red roses?”
She felt a shiver roll down her spine, meeting his intense eyes and understanding the promise they held. If she nodded, he’d make her his, right here, right now, and there would be no holding back. Her voice was barely a whisper, but steady as she asked, “Do you have a condom?”
He nodded, pulling one from his pocket with a grin, and she gave her answer with a simple nod of her own. That was all it took—Olivier growled softly, and the tension that had simmered between them finally snapped as he moved to claim her.
Meanwhile, above deck, Elise sat comfortably nestled in Marc’s arm in the warm evening air. She’d brought along a novel, one that she knew would make Marc’s interest peak— The Siren, a particularly spicy romance. Her voice was low and soft as she read aloud with the quiet rhythm of the waves against the hull.
Marc’s fingers traced small circles along her hip, occasionally drifting up to playfully tease her through the thin material of her swimsuit, his fingertips grazing her sensitive skin. Every now and then, Elise’s voice would falter, breath catching as Marc’s touch grew bolder. She pressed closer into his side, a flush creeping over her cheeks as he continued to explore her in a slow, leisurely rhythm that was both tender and maddening.
“You’re not making this easy,” she whispered, her voice barely audible as his fingers lingered over her, but Marc only chuckled, his grip firm as he held her close.
“Patience,” he murmured, his voice a steady, teasing rumble in her ear. He knew they’d have to wait until the watch change, but for now, he was content to keep her on edge, drawing soft gasps and quiet moans that no one but him could hear. Elise knew that she wouldn’t find release until Angelique and Olivier took over at 1 a.m., but that only seemed to add to the thrill, each touch from Marc heightening the tension that lay beneath the peaceful night.
As the distant lights of passing ships glided by, their engines a low hum in the night, Elise did her best to focus on reading The Siren aloud to Marc. She’d been determined to keep going despite the distraction of his hands tracing heated paths across her skin, his touch intensifying as the story’s spice level climbed.
