The skirt was slim, tapering just enough to demand mincing steps; each stride was short and composed. Her posture collar, rigid and high, cradled her jaw and lifted her chin, allowing no downward glance. A wide-brimmed hat veiled her face in fine black netting, its edge falling far over her shoulders.
The Royal Ascot grounds were a vivid spectacle of Victorian England at its most theatrical.
The wealthy and titled moved through the enclosures like costumed players, their laughter bright beneath the white marquees. The gentlemen wore morning coats in black or dove gray, the better sort pairing them with silk top hats and ivory-handled walking sticks. Some wore carnations in their buttonholes and smoked Turkish cigarettes in slender ivory holders. Their conversation flowed easily–from bloodlines of horses to politics at Westminster–spoken in clipped tones over silver flasks of brandy or champagne served in cut crystal.
The women, their dresses ablaze with color and ruffles, swirled in an ocean of silk, lace, and tulle. Parasols bloomed like flowers against the afternoon sun. They clustered near the grandstand and paddock rails, whispering names of favored jockeys and laughing softly behind gloved fingers. Feathered hats rose like architectural marvels above their heads, some teetering with absurd hauteur.
Outside the Royal Enclosure, however, the social palette darkened. Here, tradesmen, clerks, and milliners rubbed shoulders with betting touts, hawkers, and pickpockets. Ragged boys with ink-smudged faces shouted the latest odds, while stout women sold penny broadsheets listing race entries from baskets slung over their arms. Vendors offered meat pies, roasted chestnuts, and gin cups with cracked ice. The lower classes congregated around the rails, craning to catch a glimpse of the thoroughbreds or cheering with almost superstitious devotion as the horses thundered past.
In one corner, a knot of cockney bookmakers barked out odds, their flat caps bobbing as they shouted over one another. Beside them, a nervous young man in a cheap morning coat fumbled a few coins onto a race stub and hurried away, eyes wide.
Children darted between skirts and boots, some with baskets of violets for sale, others pilfering coins when they thought no one was looking. The scent of horses, cigar smoke, and hot pastry clung to the air.
Seraphina moved among them like a ghost–veiled, composed, and utterly apart. She kept to the periphery of the grandstand, her veiled gaze sweeping across the crowd. It did not take long to spot Kemal Bey.
He was dressed with the studied elegance of a man striving to project affluence–his chocolate-brown cutaway coat just a little too worn at the seams, the camel-coloured waistcoat brushed clean but fraying at the edge, and a dove-gray cravat, crumbled and straightened. A modest rosebud adorned his buttonhole, and a silver watch chain swung from his waistcoat with the casual flair of someone hoping it might distract from the threadbare quality of their outfit.
He leaned against the rail, a folded racing form in one hand, his eyes fixed intently on the betting boards. The concentration etched across his face was too grave, too purposeful, for a gentleman meant merely to be enjoying an afternoon’s leisure.
From her vantage, Seraphina observed as he entered into a terse exchange with one of the bookmakers. The bookmaker was a bald man with a reddish complexion and no eyebrows, a man known as The Egg to Mr. Pike, and mentioned helpfully in his reports as one of Mr. Bey’s creditors. He stood behind a makeshift chalkboard and spoke in brusque, impatient tones.
Kemal reached into his coat pocket, produced a handful of banknotes, and hesitated. The sum was evidently insufficient. After a glance around to ensure no one of consequence was watching, he withdrew a card and scribbled something on it–an IOU, by the look of it–then signed it with a flourish. The bookmaker accepted the note with evident relish, his grin thin and wolfish, before handing over the betting slip.
Kemal took it as though it were a banknote, folding it into his hand with visible care. He turned, his eyes scanning the racetrack with the desperation of a man who had staked more than he could afford. Seraphina, her veil concealing the intensity of her interest, moved with the crowd, keeping a measured distance behind him.
She glanced at the bookie’s chalkboard. The odds had shifted. The outsider’s numbers had shortened considerably–evidence of a large wager placed at the last moment. She allowed herself a small, inward nod. A risky bet. Foolhardy, even. The kind of gamble one made when there were no safe options left.
The race was announced, and the crowd surged toward the railings. Kemal stood near the front, his body rigid with anticipation. Seraphina lingered a few paces behind, her posture serene, her gloved hands folded at her waist. She did not watch the track; she watched him.
As the thunder of hooves erupted and the racers tore past in a blur of motion, she could see the line of his shoulders grow taut. His breathing changed, shallow and quick. And when the favourite surged ahead in the final furlong and crossed the finish to raucous cheers, she saw him sag–his spine bowed, the betting slip crumpled in his fist.
The moment was perfect.
Seraphina stepped forward without haste. Her gloved hand reached out, light and deliberate, and came to rest upon his forearm. He turned, startled–his expression flushed with disappointment, eyes wide with confusion and fear.
She slipped the envelope into his hand. Her voice, low and precise beneath the veil, followed like a blade.
“Tomorrow,” she said softly, her tone firm, with the faintest edge of command. “By the Lamassu. Be there.”
Before he could respond, before he could even fully process her presence, she had stepped back into the crowd–swallowed by parasols, hats, and colour–leaving only the faintest trace of perfume and paper in her wake, leaving Kemal with nothing but the note and the promise of the next day’s meeting.
British Museum# The following day, Seraphina instructed Amara to dress her in precisely the same attire she had worn to Ascot. She wanted Kemal Bey to recognize her silhouette and the unique constraints of her form. Her thick veil remained in place, ensuring her identity would remain hidden.
Arriving at the British Museum ahead of their meeting, Seraphina took time to familiarize herself with the Assyrian collection. She found a niche that offered a clear view of the Lamassu statues, allowing her to observe Kemal’s arrival without being seen. The museum’s hushed atmosphere, with its echoing footsteps and distant murmurs, provided the perfect backdrop for their clandestine encounter.
A few minutes before noon, Kemal Bey entered the room. He glanced around, his demeanor cautious as he positioned himself near the imposing Lamassu bull. When Kemal turned, searching for a sign of his mysterious benefactor, he found her standing just behind him–poised, veiled, and utterly unreadable. She might have stepped out of the shadows themselves, her presence silent yet commanding, as if she belonged not among the living but among the ancient stone sentinels of Assyria that loomed around them.
“Mr Bey,” she said quietly, her voice calm but unmistakably firm through the fine mesh of her veil. “I trust you received my message.”
Kemal inclined his head, studying her with a guarded expression. “Indeed,” he said. “And you have my attention. Though I must confess, I am still unsure whether I should be intrigued or alarmed.”
Seraphina did not flinch. “I can offer you one thousand five hundred pounds,” she said without preamble, her tone precise, her posture impeccable. “It will be enough to settle your debts and remove you from The Egg’s reach. I propose an advance of ten percent–enough to keep your name off his list, and buy you time.”
Kemal’s eyes narrowed. The number was no small sum. Still, his hesitation was immediate, his thoughts clearly racing.
“And in return?” he asked slowly, already suspecting the answer.
“You will seduce Lady Thistledown,” Seraphina said, her voice even. “And you will ensure that you are discovered. The disgrace must be public. Her ruin must be absolute.”
Kemal drew a sharp breath and turned away for a moment, one gloved hand pressed to his lips as if to keep the words from spilling. He began pacing–a short, agitated loop in front of the Lamassu.
“That would end her, yes,” he said at last, almost to himself. “But it would end me as well. No respectable embassy would touch me after such a scandal. My position in London would become untenable. I’d be left with nothing but exile and debt.”
“You would be free,” Seraphina replied, her voice low, persuasive but unyielding. “Free of your creditors. Free of the whispers. You could leave this city behind. Begin again–in Istanbul, or wherever your name has not yet reached. With your dignity intact. With your future paid for.”
Kemal stopped pacing and turned back to her, the tension in his frame visible even beneath his well-cut coat. “Even so, it’s not enough,” he said slowly. “Not for that. You’re asking me to leap from a high window without knowing what’s below.”
“Two thousand,” Seraphina said crisply. “In full. When the Lady is compromised and the scandal is published.”
He let out a soft, humourless breath. “That barely covers what I owe,” he said. “And what then? I crawl back to Constantinople in disgrace, with no post, no patron, and no prospects?”
“You’ll be free of the worst of them,” Seraphina said calmly. “You’ll walk away from The Egg with your skin and your name. That is more than most men manage.” She paused. “Two thousand five hundred,” she said, the tone of finality in her voice.
Kemal shook his head, slowly. “It’s not enough. I’ll need more than just my debts paid. I’ll need to live. I’ll need to eat, and work, and dress like a man not entirely fallen.” He paused, looking at her from beneath his lashes. “Three thousand five hundred.”
Seraphina tilted her head slightly, considering him from behind the veil. Then, with no further expression, she turned slightly–enough to suggest she was preparing to leave.
Kemal’s voice cracked with urgency. “Three, then,” he said, the words leaving his mouth in a rush. “Three thousand. Not a penny less. And I’ll do it.”
She paused, still turned half away, then looked back at him through the gauze of her veil. For a long moment, neither of them moved.
Then Seraphina reached into her reticule and withdrew three tightly bound packets of banknotes, each precisely folded and tied. She held them out. “Ten percent,” she said. “Three hundred pounds. Enough to buy silence and a stay of execution from your creditors. The remainder when the scandal breaks. When the Lady falls.”
Kemal accepted the envelope, the notes suddenly weightier than gold. His jaw worked silently. He looked down at the packet, then slipped it into the inside pocket of his coat.
Without another word, Seraphina inclined her head once and turned, her footsteps soft as she disappeared between the shadows of the towering Assyrian statues.
Kemal stood alone in the gallery. The great stone Lamassu watched him in silence, their eyes fixed and unreadable, guardians of a long-dead empire. He reached into his pocket and felt the paper crinkle–the money, the promise, the price. He looked up at the carved kings and whispered, half to himself, half to them.
“So be it.”
Then he turned and walked away.
Later that day, Seraphina convened with Matthew Pike, engaging his services to keep a watchful eye on both Kemal Bey and The Egg, the ruthless, bald bookie Kemal Bey owed his life and soul to. Pike, ever resourceful, agreed to the task, a standard operation in his line of business.
A week passed before Pike reported back, his findings confirming Seraphina’s expectations. He had observed Kemal paying off The Egg, the transaction conducted with a subtle air of urgency. Additionally, he had witnessed a clandestine meeting between Kemal and Lady Thistledown at a café. They had appeared quite taken with one another, their laughter and Kemal’s charm evident even from a distance.
Another week later, Pike’s reports indicated further developments. The initial signs of an affair between Kemal and Lady Thistledown were becoming increasingly clear. Their meetings had grown more frequent, the nature of their interactions unmistakably intimate.
Seraphina, receiving these updates, felt a sense of satisfaction. Her plan was unfolding as intended, each piece falling into place with precision. The scandal that would ensnare Lady Thistledown was nearing its precipice, and Seraphina remained confident that her strategy would yield the desired outcome.
Pub in Lambeth# In preparation for her intricate scheme, Seraphina had engaged Matthew Pike to make contact with some less reputable individuals. So, in the dim light of a secluded backroom in a Lambeth pub, Seraphina waited, her form shrouded in the layers of her mourning attire. The thick veil obscured her features, granting her anonymity as she prepared to meet the men Matthew Pike had recommended. The door creaked open, and two figures slipped inside, their movements fluid and practiced.
“‘Ello, ma’am,” one of them greeted, his accent rough and unrefined. “Name’s Tom. This ’ere’s my mate, Billy.”
Tom was lean and wiry, his sharp eyes flicking around the room, assessing every shadow. Billy, in contrast, was stockier, his face a map of scars and weathered lines. Despite their appearances, there was a certain pride in their demeanor, a code of honor that set them apart from common cutthroats.
“Thank you for coming,” Seraphina began, her voice low and measured. “I have a task for you, one that requires discretion and care.”
Tom leaned in, curiosity piqued. “And what might that be, ma’am?”
Seraphina produced a small pouch, the clink of coins audible even through the fabric. “There is a drawer in Lord Thistledown’s study. Inside, you’ll find a folder with important documents. I need you to retrieve it for me, with the seals intact.”
Billy’s eyes narrowed, a grin tugging at the corner of his lips. “All sealed, eh? Ain’t touchin’ nothin’ inside, that what yer wantin’?”
“Precisely,” Seraphina confirmed. “I will pay you this amount now, and the same again upon successful completion. But only if no harm comes to anyone, and the seal remains unbroken.”
Tom exchanged a glance with Billy, then nodded. “We’re on it, ma’am. You can count on us.”
The two men shook hands with Seraphina, their calloused grips firm and assured. With a final nod, they slipped back into the night, their task set.
Days later, the same backroom saw their return. Seraphina waited, her veil as impenetrable as ever. Tom and Billy entered, their expressions a mix of triumph and relief.
“Got your folder, ma’am,” Tom announced, producing the sealed packet from beneath his coat. “All there, just like you wanted.”
Billy chuckled, his voice a low rumble. “Weren’t easy, but we done it. No one the wiser, no seals broken.”
Seraphina took the folder, inspecting it carefully. The seal was indeed intact, a reassuring sight. She handed them another pouch, just as heavy as the first one.
“Well done,” she said, her voice tinged with satisfaction. “You’ve exceeded my expectations.”
Tom tipped his cap, a grin spreading across his face. “A pleasure doin’ business with you, ma’am. Anytime you need somethin’ done on the quiet, you know where to find us.”
With that, they departed, leaving Seraphina to her thoughts. The documents were now in her possession, a crucial piece of her plan to implicate the Lord in his Lady’s affairs.
One morning soon after, an errand boy arrived breathlessly at the door of Seraphina’s room. “Message for you, ma’am,” he announced between gasps, extending a slightly crumpled envelope toward her.
Seraphina took the envelope from the waiting boy. “Thank you,” she acknowledged with a nod, slipping a coin into his palm. “Please wait for the reply.”
The letter inside was unsigned, yet the handwriting was unmistakably Kemal Bey’s. “The evening of Wednesday. The Albemarle Private Hotel.” It was a confirmation, the time and place where Kemal would meet with Lady Thistledown, their indiscretion poised to be laid bare. The Albemarle Private Hotel was a discreet establishment, nestled between a gentleman’s club and a publisher’s office, known for catering to those with reputations to protect.
Wasting no time, Seraphina penned a note for the waiting errand boy to deliver to Felix Dunsley, a reporter at the Illustrated London News. Her message was anonymous, but concise: “Be present at the Albemarle Private Hotel on Wednesday evening, at the Stafford Mews entrance. Await further instructions. A scandal of considerable interest awaits.” She handed the note to the boy, who accepted it with a nod, and watched as he darted off to complete his errand.
Additionally, Seraphina instructed Pike to contact someone at the Yard. The unfolding events would soon involve a diplomatic incident requiring discreet handling.
Early on Wednesday morning, Seraphina made her way to the Albemarle Private Hotel, her form cloaked in the deep black of mourning attire. Her veil was drawn tightly around her face, allowing her to move through the city’s bustling streets with the anonymity she required. She approached the side entrance of the hotel, where staff members were beginning to arrive for their shifts.
Amid the hustle and bustle, Seraphina spotted the maid she was looking for–a young parlour maid with a polished uniform and a pretty, if somewhat vacant, face. Her appearance was immaculate, her hair neatly pinned beneath her cap, but her eyes held a certain naiveté that belied her station.
“Excuse me,” Seraphina called softly, her voice barely rising above the din of the morning. The maid paused, glancing around before her gaze landed on the veiled figure.
“Yes, ma’am?” the maid replied, her accent thick and unrefined, a stark contrast to her polished appearance.
Seraphina stepped closer, ensuring they wouldn’t be overheard. “I have a task for you,” she began, her tone measured and firm. “I need these documents placed in Room No. 9, on the third floor. The seals must remain intact.”
The maid’s eyes widened, a flicker of understanding crossing her features. “In Mr. Bey’s room, ma’am?” she asked, her voice a mix of curiosity and caution.
“Precisely,” Seraphina confirmed, her words crisp and clear. She reached into her cloak and produced a small purse, the weight of it evident even through the fabric. “This is for your trouble. It is a generous sum–a week’s wages, perhaps more.”
The maid’s eyes darted to the purse, the coins inside glinting with the promise of a small fortune. Her resolve seemed to solidify, and she nodded quickly, her expression earnest.
“I’ll do it, ma’am,” she assured, her words carrying a hint of excitement. “And I won’t breathe a word to no one. You got my promise on that.”
Seraphina inclined her head, satisfied with the response. “See that you don’t. Your discretion is of utmost importance.”
The maid tucked the purse into her apron, the gesture discreet yet definitive. “I’ll keep me mouth shut, ma’am. You can count on it.”
With the arrangement made, Seraphina turned to leave. The maid watched her go, comprehension dawning on her face as she realized the gravity of her involvement. Though her intellect might have been limited, she understood well enough that keeping this secret was essential to her own well-being.
With all the pieces set upon the board, Seraphina awaited Wednesday evening with a sense of anticipation. Her plan was poised to unfold, each element arranged with meticulous precision. As the day approached, she remained confident, knowing that the scandal she intended to orchestrate would soon come to fruition.
Albemarle Hotel# Come Wednesday evening, Seraphina once more donned her full black mourning robes, the layers of fabric and lace lending her an air of solemnity as she made her way to the Albemarle Hotel. Her attire shielded her identity, allowing her to move through the dim streets unnoticed.
Upon her arrival, she observed the dim light flickering behind the heavily curtained windows of Room No. 9 on the third floor. A Hansom cab drew up to the Albemarle Street entrance, and from it emerged Lady Agatha Thistledown. She was cloaked in darkness, her face obscured by a veil and her hands gloved. A flash of colorful dress showed briefly as she stepped down from the cab before disappearing inside.
Seraphina circled around to Stafford Mews, keeping to the shadows. She watched for Felix Dunsley and quickly spotted him as he exchanged surprised greetings with Inspector Horace Rainsford from Scotland Yard’s Special Branch. Their encounter was unfolding exactly as planned.
She beckoned a stable boy lingering near the mews, pressing a coin and a prepared note into his hand, pointing out Felix Dunsley as the recipient. The boy scampered off to deliver the message, and Seraphina slipped back into the night, her work complete. She made her way back to her room, knowing the plan was set in motion.
Dunsley received the note, its contents succinct: “Room 9.” With Rainsford in tow, the pair moved purposefully into the hotel, the inspector’s authority clearing the way past the staff. Making their way to the third floor, they found themselves outside Room No. 9.
Inside, the room was dimly lit, the faint scent of foreign incense lingering in the air. A bottle of arak with two half-finished glasses sat on the sideboard, the evidence of the night’s indulgence. Kemal Bey, out of uniform, lounged on a chaise in shirtsleeves, while Lady Agatha Thistledown reclined beside him, wearing nothing but a luxurious Turkish silk robe, clearly borrowed. Her discarded corset lay nearby, and a suggestive sketch of her in Turkish dress completed the scene.
The sketch depicted Lady Thistledown reclining languidly on a plush divan, her silhouette draped in sheer, diaphanous fabric that clung to her curves with artful precision, leaving nothing to the imagination. Her hair, usually pinned in a tight bun, cascaded loosely over her shoulders, framing her flushed face with an air of wanton abandon. A delicate veil, paired with gold bangles and harem slippers, completed the exotic ensemble, suggesting a scene of intimate abandon.
While Dunsley took notes and made his sketches for his reportage, Rainsford moved through the room with quiet efficiency, his eyes scanning for anything out of place. His search led him to a folder tucked discreetly among the personal effects. Flipping through it, he recognized the seals of the Foreign Office–correspondence that should never have left the office, now in the hands of a foreign diplomat. The seals remained intact, yet the scandal had escalated from a social disgrace to a matter of diplomatic espionage, drawing Lord Thistledown into its web of intrigue and implication.
From the Illustrated London News: Lady Thistledown Discovered in a State of Impropriety–an Encounter of Notable Indiscretion with an Eastern Envoy.
Dunsley’s piece in the Illustrated London News skirted the line of propriety, avoiding outright pornography while heavily implying carnal impropriety.
The headline read: “An English Viscountess in Eastern Silk: Whispers from Albemarle.” Choice quotes hinted at impropriety: “Lady Agatha Thistledown, clad in foreign silks, found in a compromising tableau with the illustrious Kemal Bey, raising questions of national loyalty and cultural subversion.”
Quietly, Rainsford reported Lady Agatha’s name in connection with the leak of minor yet genuine Foreign Office correspondence. The revelation triggered a silent investigation, casting a shadow over Lord Thistledown’s household and humiliating him in the process. The whiff of compromised state secrets added a layer of disgrace, compounding the personal scandal.
Seraphina, meanwhile, paid off Kemal Bey, ensuring his silence as he faced recall to Constantinople under a cloud of suspicion. The affair had tainted his reputation, leaving him with little choice but to leave London behind.
The fallout was swift. Lady Agatha became a social pariah, shunned by the society she had once graced. Her disgraceful conduct and the ensuing scandal tarnished her name, leaving her isolated and ostracized. Lord Thistledown, humiliated by his wife’s indiscretions and the implications of compromised secrets, found his standing diminished, his once-respected household now a source of whispered gossip and shame. Invitations ceased. A seat on the Reform Club board quietly disappeared. Even his name was no longer mentioned in the corridors of Whitehall.
For Seraphina, the plan had unfurled beautifully, her vengeance exacted with precision. She had dismantled the life of the woman who had once sought to control her, leaving behind a legacy of scandal and ruin in her wake. Two down, one to go.
London# As Seraphina mulled over her next move against Mrs. Blackthorn, she realized that a direct approach was out of the question. Traveling to the remote Loch Thorne would draw too much attention and risk compromising her carefully crafted anonymity. In such an isolated place, any stranger would stand out. Instead, she needed the bustling populace of a large city like London to act as her cover, allowing her to operate unnoticed amid the throngs of people.
The reformatory’s graduation ball, held annually in late July, presented the perfect opportunity. It was the event where Mrs. Blackthorn showcased her “products” to single men of good fortune and particular tastes—those desiring tightly laced and obedient wives. For Seraphina, this was the only time Mrs. Blackthorn ventured into the big city. The ball would provide not only a chance to confront Mrs. Blackthorn but also the ideal stage to escalate the scandal to a magnitude that could not be ignored or concealed.
These were not suitors in search of love. They were collectors, fetishists, seeking girls shaped into submission, trained to flinch prettily and never raise their voices. Each one expected a dress-doll wife—corseted, polished, silent. The end of school was not freedom for these girls; it was merely a transfer of control. Seraphina had edperienced their type before firsthand: men who loved the wardrobe more than the woman inside it. And Mrs. Blackthorn was only too happy to supply them.
With time running short, Seraphina knew she had to act quickly. She enlisted Pike once more, instructing him to gather dossiers on the various girls finishing at Mrs. Blackthorn’s school this year. Armed with this information, she would pinpoint the perfect target to execute her plan, ensuring the scandal would be so damaging that Mrs. Blackthorn’s reputation would be permanently tarnished.
Pike found Seraphina in her study, the afternoon light filtering through the lace curtains in delicate patterns, when he delivered his findings. He shuffled through a sheaf of dossiers, each file representing one of Mrs. Blackthorn’s recent charges. His expression was one of practiced neutrality, though his eyes flicked up occasionally to gauge her reaction.
“I’ve compiled the information you requested, ma’am,” Pike began, laying the first dossier on the table. “There are three girls this year who stand out. Troubled, they are, in different ways.”
Seraphina nodded, her interest piqued. “Tell me about them.”
Pike opened the first folder, revealing a photograph of a young woman with sharp features and defiant eyes. “This here is Emily Stokes. Bit of a firebrand, she is. Daughter of a wealthy merchant. Sent to Mrs. Blackthorn’s after she was caught leading a protest at her boarding school. Something about unfair treatment of the staff.”
Seraphina arched an eyebrow. “A protest, you say? She sounds… passionate.”
“Indeed,” Pike replied. “But her family found it unbecoming, especially for a girl of her standing. She’s got spirit, that’s for sure.”
He placed the next dossier in front of Seraphina. The photo showed a girl with soft curls and a nervous smile. “This one’s Mary Fletcher. Came from a good family, but she’s a bit of an odd duck. She’s fascinated with seances and spiritualism. They say she claims to speak with the spirits of the dead.”
Seraphina tilted her head, intrigued. “An unusual hobby for a young lady.”
“Aye,” Pike agreed. “Her family didn’t take kindly to it. Sent her to the reformatory to set her straight, so to speak.”
Finally, Pike laid the last dossier on the table. “And then there’s Charlotte Hargreaves.” He tapped the photograph of a girl with haunted eyes, her expression a mixture of vulnerability and defiance. “Youngest daughter of Rear Admiral Hargreaves. Her story’s a bit more… colorful.”
Seraphina leaned forward, her gaze intent. “Go on.”
“Officially, they say it was ‘disruption’ and ‘moral laxity,’ but the truth’s a bit spicier,” Pike explained. “She was caught in a rather compromising embrace with a parlor maid. And there are whispers of laudanum abuse and self-starvation.”
Seraphina considered the information, her mind already calculating the possibilities. “She sounds perfect,” she murmured. “A girl with a story like hers could be quite… useful.”
Pike nodded, understanding her intent—then hesitated. His fingers brushed the edge of the dossier, his voice quieter when he added, “Just be careful with her, ma’am. That one’s already been bent near breaking. You twist her any further, you might not get the shape you’re aiming for.” He held her gaze a moment longer than usual—measuring something he wasn’t sure he wanted to see.
Seraphina smiled, the pieces of her plan clicking into place. “Thank you, Mr. Pike. I believe she will be exactly what I need.”
Pike hesitated again, then cleared his throat. “If I may say so, ma’am… some girls, when you set ’em free of their cage, don’t always walk the path you give ’em. Sometimes they run wild—or straight back into the fire.” He gave a short nod toward Charlotte’s photo. “Just saying. That one’s got a storm behind her eyes.”
Seraphina needed a way to contact Charlotte and propose an opportunity for revenge against Mrs. Blackthorn—a notion Seraphina imagined Charlotte would readily entertain. From her own experiences, Seraphina had a keen understanding of what Charlotte’s life at the reformatory would have entailed: Mrs. Blackthorn’s unique brand of “restraint therapy,” likely a stint in the isolation cell to start, and of course the cane, followed by a strict regimen designed to break her spirit. Seraphina’s plan hinged on the hope that Charlotte retained a spark of defiance, a will to strike back at her oppressor.
Langham Hotel# The morning after Pike messaged her, via a messenger boy, that Mrs. Blackthorn and her girls had returned to town and were staying at the Langham Hotel, Seraphina set her plan into motion. She instructed Amara to dress her as a parlor maid in the Langham uniform—though her conditioning demanded that she be more tightly laced and higher heeled than was typical for such a position. Crucially, Amara applied a thick layer of concealing makeup to disguise her features and prevent Mrs. Blackthorn from recognizing her.
Caped and transformed, Seraphina made her way to the hotel, slipping in through the servant’s entrance alongside the morning delivery of food, bread, and milk. Once inside, she moved as swiftly as her restrictive attire allowed, navigating the labyrinth of servant’s corridors until she reached the wing where the reformatory girls were housed.
Adopting the guise of “Rose,” she approached the staff with a fabricated tale. “I’m a replacement for Becky, who’s under the weather,” she explained, her voice carrying an air of urgency. “Please, don’t rat me out to the Head Housemaid—or Becky’ll be in trouble.”
The other staff, sympathetic to her plight, nodded in understanding, and helped by distracting the Head Housemaid. This allowed Seraphina to slip into the service unnoticed, her eyes scanning for the face of Charlotte Hargreaves.
In the early light of dawn “Rose” quietly entered the room where Charlotte Hargreaves lay. The faint light revealed her form bound by the elaborate night gear mandated by Mrs. Blackthorn’s regime.
“Morning, Miss Hargreaves,” Rose announced softly, her voice carrying a note of feigned cheer.
Charlotte stirred, her expression a mix of grogginess and irritation. “Who’s there?”
“Rose, ma’am,” Seraphina replied, her hands already working to undo the mittens that encased Charlotte’s hands. “Just here to help you get ready.”
With careful precision, Rose removed the sack-like nightgown, its narrow cut restricting Charlotte’s legs. Next came the night corset, extending from Charlotte’s knees to her bust line. The release from its confines brought a fleeting moment of freedom, allowing Charlotte to stretch her limbs and breathe more deeply. Rose undid the mittens and the heel-less night boots that forced Charlotte’s feet into an en-pointe position.
Charlotte sat up, rubbing her wrists where the mittens had chafed. “Thank you,” she murmured, a trace of surprise in her voice at the unexpected kindness.

The names, the details, the illustrations—each more damning than the last—left no room for denial.
Mrs. Blackthorn did not face trial. Her friends abandoned her. Her staff disappeared. What remained of her wealth was quietly redirected to ensure a scandal of this scale did not touch more prominent names. And so, within days, she was removed from public view entirely. Doctors, summoned by her remaining family, pronounced her unfit—morally compromised and dangerously excitable. She was committed to the Bethlem Royal Hospital, known by another name on the street: Bedlam.
There, she was subjected to the very therapies she once recommended for others. Hydrotherapy. Restraint. Dietary controls. Weeks passed without real clothing. Months went by without conversation. Her hair was cut. Her corsets removed. She was bathed, examined, penned, and catalogued. No one came to visit. No one asked after her. She had once ruled over silence, obedience, and control. With her revenge complete, Seraphina found herself at a crossroads. She had achieved what she set out to do, yet the victory felt strangely hollow. The restrictive attire she wore remained a constant companion—her tightly laced corsets, towering heels, gloves, and veils were no longer tools of reform but habits embedded deep into her daily life. Much of her inheritance had been consumed in the pursuit of justice. Now, with her enemies disgraced and gone, she faced the far more mundane question of survival.
Meanwhile, the Loch Thorne Reformatory, left leaderless in the wake of scandal, stood in quiet disarray.
Loch Thorne# Seraphina sat by the window of her London hotel, watching the soft drizzle trail down the glass. The scandal had broken precisely as intended. Mrs. Blackthorn was finished—her name spoken only in hushed, scandalized tones. The reformatory, leaderless and disgraced, had gone into quiet chaos. Girls were being sent home or relocated, instructors dismissed, and the remaining staff unsure what came next.
It was the perfect opening.
Seraphina had not been named, implicated, or even mentioned in the aftermath. She was still seen as a respectable widow of impeccable bearing, a former alumna who had emerged from Mrs. Blackthorn’s care as a model of composure and restraint. But she was also nearly out of funds. Her revenge had cost her dearly—bribes, travel, layers of disguise, and the upkeep of her appearance. She needed not only shelter and security but a future.
And perhaps, more than that, she felt something stir beneath the satisfaction of revenge: the understanding that no one else would protect those girls. Not from people like Mrs. Blackthorn. Not from the men who funded the institution and demanded obedience in exchange for charity. If someone with insight, and memory, and control did not take the reins, then another woman like Blackthorn would rise in her place.
So she drafted a letter.
It was written on pale blue stationery, the handwriting elegant and steady. It was addressed jointly to Rear Admiral Hargreaves and Lord Everingham—both discreetly involved in the reformatory’s governance. She presented herself not as a petitioner but as a solution: an alumna with firsthand understanding of what made the institution effective, but also what had allowed its failures. She proposed a new model—one that retained discipline but offered dignity. Modern restraint, gentler methods, and outcomes that would appeal to both society and the press.
She emphasized her neutrality in the scandal, her respectability, and her knowledge of the girls’ needs—emotional, behavioral, and educational. She positioned herself not as a reformer, but as someone who could protect the reformatory from further scrutiny by quietly restoring its purpose under new, careful leadership.
Both men replied within the week. A luncheon was arranged. At the table, she spoke with warmth, precision, and a hint of humility. She acknowledged the difficulties ahead, but assured them she had the discretion and steadiness to lead. Lord Everingham, ever pragmatic, admired her composure. Rear Admiral Hargreaves, perhaps remembering his daughter’s troubled path, respected her poise.
Within a fortnight, a formal announcement was made—quietly, without press or notice.
Mrs. Seraphina Arabella Hartwell was appointed Headmistress of the Loch Thorne School for the Refinement of Wayward Ladies.
Soon after assuming her new role as Headmistress, Seraphina began to sense the difference between managing a vision and enforcing one. Most of the girls at Loch Thorne adapted quickly to the restructured routines—softer in tone than Mrs. Blackthorn’s, but no less exacting in detail. Yet there were a few who resisted.
Foremost among them was Elisabeth Gainsley, the daughter of a solicitor and a known sympathizer of the suffrage movement. At seventeen, Elisabeth was clever, defiant, and disinclined to cooperate with even the gentlest corrections. She refused the high collars. She shortened her curtsies. She slipped books on political theory into her embroidery basket and refused to allow her waist to be cinched beyond twenty-four inches.
She was a liability.
Seraphina summoned her to the office after several classroom disruptions. The girl stood with her arms crossed and her chin high, a stance that had once belonged to Seraphina herself, in another life.
“Miss Gainsley,” Seraphina said calmly, “you are aware that the reformatory exists to cultivate comportment, not argument.”
“And yet you argue very well, Mrs. Hartwell,” Elisabeth replied, her voice crisp. “Why shouldn’t I?”
The remark struck more deeply than Seraphina cared to admit. She dismissed the girl, saying only, “Report here tomorrow morning. We will begin a new kind of lesson.”
That night, Seraphina sat at her desk long after the halls fell quiet. The candle burned low, its light flickering across the brass surface of the Himalayan prayer machine, tucked neatly behind the cabinet doors. She stared at it for a long time.
She had promised herself she would never use it on another. But now she faced the possibility of disorder in her ranks. Elisabeth wasn’t the only girl with ideas of rebellion. And if the institution faltered under her leadership, she would not be given a second chance.
Still, as her gloved hand reached out and touched the machine’s curved handle, she hesitated. She was no longer under duress. She was not a pawn.
She was choosing.
The next morning, Elisabeth was escorted to the office under the pretense of a posture evaluation. She sat stiffly in the chair across from Seraphina, who maintained a gentle tone, even as she dimmed the curtains and unlocked the cabinet.
“What is that?” Elisabeth asked, eyes narrowing.
“Nothing harmful,” Seraphina replied. “But very helpful. Just a few minutes of focus, to ease your thoughts.”
The machine hummed to life.
Its colored wheels began to spin, casting soft, rhythmic light across the walls and over Elisabeth’s face. The girl shifted, unsettled. Seraphina remained seated, voice low and even.
“Just breathe, Miss Gainsley. Sit tall. Let yourself listen.”
Within minutes, Elisabeth’s posture changed. Her jaw slackened. Her gaze fixed. And as the pulse of light deepened its rhythm, Seraphina spoke carefully, slowly, reinforcing the patterns already etched into her own mind—obedience to male guidance, a craving for restrictive dress, a hunger for precision and order.
After twenty minutes, the machine slowed and stopped. Elisabeth blinked rapidly, swaying slightly as she stood.
“You’ll return tomorrow morning,” Seraphina said, as if the matter were routine.
“Yes, ma’am,” Elisabeth replied, her voice quieter than before.
Within days, her waist measured twenty inches. She began to speak more softly in class. When her father visited, she flushed and followed his instructions without resistance.
Seraphina observed it all with mixed feelings. The reformatory was stabilizing. Her model was succeeding. But alone in her office, she sometimes stared at the prayer machine and asked herself what Mrs. Blackthorn would have done—and how far she had come from being the girl who once fought not to be bent.
Still, she told herself, it was only one girl. Just enough to preserve the school. To protect the others. To prove she could lead.
And besides, Elisabeth looked beautiful in a corset. Peaceful. Almost grateful. It was then that Morag burst in, her cheeks flushed. “Beggin’ yer pardon, ma’am,” she said breathlessly, “but there’s a right mess in literature class. Daisy and Helen’ve been caught wi’ one o’ them vulgar penny romances—illustrated, no less. Filthy thing, if ye ask me.” Seraphina set down her pen, her thoughts already shifting. Another test of balance between discipline and leniency. As Morag waited, wringing her hands in the doorway, Seraphina stood and smoothed her skirts, her expression unreadable. “Bring them to my office,” she said calmly. “We’ll settle this before luncheon.”
Loch Thorne, Autumn 1985# The wind off the water hit harder than she’d expected.
Claire Alden stood at the edge of the narrow dock, her canvas duffel slung over one shoulder, jacket zipped to the chin. The Loch stretched before her like a piece of cut slate, dull and silver, reflecting nothing. Across the water sat the island, dense with pine and mist, and on its rise—half-choked in bracken and shadow—stood the building. The reformatory.
She hadn’t even known she had Scottish roots until the lawyer called. Something about a great-aunt several times removed. A reclusive widow. A name scratched into a will no one remembered drafting. Now, after three plane rides, two train transfers, a hired car, and one very narrow road full of sheep and fog, she was here. At the edge of her inheritance.
She still wasn’t sure what she’d inherited, exactly. When the solicitor mentioned “a mansion,” Claire had imagined something modest, maybe ivy-covered stone and a few creaking rooms. Not an island. Not that hulking silhouette rising through the mist like a fortress abandoned mid-siege. She hadn’t even known she had Scottish ancestry—no stories, no tartan, nothing passed down. Just this. Some great-aunt with a widow’s name and no known heirs, and now Claire, staring at the edge of her own family’s ghost story. She figured she’d stay a day or two, take a look around, maybe get a sense of the place. Then what? Sell it, probably. Unless it couldn’t be sold. Unless it wasn’t worth anything at all.
“Right then,” the woman beside her said. “Let’s not dawdle.”
The ferry was barely more than a boat—dark green, metal-hulled, and dented in places that suggested age and experience, like its owner.
The ferryman—ferrywoman—was named Isla Duncan. A stout woman in a thick wool sweater, with hair tied in a kerchief and boots that looked war-tested. She didn’t smile, but she wasn’t unkind.
Claire climbed aboard and sat on the metal bench as Isla pushed off with a practiced kick and turned the outboard motor. The boat trembled, then groaned forward into the water.
“Bit late in the year for sightseeing,” Isla called over the wind, voice thick with a Highland burr. “You’re the American, then?”
“I am. Claire Alden.” She offered a hand, then laughed at herself—too far to shake.
Isla nodded. “Aye, they said you’d come. Lawyer phoned MacCallum’s shop for the number. Told him I knew the way well enough.”
The wind picked up, whipping strands of Claire’s hair into her eyes. “So—what do you know about the place?”
Isla’s eyes didn’t leave the dark shape of the island. “Locals call it the Hartwell House, but that’s not what it was, not really. It was a school. Or… a kind of school. For girls. They called it a reformatory back then. Victorian times. Girls sent there to learn their place, if you catch the meaning.”
Claire raised an eyebrow. “That sounds ominous.”
“Aye. Was,” Isla said. “The women ran it—strict types. Real lace-and-discipline sort. They say the headmistress came from the colonies, India maybe, wore black every day and never once unlaced her corset. Mad as a hatter, but elegant, so they say. Mrs. Hartwell, she was called. No one saw her much in town, but the ferrymen used to bring crates for her—cases of gloves, veils, corsets, and dresses tailored too tightly for comfort. Things too fine for island living. Things meant for display, or for correction. She ran the place like a queen. Girls came off the island changed, if they came back at all.”
Claire felt a chill that had nothing to do with the weather.
“So what happened to it?”
Isla shifted in her seat, frowning. “Closed just before the war. Some say the government got interested. Some say there was a scandal. Most just say it got too strange. Last few girls weren’t right, they say. Always quiet. Posture too good. Wouldn’t speak unless spoken to.”
The island loomed larger now, its trees rising dark and still behind the broken stone wall that rimmed the landing cove.
“Weren’t any family left, not that we knew,” Isla continued. “But I suppose you’re it now. The Hartwell line, or some long thread of it.”
Claire managed a laugh, thin as the wind. “Not a name I’ve ever heard in my family.”
“No surprise. Families bury the strange ones. Easier to forget.”

The steps leading to the path had recently been scraped clean of moss. Beyond the landing, the gravel path curved up into the trees toward the house, which loomed in partial view beyond the rise.
Claire climbed out, her boots thudding against the damp planks. The trees whispered faintly now, wind curling through the pines. But there was no carriage. No figures waiting at the gate. Just the iron arch above the gravel path, its sign still faintly legible in the twilight.
Just the silence of abandonment.
Isla remained in the boat a moment longer, then reached under the bench for two crates. “Right—provisions,” she said, hauling them onto the dock. “Bit of bread, tea, tinned soup," she tapped one crate. “Greens, potatoes, and a bit of meat,” she tapped the other. “Not fancy, but enough for a few days.” She set the crates down near the steps. “Fuel was brought over three days back, and we tested the generators and boiler then. “Loch Thorne School for the Refinement of Wayward Ladies”
The lettering was worn but legible.

Isla nodded. “Aye. Might not look it now, but she was once a grand place. Strange. Beautiful. And full of rules.” She paused. “You planning to stay long?”

She turned to the uniforms again, running a hand down the boning of a corset.
“They really wore this every day?” she muttered.
There was a strange pull to it—fascination mixed with discomfort. Part of her wanted to know what it felt like. Not out of nostalgia, but curiosity. Just to understand what had been expected. She checked a few labels—yes, they’d have her size. It would be easy enough to try one on.
But she didn’t. Not yet. This wasn’t dress-up. These weren’t costumes. Whatever this place had been, it took itself seriously. And it had taken its girls even more seriously.
Claire closed the cupboard gently and stepped back into the corridor, the overhead lights flickering as if deciding whether to stay on.
Then she found it.
At the end of the west wing, behind a pair of heavy doors that stuck in their frame, lay a room unlike the others. Tall-ceilinged. Almost bare. The air was warmer, filled with golden late afternoon light that poured through an enormous arched window. And in the center of the room, on a large carved table, stood a box catching the sun.
She turned to the table itself—a broad slab of carved wood, its surface cleared for the box, but with several drawers beneath.
One stuck slightly, then gave. Inside lay a thick ledger, leather-bound, its edges gilded and worn with use. The cover bore no title—just a single embossed monogram: S.H.
Claire lifted it out, blowing dust from the top.
Inside: names. Lines and lines of entries in tidy script, columns dated between 1901 and 1935.
Pupil Name. Parent or Guardian. Cause for Admission. Tier of Treatment. Annual Fee. Outcome.
She skimmed:
“Beatrice Weatherby – Col. Weatherby (ret.) – Improper correspondence with stablehand – Advanced Therapy – £700 – Married, 1912 (Brig. Saunders, 1st Lancers)”
“Diana Fortescue – Lady Fortescue – “Strong-mindedness,” refusal to wear proper dress – Advanced Therapy – £700 – Married, 1914 (A. Calthorpe, solicitor)”
“Eleanor Macintyre – Mrs. J. Macintyre – Disobedience, chronic lateness, academic pride – Standard Instruction – £100 – Emigrated to Canada, 1925”
Claire turned quickly through the pages. There were dozens more. Maybe hundreds.
The handwriting changed after 1919, but the pattern didn’t. Always the same: cause, fee, outcome. “Advanced Therapy” appeared in bold, with extra ticks and occasional notes in the margin.
“Mild resistance in months 2–5. Breakthrough after corset regimen intensified. Full compliance observed by 8th month. Advanced therapy recommended bimonthly thereafter.”
Claire’s pulse quickened. “Advanced therapy? What the hell was that?” Claire stared at the pages, the tidy handwriting suddenly grotesque. These weren’t just school records. They were product sheets. Girls sent in, behavior cited, price paid, and outcome—always marriage, always to someone who wanted a wife shaped just so. It read like livestock entries. As if “strong-mindedness” were an illness. As if “full compliance” were a goal. Her stomach turned.
This wasn’t a school. It was a factory. And “Advanced Therapy” wasn’t education—it was correction. Reform, maybe. Or erasure.
She looked around the room again, newly unsettled by the silence, by the neatness. Whoever ran this place had done so with purpose. And someone—several someones—had paid for it. Encouraged it. Expected it. Handed over their daughters who did not conform to the standards their families demanded, reshaped into model women fit for marriage, society, or silence.
Claire exhaled slowly, the air thick in her lungs. She closed the ledger gently, as if shutting the book might muffle what she’d just learned. It didn’t.
A second book in that drawer was obviously a diary. She flipped forward, past faded ink, until she came to a marked entry near the middle.
August 17th, 1899
Today marks the final settlement of accounts with the Hargreaves estate. With the Rear Admiral’s passing and no male heir to contest, I have at last secured full ownership of the institution. Lord Everingham proved gracious, as ever—his patronage remains vital, but he sees the wisdom in unified leadership. A school cannot thrive by committee. Continuity has been preserved. I have written to the solicitor confirming the dissolution of the founding consortium. I hold the deeds myself now. The reformatory’s future is mine to shape, without compromise, without interference.
May it remain a place of discipline and order in an era increasingly given over to indulgence. I shall carry forward its mission—refined, yes, but unswerving.
Claire frowned. She flipped to the front, toward the earliest entries, and read.
January 2nd, 1885 It is not without some heaviness of heart that I accept the burden placed upon me today. The reformatory was never my ambition, nor do I imagine myself a natural schoolmistress. But with my husband’s affairs concluded, and my situation pressing as it is, I cannot afford discretion. And yet I do not despair.
With Mrs. Blackthorn’s… departure—at last—and with her, I pray, the cruelty she so thinly veiled as correction. I will run the school differently. Not softly, but justly. The girls must be guided, not broken. Restrained, but not humiliated. There is dignity in discipline if meted with compassion.
This place can change them for the better, I am sure of it. It need only change its heart first.
Claire closed the book.
It didn’t add up. That first voice—tentative, almost tender—was a world away from the cold precision of the ledger. Somewhere between that winter and the turn of the century, Mrs. Hartwell had changed. Or the school had. Or both.
And whatever “Advanced Therapy” was, it hadn’t been born of compassion. Claire needed to understand what had truly happened in this place.
Her gaze drifted back to the box.
It didn’t belong here. Not in a Victorian stone mansion tucked away in the Scottish highlands. The box was made of dark, polished wood—almost black, with a lacquered sheen—and carved all over in intricate, swirling patterns that shimmered faintly when the light hit them. Not floral. Not quite geometric. Almost… alive. The corners were inlaid with what looked like jade, cool and green, while the panels shimmered with embedded stones: turquoise, lapis, violet glass, flakes of gold. Delicate scrolls and cylinders were integrated into the design, like a music box crossed with something religious. The whole thing radiated presence. Not just exotic—ritualistic. As if it had come from somewhere older, deeper, and far from here.
Claire stepped forward, holding her breath, and laid both hands on the lid. It opened like a triptych. The outer panels folded back with a soft click, revealing a strange, layered interior: brass rods, interlocked gears, scrollwork spindles, and etched plates that caught the sunlight like fire.
She had no idea what it was.
But she was certain it had been used. Many times.
She turned one of the cylinders. It moved with a gentle resistance, then clicked into place.
A hum began. Low and deep. It settled into her chest like distant thunder rolling through stone. Behind the embedded gems, lights began to stir—faint at first, then brightening into a full cascade of motion and color. Sapphire, emerald, violet, gold—reflections spun across the walls and floor like living prisms gone wild.
Claire watched.
She meant to look away. She even tried, just for a second. To laugh. To mutter “What the hell is this thing?” But she didn’t. The lights pulsed in slow rhythm, each wave of color drawing her deeper inward. The hum settled into her bones. Her breath slowed.
Her shoulders lowered.
The buzz of thought began to fade, smoothed into stillness. Behind her eyes, the tightness unwound.
She sat down without thinking—on the edge of a trunk, or maybe a stool—her gaze still locked on the machine. It moved in delicate motion now, cylinders turning, light shifting in time. She couldn’t look away. Didn’t want to.
Time stuttered, then vanished.
The light seemed to fill the space where thought had been. Her limbs were heavy. Her mind, warm. The outside world dulled into quiet.
She blinked once.
The machine continued. The lights shimmered. The hum vibrated low and sweet.
She didn’t move.
And then—softly, like a thought not quite hers—came a voice beneath the hum, a whisper inside the stillness:
You don’t have to think right now. Just listen.

Introduction# Sonia: Meet LASS-VASH-2024# Subject: Meet LASS-VASH-2024
Anna,
I am back in Shenzhen airport, half dead, under-caffeinated, and carrying a sample that makes no sense.
The local reports call it the Large Self-Stabilizing Viral Airborne Shenzhen Strain. I shortened that to LASS-VASH-2024 because I refuse to type the full thing every time. The symptoms sound almost insulting for something this elaborate: three to five days of fever, vomiting, headaches, and unusually vivid dreams. Nasty, yes. Catastrophic, no.
But the genome is absurd.
I am not talking about “unusually large.” I am talking about something engineered by a team that wanted to show off. It is far too stable for its size. Whole sections look less like viral code and more like stored data with built-in correction. It should fall apart. It does not.
I keep circling back to the same thought: nobody builds something this complicated to cause a bad cold and a few ugly nights.
I’m bringing a chilled sample under permit. If you still want it, I can bring it straight to the lab after I land. Coffee after that, if neither of us is infected with the thing.
Sonia
Anna: Re: Meet LASS-VASH-2024# Subject: Re: Meet LASS-VASH-2024
Sonia,
Of course I still want it.
You had me at “far too stable for its size.” If the sequencing confirms what you think it does, this is not just unusual. It is designed.
Bring the sample straight to GAIA when you get back. I’ll keep the sequencers ready. We won’t get a full readout right away, but if the structure is as strange as you say, we should at least get enough to know whether we’re looking at something artificial.
And yes, coffee after. Assuming you’re not delirious and I’m not buried under a mountain of data.
Travel safe.
Anna
Sonia: Maylee Shufoo# Subject: One more thing from Shenzhen
Anna,
There is something else here you’d enjoy hating.
A boutique chain called Maylee Shufoo keeps turning up in the shopping districts here. The name is written in Chinese on the windows, and the whole thing looks like a very expensive dare.
The style is impossible to miss. Pencil skirts so tight they change the way women walk. High collars that look half blouse, half restraint. Gloves with too many buttons. Corsets sold as if they were office basics. Some pieces look Victorian, some look like polished corporate wear, some look almost ceremonial. It has that fascinating thing you sometimes get here, where fashion crosses over into discipline and nobody acts as if that is strange.
The almost open, everyday bondage aspect is wild. Not nightclub fashion, not costume, not even subculture exactly. Just a shop on a normal street selling elegance, restraint, and inconvenience as if every woman obviously wants that.
It should look ridiculous. Instead it looks expensive, polished, and weirdly convincing.
I took a photo.
Maybe it means nothing. Maybe it is just Shenzhen being Shenzhen and me being too sleep-deprived to walk past a novelty shop without writing you a field report.
See you tomorrow if I survive customs and jet lag.
Sonia
Anna: Re: Maylee Shufoo# Subject: Re: One more thing from Shenzhen
Sonia,
That shop looks like someone crossed a boardroom, a bridal salon, and a fetish house, then hired a very serious art director.
So yes, I hate it already.
It also looks like Fifty Shades of Shenzhen opened a flagship store and got a tax break.
I would like to see you wear that blouse with the impossible collar purely in the interests of international cultural understanding.
Bring the photo. Bring the sample. Bring yourself in one piece. If this thing really is engineered, I want to know who made it and what they thought they were doing.
Anna

Dressing Sonia# The room held a faint chill, the sort of coolness that clung to early mornings in winter. Sonia lay still, her eyes open to the dim light filtering through the heavy curtains. Her night corset held her firmly in its unyielding embrace. Her silk nightgown ran over it, clinging to her skin where warmth had built beneath the layers, and her hands, trapped in thumbless locking mittens, rested uselessly at her sides.
Her bladder ached, a steady, insistent pressure that she had tried to ignore for over an hour. She wiggled her fingers inside the mittens, an exercise in futility – she knew they held her without a possibility of escape. The tightly-laced corset offered no leeway for her movements; it ran from her knees to over her bust, covering her completely, unbendable and pulling knees closely together. Her arms were lashed to her waist at the elbows, allowing her a few inches of movement.
At the first stirrings of Henry beside her, Sonia turned her head as much as her restraints would allow. His slow, deliberate breath became a slight groan as he shifted, and finally, his eyes opened. She whispered, her voice a mix of urgency and practiced patience. “Sir, please, I need your help.”
He sat up, running a hand through his tousled hair. Without hesitation, he swung his legs over the side of the bed and leaned toward her. The mittens were the first to go. He pulled the small key from the nightstand drawer, the faint clink of metal against metal heralding her first taste of freedom. As he unlocked each mitten, his fingers brushed the soft skin of her wrists, now slightly reddened from the night’s confinement.
“Up you come,” he said, offering his hands. Sonia allowed him to help her stand her up, a task that required his strength and her trust, since her corset extended down to her knees, locking her legs closely together. The corset resisted, but Henry’s steady grip made short work of the motion. She stood, with him balancing her, feeling the strain of the boning against her ribs and the relief of no longer being flat on her back.
He turned her gently, removed the elbow lashes, and moved on to finding the tiny buttons at the back of her nightgown. Each one surrendered to his touch with a satisfying pop. The gown fell forward, pooling at her legs and revealing the taut laces of the night corset beneath. He moved behind her, fingers tracing the web of laces before beginning the slow process of unbinding her.
With every inch of loosening, her skin responded, goosebumps rising along the path his fingers took. When the corset finally came away, her body seemed to sigh in relief. He traced the imprints left behind, ridges of pressure that ran where the boning had strained against her skin. His touch was warm and deliberate, a gentle acknowledgment of her endurance. Her breath hitched as his fingers lingered on a particularly deep mark along her side.
“You’re beautiful like this,” he murmured, gently kissing her shoulder.
She wanted to lean into the kiss, but didn’t linger. The urgency returned, and she excused herself hurriedly, padding barefoot to the adjoining bathroom, the cool tiles under her foot. Once inside, she handled her needs with swift efficiency, the relief almost euphoric as she answered her body’s demands. She washed herself at the basin, quickly, relishing the warmth of the water and toweling herself dry.
Returning to the bedroom, Sonia found Henry seated at her vanity. The wooden chair creaked faintly under his weight, and he pointed to her usual spot at his feet, in front of him She knelt, presenting her back.
He removed her nightcap with unhurried motions and let her hair fall free. It was waist-long and still slightly wavy from the day before, spilling down her back. He gathered it in his hands, brushing through it with steady strokes. The bristles tugged gently at her scalp, a sensation that sent shivers down her spine. The regular motions were soothing, the familiar ritual calming, allowing her to gather herself for the day.
When her hair shined and fell straight, he began to braid it, his fingers weaving the strands with practiced precision. He did a tight single braid and finished by rolling it into a neat coil, pinning it at the back of her head.
Henry rose from his seat, and helped Sonia stand, turning around to face him. The imprint of the boning lingered on her torso like a map of discipline, faint red lines marking her flesh.
She stepped towards her wardrobe, and took a slip. Its silk slid over her fingers as she picked it up, the fabric cool and whisper-soft. She pulled it over her head and it fall into place, the hem settling high, just past her mons. It was a mere prelude to the ensemble she would build, but the feeling of it against her skin sent a small shiver of anticipation through her.
She turned to the small drawer atop the vanity, retrieving a pair of short cotton gloves. The gloves blunted her nails safely to handle the delicate stockings without risk. She rolled each stocking carefully, guiding the sheer fabric up her legs. The smooth slide over her calves and thighs was a practiced motion, the stockings clung perfectly, their tops sitting just above mid-thigh, leaving a sliver of bare skin where the garters would soon connect.
Henry approached her, holding her corset out for her. The embroidery caught the morning light, floral patterns dancing across the fabric. This corset was new, unbroken, and it promised both challenge and reward.
She stepped into the embrace of its structure, positioning it around her torso. The boning pressed into her hips as she closed the busk with a series of clicks and practised wiggles. Once secured, she adjusted herself within the cups, her fingers working under the edge of the corset to sort and lift. The garment’s push-up design worked marvelously, forcing her breast upward, creating a dramatic silhouette she could feel as much as see.
She bent slightly, attaching the garters to the tops of her stockings, starting with the front and side clips. She stepped aside slightly as Henry moved behind her, his fingers brushing the backs of her thighs as he fastened the rear garters. The contact left her skin tingling in its wake.
Standing once more, she braced herself as Henry began the first round of lacing. The corset drew tight against her body, compressing her waist in increments. She exhaled deeply, preparing for each pull of the laces. The new corset resisted, its fabric stiff and unyielding, but Henry’s hands were steady. He worked methodically, tightening the garment with a precision she had come to depend on.
The pressure built slowly, a familiar embrace that transformed into something sharper as the laces drew her waist smaller. The boning dug into her ribs and hips, not unkindly, but with the insistence. She breathed carefully, shallow but controlled, each inhale reminding her of the limits this corset imposed.
Her dependency on corsetry was no secret, least of all to herself. Without the support, her body felt adrift, weak. This newest piece, however, demanded more of her, its narrower cut a challenge even for her seasoned frame. She reveled in it, though—the strain, the discipline, the way it forced her into perfection. It was a struggle she embraced.
Henry stepped back for a moment, his hands resting lightly on her waist, feeling the firmness of her silhouette. “Not yet fully tight, my dear,” he said.
“I know,” Sonia replied.
Sonia eased herself into the chair at her vanity, her corseted waist held upright without touching the backrest. The slight constriction was already familiar, her body beginning to meld with the unforgiving structure. She took off the short cotton gloves. Laying them aside, she opened her makeup case.
She started with a liquid foundation, dabbing it onto her skin with a sponge, then blending it into an even canvas. The cold cream smoothed over her cheeks and forehead. Next, she selected a small pot of rouge, dabbing just enough onto the apples of her cheeks to create a soft flush, blending it into a smooth gradient. Her lips followed, the lip brush tracing a perfect bow with a rich, glossy red, the pigment shimmering faintly under the light.
Her eyes demanded precision. She applied a thin line of black kohl along her upper lash line. A small angled brush smudged it slightly, creating a sultry effect. Mascara followed, the wand curling through her lashes, adding length and volume until they framed her gaze like dark fans. Finally, she brushed a faint shimmer of pearlescent powder onto her lids and just below her brows, catching the light with every subtle movement.
Satisfied, she cleaned her fingers with a moist paper towel. Her skin felt fresh, her makeup pristine, every detail deliberate. She turned in her rotating chair, her corset creaking slightly, and faced Henry.
He knelt before her, lifting one of her legs to rest her foot on his thigh. The leather of her very high-heeled kneeboots gleamed in the morning light. She slid her stockinged foot into the snug confines of the boot, the interior buttery soft yet unyielding as it molded to her foot and ankle. Henry laced them with care, starting at the toe and working his way upward. The tight laces pulled the leather snug around her calf, each pass of the lace cinching closer, the fit both restrictive and supportive. He tied them off with a double bow just below her knee before moving to the other boot, repeating the ritual with the same methodical precision. The heels forced her feet into a severe arch, the soles pressing forward, her balance already altered even as she remained seated.
By now, the corset had warmed to her body, the rigid boning flexing just slightly, signaling it was time for the second round of lacing. Sonia rose and Henry moved behind her. He began at the top, drawing the laces down to her waist, pulling the fabric tighter with each pass. The pressure increased, her ribs compressed, her breaths shallower. He paused, allowing her a moment to adjust before continuing from the bottom, drawing the laces upward to meet at her waist. The second pass was firmer, the corset gripping her torso like a second skin. Though the back still showed a gap, it was acceptable for the first wearing.
“You’ll have to last the whole day,” Henry reminded her gently. “Be sensible.”
Sonia nodded, her breath catching slightly as he adjusted the shoulder straps. He crossed them behind her back, pulling them over her shoulders to the front, and passing them back under the shoulders again, fastening them tightly to the lashes just above her waist. Positioned this way, the straps would have maximum leverage, but the lashes would sit invisibly at her back, her lines unmarred. The straps bit into her shoulders, pulling them downward and backward, locking her posture into an elegant, regal pose. She could no longer raise her shoulders, nor could she lean forward or twist her upper body. Every movement would now radiate poise and control.
Henry held out the hobbling underskirt, the Yoyah Sheengzoh, for her to step into. She grasped his shoulders for balance as she lowered herself into it, the fabric wrapping tightly around her hips and thighs. Once in place, he fastened it to hooks at the front of her corset, ensuring the skirt wouldn’t shift or slip. He worked his way around to the back, securing the dozens of tiny buttons that completed the garment. The skirt restricted her stride to minuscule steps, forcing her to adopt a delicate, gliding motion.
Next came her gloves, a pristine pair of white kid leather that reached just past her elbows. She slipped her hands into them, the snug fit requiring effort as Henry used a button hook to close the tiny buttons at the mousquetaire and the upper hem. The leather encased her fingers tightly, smoothing over her skin and leaving no room for error in her movements.
Her blouse followed, a Victorian piece with dramatic ruffles at the collar and cuffs. The high, boned collar pressed against her neck, a constant reminder to keep her head upright and forward. She felt its bite when she leaned slightly, a correction that made her adjust to the regal posture it demanded. The cuffs buttoned seamlessly to her gloves, preventing any slippage or gaps, ensuring a pristine presentation. Henry stood behind her, fastening the long line of buttons from her lower back to the nape of her neck.
Henry moved with calm efficiency as Sonia stood, perfectly still, awaiting the final layers of her ensemble. He retrieved the structured boning for her bustle, its rigid supports gleaming faintly. He positioned it at the back of her corset, the curved frame extending behind her like a cage designed to exaggerate her silhouette. He tied it around her waist, letting the structure fall down from there, and draped a petticoat over it to smooth out the lines from the boning.
Finally, it was time for the overskirt, its elaborate embroidery shimmering in the soft morning light. Henry draped it over the petticoat, its layers cascading like a waterfall of fabric. The heavy folds swished faintly as he adjusted them, smoothing the drape so that each pleat and line fell perfectly. He buttoned the skirt into place, attaching it to the bodice with a row of small, discreet buttons along her hips. The overskirt flared dramatically behind her.
To complete the look, he added the apron. The front panel fell neatly over her overskirt, its fabric slightly stiffer to maintain its crisp shape. The apron’s edges were lined with intricate lacework, a delicate contrast to the structured silhouette beneath. Henry gathered the ties behind her, pulling them taut. The action cinched her waist even further, emphasizing the narrow curve of her corseted middle. He tied a large decorative bow at the back, the loops perfectly symmetrical, and secured it with another pin.
Henry stepped back to admire his work, his gaze lingering on the way her figure was both framed and confined by the meticulous layering. “Nearly there,” he murmured, retrieving the bonnet.
Its wide brim formed a deep poke that framed Sonia’s face, shielding it from view and narrowing her vision. He placed it carefully over her head, guiding the rubberband on the inside to clasp securely around the knot of braided hair at the back of her neck. Sonia felt the slight tug as it locked into place, the weight of the bonnet settling firmly on her head.
Deep inside the poke, directly in front of her face, hung the fine mesh veil. Its delicate pattern obscured her features further, another layer of modesty. Henry reached under the band of the bonnet, securing the veil so it hung evenly, its edges tucked neatly out of sight.
The final step was the wide band of the bonnet itself. Henry brought it under her chin, crossing it there with deliberate care, securing the veil. The fabric grazed her skin, snug but not cutting. He wrapped it once around her high, boned collar, the band pulling the bonnet’s weight more securely against her head. At the nape of her neck, he tied it into a firm bow, again securing the knot with a decorative pin.
The bonnet’s restraint forced Sonia to hold her head perfectly upright, the poke keeping her vision narrowly focused. The veil added a muted softness to the world beyond, its presence a constant reminder of the modesty imposed upon her. The tightness of the band around her neck reinforced the upright posture demanded by her corset and collar.
Henry stepped back again, this time fully satisfied. “You’re ready,” he said, his voice carrying a note of approval. Sonia lifted her gloved hands to smooth the apron, her movements restricted yet deliberate. She felt the weight of every layer, every strap and bow and bone that confined her. Yet, beneath the pressure, there was an undeniable satisfaction—a pride in her presentation.
Sonia minced carefully across the room, her tiny, deliberate steps a symphony of restricted motion. The Yoyah Sheengzoh underskirt allowed no room for error, its tight embrace forcing her movements into a rhythm of gliding grace. Each step carried her toward the full-length mirror, where she stopped and stood tall, her corset and collar dictating every inch of her posture.
She turned her head slightly, as much as the bonnet and high collar would allow, and inspected her reflection. The layers of fabric and lace created a vision of disciplined elegance. The apron cinched her waist with ruthless precision, emphasizing the dramatic curves achieved by the corset. The veil inside her bonnet softened her features, adding an ethereal quality, while the poke framed her head in modesty and mystery. She could feel the bite of the collar against her neck, a reminder to keep her chin raised and her posture impeccable.
Satisfied, she pivoted gracefully, the heavy skirts and bustle swaying subtly with the motion. “Sir,” she said softly, her voice deferential, “may I have my cape? I mustn’t keep Anna waiting.”
Henry, standing nearby with his usual composed demeanor, nodded. “Of course, my dear.” He retrieved the ankle-length cape from the hook by the door. Its dark fabric shimmered faintly, the lining weighted at the hem to ensure it would always drape correctly. He unfolded it with care and stepped behind her, draping it across her shoulders. The weight settled around her, its embrace both protective and restricting.
“Arms, please,” he instructed. Sonia raised her gloved hands, her elbows bent, allowing him to guide them through the elasticated hand slips inside the cape. The slips snapped snugly around her wrists, locking her arms into place. She flexed her fingers slightly, the tight kid leather gloves stretching but allowing no real dexterity.
Henry moved to the front and began fastening the cape. The buttons ran from the weighted hem to the high collar at her neck, each one securing her further within the garment. As he reached the final button, just beneath her chin, he smoothed the fabric over her shoulders.
“There,” he said, stepping back to assess his work. The cape restricted her hands, pinning them in front of her at hip height with no room for separation beyond a narrow span. Yet it covered her entirely, leaving only the hem of her dress and the tips of her boots visible below.
Sonia glanced down at her bound hands, testing the limits of her motion. She couldn’t raise them higher or spread them further, but it didn’t matter. She was perfectly prepared to go out. “Thank you, Sir,” she murmured.
Henry moved to the door, opening it wide for her. Sonia minced toward him, the soft swish of her skirts and the faint click of her heels on the floor the only sounds in the room. As she passed through the doorway, the weighted cape swayed gently, reinforcing the elegance of her constrained movement.
The fresh air outside greeted her as she stepped into the world, her pace unhurried yet precise. Anna would be waiting, and Sonia would arrive in nothing less than perfect form, her every step a testament to the discipline and care invested in her appearance. Henry’s gaze followed her, watching her glide down the path with quiet satisfaction.

A secret CERN experiment rips open gateways to alternate Earths, where a captive scientist is forced to explore worlds that should never exist. At CERN, she uncovered traces of a facility that did not exist, a hidden collider where exotic matter tears reality apart. Lured into Point 4, a site buried beneath the French countryside, she became a prisoner of the Exotic Transdimensional Gateway, an experiment that opens doorways to alternate Earths. Some are nightmarish, some uncanny, and some more dangerous than anything imagined. Forced into these worlds as an unwilling explorer, Zoë discovers that the real threat may not be what lies on the other side, but the people who control the gateway.
